data.title: Note-Making and Summary Writing
notes: What Is Note-Making?

Note-making is the process of extracting key information from a passage and organising it into a structured format using headings, sub-headings, and bullet points. In the NEB Class 11 English examination, note-making is a tested skill (typically 5-8 marks) that assesses a student's ability to identify important information, organise it logically, and present it concisely. Note-making is different from note-taking: note-making is done after reading a passage, while note-taking is done during a lecture or speech.
Format of Notes

A well-structured set of notes includes: (1) Title — a concise heading that captures the main topic (e.g., 'THE IMPORTANCE OF READING NEWSPAPERS'). (2) Main points — the key ideas from the passage, numbered or lettered (A, B, C...). (3) Sub-points — supporting details under each main point, indented and numbered (1, 2, 3... or a, b, c...). (4) Abbreviations — standard abbreviations can be used to save space (e.g., 'govt' for government, 'edu' for education, 'adv' for advantage, 'disadv' for disadvantage). The notes should fit on one page and use a clear hierarchical structure.
Steps in Note-Making

To make effective notes: (1) Read the passage carefully — understand the main idea and structure before writing notes. (2) Identify the main topics — look for the central themes or arguments (usually 3-5 main points). (3) Create a title — write a concise heading that covers the entire passage. (4) Write main points — phrase each main idea in a short heading (not a full sentence). (5) Add sub-points — under each main point, add supporting details, examples, or evidence. (6) Use abbreviations — replace long words with standard abbreviations. (7) Review — check that the notes capture all key information and are logically organised. This process typically takes 10-15 minutes for a standard passage.
Summary Writing: Definition and Purpose

A summary is a concise restatement of a passage's main ideas in the writer's own words. It is shorter than the original (typically 1/3 to 1/4 the length) and includes only the essential information, omitting examples, details, and repetitions. In the NEB exam, summary writing typically carries 5-8 marks. A good summary: (1) preserves the main ideas in logical order, (2) is written in your own words (not copied from the passage), (3) is concise (usually 80-120 words for a 200-300 word passage), (4) uses third person and present tense (unless the passage is in past tense), (5) does not include personal opinions or new information.
Steps in Summary Writing

To write an effective summary: (1) Read the passage thoroughly to understand the main idea. (2) Identify the main points — what are the key arguments or facts? (3) Draft the summary — write the main points in your own words, following the passage's logical order. (4) Eliminate details — remove examples, statistics, quotations, and repetitions. (5) Check length — ensure the summary is approximately 1/3 to 1/4 of the original passage. (6) Review for accuracy — ensure the summary faithfully represents the passage without adding personal interpretation. A common mistake is to copy sentences directly from the passage — this is never acceptable in a summary.
Difference Between Note-Making and Summary Writing

While both note-making and summary writing involve condensing information, they differ in format and purpose: Note-making is presented in a structured, hierarchical format with headings, sub-headings, and bullet points. It is a visual organisation of information. Summary writing is presented as a continuous paragraph in prose form. It is a condensed restatement of the passage's content. Note-making tests organisational skill; summary writing tests comprehension and paraphrasing skill. Both are commonly tested in NEB exams, sometimes together from the same passage.
Common Mistakes in Note-Making

Avoid these errors: (1) Writing full sentences in notes — notes should use headings and phrases, not complete sentences. (2) Including too many details — notes should be concise; omit examples and minor points. (3) Poor organisation — main points should be logically ordered, with clear hierarchy between main and sub-points. (4) No title — every set of notes must have a title. (5) Copying from the passage — notes should paraphrase, not copy. (6) Using abbreviations that are unclear — only use standard, widely understood abbreviations (govt, edu, adv, dis, approx, etc.).
Common Mistakes in Summary Writing

Avoid these errors: (1) Copying sentences verbatim — a summary must be in your own words. (2) Including minor details — examples, statistics, and illustrations should be omitted. (3) Adding personal opinion — a summary is objective, not evaluative. (4) Being too long — a summary should be approximately 1/3 to 1/4 of the original. (5) Changing the meaning — ensure your summary accurately reflects the passage. (6) Using first person — summaries are written in third person. (7) Not using a title — a summary should have a concise title that captures its main idea.
confusion: Note-making vs. Note-taking: Note-making is done after reading a passage, organising information into a structured format with headings and sub-headings. Note-taking is done during a lecture or speech, capturing key points in real-time. Note-making is a structured academic skill; note-taking is a practical study skill.

Summary vs. Abstract: A summary condenses a passage's main ideas in the writer's own words (1/3 to 1/4 length). An abstract is a brief summary of a research paper or report, usually including the purpose, method, and findings. In NEB exams, 'summary' is the required term; 'abstract' is not used. Both are concise, but an abstract has a more rigid academic structure.

Notes vs. Outline: Notes are presented in a hierarchical format with headings, sub-headings, and bullet points (visual structure). An outline is a linear list of main points and sub-points, usually using Roman numerals and letters (I, A, 1, a). In NEB exams, 'notes' and 'outlines' are sometimes used interchangeably, but the expected format is the heading/sub-heading structure.

Paraphrasing vs. Summarising: Paraphrasing rewrites a specific passage or sentence in your own words (same length, same detail). Summarising condenses a longer passage to its main ideas (shorter length, fewer details). Paraphrasing preserves all the information; summarising selects only the most important information.

Main idea vs. Topic: The topic is the subject of the passage (one phrase: 'Environmental Pollution'). The main idea is what the author says about the topic (a complete sentence: 'Environmental pollution is the most pressing challenge facing developing nations today'). Notes should have a title (topic), while a summary should express the main idea in the opening sentence.

data.title: Introduction to Short Stories
notes: What is a Short Story?

A short story is a brief work of prose fiction that can normally be read in one sitting. It focuses on a single incident, character, or idea, and develops it with economy of language. Unlike a novel, a short story usually has a limited number of characters, one central conflict, and one main effect. Edgar Allan Poe famously argued that a short story should aim at a single effect — every word, every image, every detail should contribute to one unified impression.
Key Elements of a Short Story

Plot: the sequence of events in the story — exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Character: the people (or animals, or forces) in the story; they can be round (well developed, changing) or flat (simple, unchanging). Setting: the time and place of the action, which influences mood and conflict. Theme: the central idea or message of the story — what the story means beyond its events. Point of view: the perspective from which the story is told — first person (I), second person (you), or third person (he/she/they; limited or omniscient). Conflict: the struggle at the heart of the story — internal (man vs self) or external (man vs man, man vs nature, man vs society).
How a Short Story is Built

A good short story starts with a hook that creates curiosity, moves through rising tension to a climax (the turning point), and ends with a resolution — which may be closed (everything is settled) or open (leaving the reader to decide). Writers often use foreshadowing (hints of what will come) and symbolism (objects or actions standing for larger ideas) to deepen meaning.
Short Stories in the NEB English Syllabus

In the NEB (Nepal Education Board) English curriculum, short stories are studied to develop skills of comprehension, analysis and interpretation. Students are expected to identify the elements above, explain the theme in their own words, relate the story to real life, and answer questions about character, setting, plot and moral values.
The Six Universal Elements of Fiction

Every short story, regardless of culture or period, contains six fundamental elements: (1) Character — who the story is about; (2) Setting — when and where it takes place; (3) Plot — what happens; (4) Conflict — the central problem or tension; (5) Theme — the underlying message; (6) Style/Tone — how the author tells the story. These six elements work together like instruments in an orchestra: remove one and the story loses its coherence. When analysing any short story for an exam, systematically address each of these six elements to build a complete answer.
Types of Short Story

Short stories can be classified by their structure and intent: Fable — a short tale with animals as characters, ending with a moral (e.g., Aesop's Fables). Parable — a short narrative that illustrates a moral or spiritual lesson (often found in religious texts). Anecdote — a brief account of an interesting or amusing incident. Vignette — a short piece that captures a mood or moment rather than telling a complete story. Sketch — a brief, impressionistic portrayal of a character or scene. Flash fiction — an extremely short story (under 1,000 words) that delivers a complete narrative arc. Understanding which type you are reading helps you interpret the author's intentions and the story's effect on the reader.
Characterisation: Flat vs. Round, Static vs. Dynamic

W.E. Forster introduced the distinction between flat characters and round characters. A flat character is built around a single idea or quality — they are easily described in one sentence. A round character is complex, contradictory, and capable of surprising the reader in a convincing way. Similarly, a static character does not change significantly during the story, while a dynamic character undergoes an important inner change. Protagonists in literary short stories tend to be round and dynamic; supporting characters are often flat and static. In exam answers, always specify which type each character is and give textual evidence.
Setting and Atmosphere

Setting is more than just a backdrop — it shapes the mood (atmosphere), reflects the characters' psychological states, and can even function as a symbol. A stormy night may mirror a character's turmoil; a pristine garden may represent innocence. Key questions to ask about setting: When does the story take place? Where does it take place? How does the setting affect the characters' behaviour? How does the author use descriptive language (imagery, sensory details) to create atmosphere? In many classic stories — for example, those by Thomas Hardy or D.H. Lawrence — the landscape of rural England is as much a character as the people in the story.
Point of View and Narrative Voice

Point of view (POV) determines how the reader receives the story's information. First-person POV ("I") gives intimate access to the narrator's thoughts but limits knowledge of other characters. Third-person limited ("he/she") follows one character closely and shares their perceptions. Third-person omniscient ("he/she/they") gives access to the thoughts of multiple characters. Second-person POV ("you") is rare in fiction but creates a sense of direct address. The reliable narrator tells the truth as they know it; an unreliable narrator distorts or lies to the reader, creating irony. Identifying the narrative voice correctly is essential for understanding the author's intended meaning.
Literary Devices in Short Stories

Short story writers employ a rich array of literary devices: Metaphor — a direct comparison without "like" or "as" ("Life is a journey"). Simile — a comparison using "like" or "as" ("Her smile was like sunshine"). Personification — giving human qualities to non-human things ("The wind whispered through the trees"). Imagery — vivid sensory language that appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste, or touch. Irony — a contrast between expectation and reality (situational, dramatic, or verbal). Allusion — a reference to another literary work, historical event, or myth. Hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration for effect. Understatement — deliberately expressing less than is meant. These devices enrich the text and reward close reading.
Theme vs. Moral

A theme is a central idea or insight about life that a story explores — it is implicit and often complex. Themes can be stated in a single sentence, such as "Love can be both healing and destructive" or "Power corrupts those who seek it." A moral, on the other hand, is an explicit lesson that the story teaches — it is usually a direct instruction: "Honesty is the best policy." All stories have themes, but not all stories have morals. Fables and parables typically have morals; literary short stories tend to have themes. In exam answers, always express the theme as a complete, nuanced statement — never simply name it as a single word ("friendship") without elaboration.
Understanding Conflict in Depth

Conflict is the engine of narrative. Without conflict, there is no story. The main types are: Man vs. Man — a struggle between two characters (e.g., a hero and a villain). Man vs. Self — an internal struggle within a character's mind (guilt, doubt, desire). Man vs. Nature — a battle against natural forces (a storm, a wild animal, disease). Man vs. Society — a character at odds with social norms, laws, or expectations. Man vs. Fate/Supernatural — a struggle against destiny or forces beyond human control. Most stories contain a primary conflict and one or more secondary conflicts. Identifying and categorising conflict is a core skill in literary analysis and a frequent exam question.
The Importance of Opening and Closing Lines

In a short story, every word counts, but opening and closing lines carry special weight. A strong opening establishes voice, setting, and conflict quickly — it is the author's promise to the reader. Consider the opening of Kafka's The Metamorphosis: "One morning, when Gregor Samsa woke from troubled dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a horrible vermin." The closing resolves (or deliberately refuses to resolve) the tension and leaves the reader with a final impression. In exam preparation, memorise and analyse the opening and closing lines of the stories in your syllabus — they are prime material for close-reading answers.
How to Read a Short Story for Exam Preparation

Follow this systematic approach: First reading — read for enjoyment and general understanding; note the overall impression. Second reading — annotate actively: underline key passages, note literary devices, track character development, and mark the turning point (climax). Third reading — focus on theme and craft: ask why the author made specific choices (structure, language, imagery). Prepare by writing a summary of each story (150-200 words), a character sketch of each major character, a list of themes with supporting evidence, and key quotations you can cite in your answers. This three-pass method ensures both comprehension and analytical depth.
Summary Writing: A Core Skill

Summary writing is a tested skill in the NEB English exam. A good summary: (1) preserves the main events in chronological order; (2) omits minor details, dialogue, and examples; (3) is written in your own words, not copied from the text; (4) maintains third-person and past tense ("The protagonist faced..."); (5) is concise — typically 150-200 words for a short story summary. A common mistake is to retell every detail; a summary is not a retelling but a distillation. Always check: does my summary include the main characters, the central conflict, and the resolution? If yes, it is on the right track.
Developing Critical Vocabulary

To write strong analytical answers, you need a working vocabulary of critical terms: Protagonist — the main character. Antagonist — the character or force opposing the protagonist. Narrator — the voice telling the story (not always the author). Exposition — the introductory section that provides background information. Rising action — events that build tension toward the climax. Climax — the turning point or moment of highest tension. Falling action — events after the climax. Resolution/Denouement — the conclusion where loose ends are tied up. Epiphany — a sudden moment of insight or revelation experienced by a character. Using these terms accurately in your answers demonstrates deep understanding and impresses examiners.
confusion: Short story vs. novella: A short story is typically under 7,500 words and focuses on a single incident, while a novella is between 17,500 and 40,000 words and allows for more complex plots and character development.

Theme vs. subject: The subject is what the story is about in one word (e.g., 'war', 'love', 'jealousy'). The theme is what the story says about that subject — it is a complete statement (e.g., 'War destroys the innocence of youth'). Never write a theme as a single word in an exam.

Plot vs. story: The story is everything that happens in the narrative world in chronological order. The plot is the specific arrangement and selection of events as presented by the author — events may be reordered, skipped, or emphasised. A story might be told out of order (flashback, flashback within flashback), but the plot is what the reader actually experiences.

First-person narrator vs. author: The narrator is a fictional voice inside the text — not the author. Even when a story is written in first person ('I'), the 'I' is a character, not the real person who wrote the story. Confusing narrator with author leads to misinterpretation, especially with unreliable narrators.

Foreshadowing vs. flashback: Foreshadowing provides hints or clues about events that will happen later in the story. Flashback is a scene that interrupts the present action to show events from the past. One points forward; the other points backward. Both are common in short stories but serve very different narrative functions.

data.title: Reading Comprehension: Passage Analysis
notes: Systematic Passage Analysis

Systematic passage analysis is a structured approach to understanding and answering questions about an unseen prose passage. In the NEB Class 11 English examination, comprehension passages typically carry 10-15 marks and may include factual questions, inferential questions, vocabulary-in-context questions, and short-answer questions. A systematic approach ensures that students extract maximum information from the passage and answer all questions accurately and efficiently.
Step 1: Preview the Passage

Before reading in detail, spend 30-60 seconds previewing: (1) Read the title (if given) — it often reveals the topic and sometimes the author's position. (2) Skim the first paragraph — it usually introduces the topic and main idea. (3) Skim the last paragraph — it often summarises or concludes the argument. (4) Note the paragraph topics — read the first sentence of each paragraph to understand the structure. This preview takes 1-2 minutes and provides a mental framework for detailed reading.
Step 2: Active Reading

During active reading, engage with the text: (1) Underline key terms — names, dates, technical terms, repeated ideas. (2) Marginal notes — write brief summaries of each paragraph in the margin (2-3 words per paragraph). (3) Note transitions — pay attention to words like 'however', 'therefore', 'moreover', 'nevertheless' — these signal shifts in argument or emphasis. (4) Identify the author's stance — is the author supportive, critical, neutral, or balanced? (5) Mark difficult words — circle words you don't know and try to infer their meaning from context. Active reading takes 3-5 minutes for a standard passage and significantly improves comprehension and retention.
Step 3: Answering Questions Strategically

When answering comprehension questions: (1) Read the question first — this tells you what to look for. (2) Locate the relevant section — scan the passage for keywords from the question. (3) Read the surrounding sentences — one sentence may not contain enough information. (4) Quote directly for factual questions — use the passage's exact words where possible. (5) Paraphrase for inferential questions — express implied meaning in your own words. (6) Keep answers concise — answer only what is asked; avoid unnecessary information. (7) Check your answer — ensure it is supported by the passage, not your own opinion. This strategic approach saves time and improves accuracy.
Types of Comprehension Questions

NEB comprehension questions fall into these categories: Factual recall — questions asking for information directly stated in the passage (Who? What? When? Where?). Inference — questions asking for meaning that is implied but not directly stated (Why? How? What can be inferred?). Vocabulary in context — questions asking for the meaning of a word or phrase as used in the passage. Main idea — questions about the central theme or purpose of the passage. Tone and attitude — questions about the author's feeling or perspective. Structure — questions about how the passage is organised. Application — questions asking students to apply ideas from the passage to a new situation. Different question types require different reading strategies and answer formats.
Handling Vocabulary-in-Context Questions

When asked to explain a word's meaning in context: (1) Read the entire sentence containing the word. (2) Read the sentences before and after — context extends beyond the immediate sentence. (3) Look for context clues — definitions, examples, contrasts, and restatements that reveal meaning. (4) Consider the word's root — knowing Latin or Greek roots can help (e.g., 'bene' = good, so 'benevolent' = good-willed). (5) Eliminate obviously wrong options — in MCQ format, eliminate answers that don't fit the context. (6) Substitute your answer — replace the word with your meaning in the sentence to check if it makes sense. Vocabulary-in-context questions test your ability to use surrounding information to determine meaning, not just recall dictionary definitions.
Writing Effective Short Answers

For short-answer comprehension questions (2-4 marks): (1) Answer in complete sentences — even for short answers, use proper sentence structure. (2) Be specific — include relevant details from the passage. (3) Use textual evidence — reference specific parts of the passage to support your answer. (4) Stay within the passage — do not bring in outside knowledge unless asked. (5) Keep it concise — 2-4 sentences are usually sufficient for 2-4 mark questions. (6) Address all parts — if a question has two parts, answer both. For longer answers (5-8 marks): write 4-6 sentences with clear structure (topic sentence, supporting details, conclusion). Always write in your own words when paraphrasing, and use direct quotes when the passage's exact wording is important.
Time Management in Comprehension

Effective time management for comprehension sections: (1) Preview (1-2 minutes) — skim title, first/last paragraphs, and topic sentences. (2) Active reading (3-5 minutes) — read carefully, underline key points, make marginal notes. (3) Answer factual questions (2-3 minutes) — these are usually the easiest and fastest to answer. (4) Answer inferential questions (3-5 minutes) — these require more thinking and evidence-gathering. (5) Answer vocabulary questions (2-3 minutes) — use context clues and elimination. (6) Review (2-3 minutes) — check answers for completeness and accuracy. Total time: approximately 15-20 minutes for a standard comprehension passage. Practising with a timer builds speed and accuracy.
confusion: Inference vs. Opinion: An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from evidence in the passage — it must be supported by the text. An opinion is a personal belief or judgment that may or may not be supported by the text. In NEB exams, inference questions require textual evidence; opinion questions ask for your personal response. Confusing these leads to answers that are either unsupported (opinion presented as inference) or redundant (stating the obvious).

Main idea vs. Topic sentence: The main idea is the central point of the entire passage — it may be stated explicitly in a topic sentence or implied throughout. The topic sentence is a single sentence (usually at the beginning of a paragraph) that states the paragraph's main point. The main idea of a passage may not have a single topic sentence — it may be developed across multiple paragraphs. In NEB exams, 'main idea' questions require synthesising information from the entire passage.

Author's purpose vs. Author's main idea: The author's purpose is WHY the author wrote the passage (to inform, to persuade, to entertain, to describe). The author's main idea is WHAT the author is saying (the central argument or message). Purpose is about function; main idea is about content. A passage may have the purpose of persuading with the main idea that 'vaccination is essential for public health.' These are related but distinct concepts tested in NEB comprehension questions.

Literal meaning vs. Figurative meaning: Literal meaning is the direct, dictionary definition of words — what they say on the surface. Figurative meaning is the implied, non-literal meaning — what the author suggests beyond the surface. In comprehension, literal questions ask for information directly stated; figurative questions ask for implied meaning (inferences, themes, symbolic interpretations). Students often miss figurative meaning by taking language too literally.

Summary vs. Paraphrase: A summary condenses the entire passage to its main ideas in significantly fewer words (1/3 to 1/4 length). A paraphrase restates a specific passage or sentence in your own words, maintaining approximately the same length. Summaries are selective (only main ideas); paraphrases are comprehensive (all details in new words). In NEB exams, summary questions ask for a condensed version; paraphrase questions ask for restatement of a specific passage.

data.title: Synonyms and Antonyms
notes: What Are Synonyms and Antonyms?

Synonyms are words that have the same or similar meanings in certain contexts (e.g., big/large, happy/joyful, smart/intelligent). Antonyms are words with opposite meanings (e.g., hot/cold, brave/cowardly, abundant/scarse). In the NEB Class 11 English examination, synonym and antonym questions typically carry 3-6 marks and appear in objective (MCQ) and subjective (one-word substitution) formats. Mastering synonyms and antonyms is essential for vocabulary expansion, improving writing quality, and performing well in comprehension passages where precise word choice matters.
Types of Synonyms

Synonyms can be classified into several types: Absolute synonyms — words that are interchangeable in all contexts (rare in English — 'lift' and 'elevator' are close but used in different registers). Relative synonyms — words with similar meanings but different connotations, registers, or collocations (e.g., 'slim' vs. 'thin' vs. 'skinny' — all mean 'not fat' but with different emotional overtones). Contextual synonyms — words that are synonyms only in specific contexts (e.g., 'start' and 'begin' are synonyms when referring to an action, but not when 'start' means 'engine ignition'). NEB exams typically test relative and contextual synonyms.
Types of Antonyms

Antonyms can be classified into three types: Gradable antonyms — words that exist on a spectrum and can be modified (hot/cold — something can be very hot or slightly cold). Complementary antonyms — words that are absolute opposites with no middle ground (dead/alive, present/absent, true/false). Converse antonyms — words that express a reciprocal relationship (buy/sell, teacher/student, above/below). Understanding these types helps students choose the correct antonym in context. NEB exams may ask students to identify antonyms from a list or to choose the best opposite for a word in a given sentence.
Strategies for Learning Synonyms and Antonyms

Effective strategies include: (1) Learning in context — study words as they appear in sentences, not in isolation. Context reveals the appropriate register and connotation. (2) Word families — learn related words together (happy, happiness, happily, unhappy, unhappy, happiness). This builds understanding of word formation and relationship. (3) Flashcards — write the word on one side, synonyms/antonyms and example sentences on the other. (4) Reading widely — exposure to diverse texts naturally builds vocabulary. (5) Using a thesaurus wisely — a thesaurus lists synonyms but does not explain connotations — always check usage in context. (6) Regular review — spaced repetition is essential for long-term retention.
Common Synonym/Antonym Patterns in NEB Exams

NEB exams frequently test the following word pairs and patterns: Abstract nouns from adjectives: happy → happiness, sad → sadness, kind → kindness. Opposite prefixes: happy/unhappy, possible/impossible, careful/careless, honest/dishonest. Contextual meaning: The word 'bright' has different antonyms depending on context — 'bright light' (antonym: dim) vs. 'bright student' (antonym: dull) vs. 'bright future' (antonym: bleak). NEB exams sometimes test this contextual sensitivity by providing a sentence and asking for the appropriate synonym or antonym.
Avoiding Common Mistakes

Common errors in synonym/antonym questions: (1) Choosing a word with the wrong connotation — 'slim' and 'fat' are antonyms, but 'skinny' and 'fat' are not appropriate in formal contexts. (2) Ignoring context — choosing a synonym that fits the dictionary definition but not the specific sentence. (3) Confusing synonyms with related words — 'result' and 'consequence' are related but not perfect synonyms. (4) Choosing antonyms from the wrong category — 'hot' and 'cold' are gradable antonyms; 'hot' and 'spicy' are not antonyms (spicy describes taste, hot describes temperature). (5) Using words that are too extreme — the antonym of 'small' is 'large', not 'enormous' (which implies a different degree). Always choose the most precise and context-appropriate word.
confusion: Synonym vs. Equivalent: A synonym is a single word with nearly the same meaning as another word in most contexts (big ≈ large). An equivalent may be a phrase or expression that conveys the same idea (very big ≈ enormous). In NEB exams, synonym questions ask for a single-word replacement. One-word substitution is related but more specific — it provides a definition and asks for the single word that matches it.

Antonym vs. Opposite: An antonym is a specific vocabulary term for a word with the opposite meaning (hot/cold, brave/cowardly). An 'opposite' is a broader concept that includes antonyms but also refers to anything contrary. In NEB exams, use 'antonym' when referring to vocabulary relationships. Some words have multiple antonyms depending on context — 'light' (weight) → antonym: heavy; 'light' (illumination) → antonym: dark.

Contextual synonym vs. Absolute synonym: Absolute synonyms (words interchangeable in ALL contexts) are extremely rare in English. Most so-called synonyms are contextual — they are interchangeable only in specific situations. For example, 'begin' and 'start' are often synonyms, but 'start the car' is correct while 'begin the car' is not. NEB exams sometimes test this distinction by providing a sentence where only one of two similar words is appropriate.

Gradable vs. Complementary antonyms: Gradable antonyms (hot/cold, big/small) exist on a continuum — something can be more or less of either. Complementary antonyms (dead/alive, present/absent) are absolute opposites — something cannot be both or neither. This distinction matters in NEB exams because it affects how antonyms are used in sentences. For example, 'not hot' does not necessarily mean 'cold' (it could be warm), but 'not dead' necessarily means 'alive' (in the complementary pair).

Connotation vs. Denotation in synonym selection: Two words may have the same denotation (dictionary definition) but different connotations (emotional/cultural associations). 'Thin' and 'slim' both mean 'not fat', but 'slim' has a positive connotation while 'thin' can be neutral or negative. In NEB synonym questions, the correct choice depends on the connotation that fits the context, not just the dictionary definition.

data.title: Vocabulary: Word Formation, Idioms, and Phrases
notes: Word Formation

Word formation is the process of creating new words from existing words using affixes (prefixes and suffixes), compounding, conversion, or blending. In the NEB Class 11 English examination, word formation questions (typically 3-5 marks) ask students to change a given word into a different part of speech or to fill in a blank with the correct derived form. Prefixes are added to the beginning of a word (un-, dis-, re-, pre-, mis-). Suffixes are added to the end ( -ness, -ment, -tion, -able, -ful, -less, -ly, -er, -ist). Understanding word formation patterns is essential for vocabulary expansion and grammar accuracy.
Common Prefixes and Their Meanings

Key prefixes tested in NEB exams: un- (not, opposite): unhappy, unlock, unfair. dis- (not, opposite, removal): disagree, disappear, dishonest. re- (again): rewrite, rebuild, reinstall. pre- (before): prehistoric, prepaid, preview. mis- (wrongly): misunderstand, mislead, misplace. in-/im-/il-/ir- (not): impossible, illegal, irregular, incomplete. anti- (against): antibiotic, anti-social. semi- (half): semifinal, semicircle. sub- (under): submarine, submodule. over- (too much): overwork, overeat. under- (too little): underpaid, underestimate. Memorising these prefixes helps in solving word formation and vocabulary questions efficiently.
Common Suffixes and Their Functions

Key suffixes tested in NEB exams: -ness (forms nouns from adjectives): happiness, kindness, darkness. -ment (forms nouns from verbs): achievement, agreement, development. -tion/-sion (forms nouns from verbs): education, decision, admission. -able/-ible (forms adjectives from verbs): readable, visible, accessible. -ful (forms adjectives from nouns): helpful, beautiful, careless. -less (forms adjectives meaning 'without'): hopeless, fearless, endless. -ly (forms adverbs from adjectives): quickly, carefully, happily. -er/-or (forms nouns indicating doer): teacher, actor, writer. -ist (forms nouns indicating specialist): artist, scientist, pessimist. -ity (forms nouns from adjectives): ability, purity, activity. -ous/-ious (forms adjectives from nouns): dangerous, nervous, famous.
Idioms: Fixed Expressions with Figurative Meaning

Idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of individual words. Examples: 'Break the ice' = to initiate conversation in a social setting. 'Hit the nail on the head' = to describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem. 'A dime a dozen' = very common and not valuable. 'Bite the bullet' = to face a difficult situation courageously. 'Cost an arm and a leg' = to be very expensive. 'Let the cat out of the bag' = to reveal a secret accidentally. 'Beat around the bush' = to avoid talking about something directly. 'Once in a blue moon' = very rarely. Idioms are extensively tested in NEB exams through gap-filling, sentence completion, and meaning-matching questions.
Common Phrasal Verbs

Phrasal verbs are combinations of a verb + particle (preposition or adverb) that create a new meaning. Examples: give up = stop trying / surrender. look after = take care of. run out of = use all of something. put off = postpone. turn up = appear / arrive. break down = stop working (machine) / lose control (emotion). carry on = continue. get along = have a good relationship. come across = find by chance. figure out = understand / solve. Phrasal verbs are one of the most challenging aspects of English vocabulary for Nepali students, as Nepali does not have an equivalent particle system.
One-Word Substitution

One-word substitution replaces a phrase or group of words with a single word that has the same meaning. Common examples tested in NEB exams: Belonging to one state only = Native. Love of books = Bibliophile. Study of words = Lexicography. Love of humanity = Philanthropist. That can be felt = Sensible. That cannot be felt = Insensible. A person who knows many languages = Polyglot. A person who loves peace = Pacifist. That cannot be destroyed = Indestructible. A short, witty remark = Epigram. One-word substitution questions typically carry 2-4 marks in NEB exams and require extensive vocabulary preparation.
Synonyms and Antonyms

Synonyms are words with similar meanings (big/large, happy/joyful, smart/intelligent). Antonyms are words with opposite meanings (hot/cold, brave/cowardly, abundant/scarse). In NEB exams, synonym and antonym questions may appear as: (1) Direct identification ('Choose the synonym of 'enormous': (a) small (b) huge (c) weak'). (2) Odd-one-out ('Which word is different?'). (3) Context-based ('Choose the word nearest in meaning to...'). Effective preparation involves learning word pairs in context, not in isolation, because many words have multiple meanings depending on context.
Strategy for Vocabulary Preparation

To build vocabulary effectively for NEB exams: (1) Read widely — newspapers, magazines, and literature expose you to new words in context. (2) Learn word families — study a word's forms (happy, happiness, happily, unhappy) to understand word formation patterns. (3) Use flashcards — write the word on one side, meaning and example on the other. (4) Practice in context — use new words in sentences to reinforce understanding. (5) Review regularly — spaced repetition improves long-term retention. (6) Focus on high-frequency words — prioritize words that appear frequently in NEB exams and common English usage. Vocabulary is a cumulative skill that requires consistent daily practice over months, not last-minute cramming.
confusion: Idiom vs. Phrasal verb: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is figurative and unpredictable from its parts ('break the ice' ≠ literally breaking ice). A phrasal verb is a verb + particle combination where the meaning may be literal or figurative ('give up' can mean 'stop' (figurative) or 'hand over' (literal)). All phrasal verbs are not idioms, and not all idioms are phrasal verbs.

Synonym vs. Equivalent: A synonym is a word with nearly the same meaning as another in most contexts ('big' and 'large'). An equivalent may be a phrase that expresses the same idea ('very big' ≈ 'enormous'). In NEB exams, synonym questions typically ask for a single-word replacement, not a phrase. One-word substitution is related but more specific — it replaces a definition with a single word.

Prefix vs. Suffix: A prefix is added to the BEGINNING of a word (un-happy, re-write, mis-lead). A suffix is added to the END of a word (happi-ness, write-r, lead-er). Both change the meaning or grammatical function of the base word. Confusing prefix with suffix is a common error in word formation questions.

Connotation vs. Denotation: Denotation is the literal, dictionary definition of a word ('home' = a place where one lives). Connotation is the emotional or cultural association of a word ('home' = warmth, safety, family). Two words may have the same denotation but different connotations ('thin' vs. 'slim' vs. 'skinny'). NEB exams sometimes test this distinction in vocabulary questions asking for the 'best' word choice.

Antonym vs. Opposite: An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning (hot/cold, brave/cowardly). An 'opposite' is a broader concept that may include antonyms but also refers to anything contrary. In NEB exams, use 'antonym' when referring to vocabulary words. The relationship between antonyms can be gradable (hot/cold — on a spectrum), complementary (dead/alive — no middle ground), or converse (buy/sell — relational opposites).

Homonyms vs. Homophones vs. Homographs: Homonyms are words that are spelled and pronounced the same but have different meanings ('bank' = financial institution / 'bank' = river edge). Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently ('their' / 'there' / 'they're'). Homographs are spelled the same but pronounced differently ('lead' = metal / 'lead' = to guide). NEB exams typically test homophones through gap-filling questions.

data.title: Essay Writing — argumentative, descriptive, narrative, ex…
notes: **What it is:** an essay argues, describes, narrates or explains a topic in organised paragraphs. The examiner marks STANCE + STRUCTURE + evidence, not length.

**Universal skeleton:** Introduction (hook + thesis) → Body paragraphs (ONE reason each: topic sentence → explanation → example) → optional counter-argument (acknowledge, then rebut) → Conclusion (restate thesis + consequence).

**Four types:** *Argumentative* (clear side, reasons, admit the other side), *Descriptive* (5 senses, spatial order, show-don't-tell), *Narrative* (one incident: setup → conflict → climax → reflection), *Expository* (explain causes/process in numbered factors, no opinion).
**Tense logic:** essays live in PRESENT for general truths; past only inside narrative examples; predictions use will/would.

data.title: Paragraph Writing
notes: **What it is:** ONE controlling idea in 4–6 sentences — the engine behind every essay, letter and report.

data.title: Formal Letter Writing — editor, application, complaint, i…
notes: **What it is:** a letter to someone you do NOT know (editor, manager, office). Half the marks are the fixed BLOCK LAYOUT; the other half is polite business tone.

**Block order:** Sender's address → Date → Recipient's designation + address → Subject line → Salutation ('Dear Sir/Madam') → Body (3 short paragraphs: who you are + purpose / details / polite request) → Complimentary close → Signature + full name in capitals.
**The pairing rule that trips everyone:** 'Dear Sir/Madam' → end **Yours faithfully**; 'Dear Mr/Ms Sharma' (real name) → end **Yours sincerely**.
**Tone grammar:** no contractions (*do not*, *I am*); polite modals (*would*, *could*, *may*); passive voice for formality ('the matter is being investigated').

**Variants:** *Editor* (public issue + call for action), *Job application* (post + skills + 'Enclosure: CV'), *Complaint* (what, when, defect + remedy + deadline), *Inquiry/Order* (price/availability/terms).
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Report Writing and Summarisation
notes: **What it is:** factual, third-person, past-tense reporting of an event (sports day, blood donation camp) — not a story, not an opinion.

**Tense/voice grammar:** past simple for every event; passive voice is standard for ceremony facts ('trophies were distributed'); reported speech for quotes; third person only — never 'I'.
**Summarisation partner skill:** compress any passage into its core idea in your own words within the word limit — keep the author's viewpoint, drop examples and repetition.

data.title: Story Writing
notes: **What it is:** a COMPLETE narrative arc judged on plot — situation → problem → turning point → resolution → (often) a quiet moral.

**Structure:** Opening (if the prompt gives a first line, USE it verbatim and continue) → Complication → Rising action → Climax (the decisive moment — slow down here) → Resolution + realisation/moral.

**Tense machinery:** past simple drives the plot; past continuous paints background ('I was dawdling home'); past perfect marks earlier events ('which she had lost'); direct speech at the climax adds life.
**Keep ONE tense zone and ONE narrator** — drifting between present and past, or I/he, breaks the story.

data.title: Comprehension and Unseen Passage
notes: **What it is:** extracting and restating passage information — the trap is copying whole sentences; the skill is locate-then-restate.

**Method:** skim for gist → scan for the question's keywords (the answer lives nearby) → answer in complete sentences with synonyms → match the question type (WH → answer the WH; 'Why' → 'Because…'; true/false → quote evidence) → verify against the text.

**Grammar of answers:** convert passage nouns into clauses ('its existence' → 'that it exists'); use report frames ('the passage states that…'); keep the passage's tense zone; quote marks ONLY when demanded.
**Length discipline:** 1-mark answers = one sentence; 2-mark answers = answer + reason/evidence.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**The four-step comprehension method:** (1) SKIM — read the passage once quickly (60 seconds) to get the gist. Don't stop for unknown words. (2) SCAN — read the questions FIRST, then scan the passage for keywords related to each question. (3) LOCATE — find the exact sentence(s) that contain the answer. Underline them. (4) RESTATE — write the answer in YOUR OWN WORDS using complete sentences. Never copy the passage verbatim.

**Why copying is the #1 comprehension error:** Examiners explicitly penalise copied sentences. If the passage says 'The river was polluted with industrial waste,' and you write 'The river was polluted with industrial waste,' you get ZERO marks for that answer. You must PARAPHRASE: 'Industrial waste had contaminated the river.' This proves you UNDERSTOOD the meaning, not just your ability to copy.

**Paraphrasing techniques for exam success:** (1) *Synonym swap*: 'happy' → 'joyful', 'big' → 'large', 'sad' → 'sorrowful'. (2) *Word class change*: 'The government decided' → 'The government's decision was…' (3) *Voice change*: 'They built the bridge' → 'The bridge was built by them.' (4) *Clause reduction*: 'Although it was raining heavily, they went out' → 'Despite the heavy rain, they went out.' (5) *Active to passive*: 'The teacher gave the students homework' → 'The students were given homework by the teacher.'

**Question type mastery — WH questions:** (1) *What* — answer with a noun or clause: 'What caused the flood?' → 'Heavy rainfall caused the flood.' (2) *Why* — answer with a reason: 'Why did she refuse?' → 'She refused because she had lost faith in the system.' (3) *How* — answer with a method or manner: 'How did they solve the problem?' → 'They solved it by combining traditional knowledge with modern techniques.' (4) *When/Where/Who* — direct factual answers. ALWAYS use complete sentences unless told otherwise.

**Question type mastery — true/false/not given:** (1) *True* — the passage explicitly confirms the statement. (2) *False* — the passage explicitly contradicts the statement. (3) *Not Given* — the passage doesn't mention the information at all. 'Not Given' is different from 'False' — it means the information is simply absent, not wrong. This distinction is heavily tested.

**Question type mastery — short answer vs. long answer:** (1) *Short answer* (1 mark): one sentence, direct to the point. (2) *Long answer* (2-3 marks): answer + supporting evidence/reason from the passage. For 2-mark questions, always include BOTH the answer AND the evidence. Format: 'X happened because Y [evidence from passage].' Don't just state the answer — justify it.

**Vocabulary-in-context questions:** When asked 'What does the word X mean in the passage?', do NOT write a dictionary definition. Write what the word means IN THAT CONTEXT. 'In the passage, "reluctant" means unwilling or hesitating because the character had no choice but to agree despite her reservations.' Always anchor your answer in the passage's context.

**Inference questions — reading between the lines:** Inference questions ask you to deduce something NOT explicitly stated. 'What can you infer about the author's attitude?' Strategy: (1) Find the sentence with the relevant information. (2) Ask 'what does this imply?' (3) Write the implication as your answer. Don't go beyond the text — stay close to the passage. 'The author's use of the word "heartbreaking" suggests they feel deep sorrow about the situation.'

**Reference questions — what does 'it/this/that' refer to?** These questions ask you to identify what a pronoun or demonstrative refers to in context. Strategy: (1) Find the pronoun in the passage. (2) Look at the preceding sentence(s). (3) Identify the noun that the pronoun replaces. Answer: 'It refers to [the specific noun from the passage].' Never answer with another pronoun.

**Tone and attitude questions:** 'What is the author's tone?' Possible answers: formal, informal, objective, subjective, sympathetic, critical, sarcastic, hopeful, pessimistic, nostalgic, indifferent. 'What is the author's attitude towards…?' Possible answers: positive, negative, neutral, ambivalent, critical, admiring. Always support your answer with a specific word or phrase from the passage.

**Main idea and title questions:** (1) *Main idea*: Read the first and last sentence of each paragraph. The main idea is what connects ALL paragraphs. (2) *Title*: Choose a title that covers the WHOLE passage, not just one paragraph. A good title is specific but not too narrow. Bad title: 'Pollution in Kathmandu' (only covers one paragraph). Good title: 'Environmental Challenges in Urban Nepal' (covers all paragraphs).

**Comprehension time management:** For a 30-mark comprehension section with a 300-400 word passage and 10-12 questions: (1) Spend 2 minutes skimming. (2) Read questions in 1 minute. (3) Each question takes 2-3 minutes (locate + restate + verify). (4) Leave 2 minutes for review. Total: ~30 minutes. Don't spend 10 minutes on one question — move on and come back. Speed and accuracy matter.

**The verification check — your last step:** After writing every answer, go back to the passage and ask: (1) Does my answer match the passage? (2) Have I answered the question asked, not a different one? (3) Is my answer in my own words? (4) Is it in a complete sentence? (5) Does it fit the word limit? If any answer fails these checks, rewrite it. Verification catches 60% of comprehension errors.

confusion: Copying vs. paraphrasing: Copying = writing the exact words from the passage (0 marks). Paraphrasing = expressing the SAME MEANING in YOUR OWN WORDS (full marks). Example: Passage says 'The children played joyfully in the garden.' Copy: 'The children played joyfully in the garden' (wrong). Paraphrase: 'The kids had fun playing outdoors in the garden' (correct). Always paraphrase unless the question says 'quote from the passage.'

Inference vs. opinion: An inference is a LOGICAL conclusion drawn from evidence in the passage. An opinion is YOUR PERSONAL belief that may or may not be supported by the passage. Inference: 'The character was likely anxious because she kept checking her watch.' Opinion: 'I think the character was anxious because I get nervous too.' Inferences use passage evidence; opinions use personal experience. Examiners want inferences.

True vs. Not Given: True = the passage CONFIRMS the statement. False = the passage CONTRADICTS the statement. Not Given = the passage NEITHER confirms nor contradicts — the information is simply absent. Example: Passage says 'Rahul went to school.' Statement: 'Rahul walked to school.' This is NOT GIVEN — we know he went, but not HOW. Don't assume; stick to what's in the passage.

Short answer vs. long answer format: A short answer (1 mark) is one complete sentence that directly answers the question. A long answer (2-3 marks) is answer + evidence/reason. Format for long answers: 'The answer is X because Y [with reference to the passage].' For short answers, skip the 'because' — just state the answer directly. Over-answering short questions wastes time; under-answering long questions loses marks.

Main idea vs. topic: The TOPIC is what the passage is about (one word or phrase: 'deforestation'). The MAIN IDEA is what the passage says ABOUT the topic (a complete sentence: 'Deforestation in Nepal is accelerating due to population pressure and policy failures'). Don't confuse them — a topic is a label; a main idea is a claim.

Comprehension skills are tested in virtually every English examination worldwide — NEB, CBSE, ICSE, Cambridge IGCSE, IELTS, TOEFL. The 'locate-then-restate' method (find the answer in the text, express it in your own words) is the universal standard across all these exams.

In the NEB English exam, comprehension typically carries 15-20 marks out of 60-80 total. It is the single highest-weighted section. Mastering comprehension technique can add 5-8 marks to your total score — more than any other single skill.

Research by reading specialists shows that students who practice 'active reading' (predicting, questioning, visualising, summarising) score 25-30% higher on comprehension tests than students who read passively. The four strategies above (skim-scan-locate-restate) are a practical application of active reading.

The most common comprehension error across all levels is copying from the passage. Studies of examiner reports show that 40-60% of students who lose marks in comprehension do so because they copied sentences instead of paraphrasing. This single habit is the biggest barrier to high comprehension scores.

Paraphrasing is a transferable skill — it is used not just in comprehension but also in summarisation, note-making, essay writing, and even in professional contexts like research and journalism. Mastering paraphrasing in exam preparation benefits your overall English proficiency.

data.title: Grammar for Writing — sentences, clauses, punctuation
notes: **Sentence types as tools:** simple (one clause — POWER), compound (two main clauses via and/but/so or a semicolon — equal weight), complex (main + subordinate clause via because/although/when/if — shows the relation between ideas). Mix them: examiners reward rhythm.

**Clauses vs phrases:** a phrase has no subject-verb pair and cannot stand alone; a dependent clause has one but leans on the main clause ('Because it rained.' alone is a fragment). Relative clauses (who/which/that) add noun detail — commas only for extra information.

**Punctuation logic:** full stop ends a thought; comma separates list items, follows openers, precedes and/but/so between full sentences; semicolon joins balanced sentences; colon introduces; apostrophe = possession or contraction (its vs it's is the classic trap). Comma splice = two full sentences joined by only a comma — fix it.

**Tense + agreement discipline:** pick a tense zone per paragraph (essays: present; reports: past); subjects agree with verbs ('Each of the students WAS present'); a/an by SOUND ('an hour', 'a university').
