data.title: Email Writing
notes: What Is Email Writing?

Email writing is the composition of electronic messages for personal or professional communication. In the NEB Class 11 English examination, email writing (often grouped with letter writing) carries 5-8 marks. While emails share similarities with formal and informal letters, they have distinctive features: a subject line, shorter body, and a more modern structure. Understanding the conventions of email writing is essential for both academic and real-world communication.
Structure of a Formal Email

A formal email follows this structure: (1) Subject line — a concise phrase stating the purpose (e.g., 'Subject: Application for Scholarship Programme'). (2) Salutation: 'Dear Sir/Madam' or 'Dear Mr. Sharma'. (3) Opening — state the purpose clearly in the first sentence. (4) Body — provide relevant details in 2-3 short paragraphs. (5) Closing — 'Yours faithfully' (unknown name) or 'Yours sincerely' (known name). (6) Signature — full name and contact information. The body should be 80-120 words for NEB exams. Unlike letters, emails do not require sender/receiver addresses at the top.
Structure of an Informal Email

An informal email to a friend or relative is less rigid: (1) Subject line — optional but recommended (e.g., 'Subject: Weekend Plans'). (2) Salutation: 'Dear Ram,' 'Hi Sita,'. (3) Opening — personal greeting and well-wishes ('I hope you are doing well'). (4) Body — share news, ask questions, express feelings in a warm tone. (5) Closing: 'Write soon', 'Best wishes', 'Your friend'. (6) Signature — first name only. Contractions, colloquial expressions, and exclamations are acceptable. The body should be 80-100 words for NEB exams.
Email vs. Letter: Key Differences

Key differences between email and letter writing: (1) Addresses — letters require sender's and receiver's addresses; emails do not. (2) Subject line — emails require a subject line; letters do not. (3) Length — emails are generally shorter and more concise. (4) Speed — emails are sent immediately; letters involve postal delay. (5) Formality — both formal and informal emails exist, but even formal emails tend to be slightly less rigid than formal letters. (6) Attachments — emails can include files; letters cannot. In NEB exams, if the question specifies 'email', follow email format; if it says 'letter', follow letter format. Using the wrong format costs marks.
Subject Line: The Most Important Element

The subject line is unique to email and is critical for effective communication. A good subject line is: (1) Concise — 5-10 words maximum. (2) Informative — it should tell the reader exactly what the email is about. (3) Specific — avoid vague subjects like 'Hello' or 'Important'. Examples: 'Subject: Request for Leave on 15th November' (good) vs. 'Subject: Something important' (bad). In NEB exams, omitting the subject line in an email question is a common error that costs marks. The subject line should be underlined or placed on its own line.
Common Email Topics in NEB Exams

Frequently assigned email topics include: (1) Formal email to principal — requesting permission, applying for something, complaining about facilities. (2) Formal email to editor — raising a civic issue. (3) Informal email to friend — inviting, congratulating, sharing news. (4) Informal email to relative — family news, festival greetings, apologies. (5) Professional email — job application, enquiry about a course, product complaint. For each type, the format and tone change appropriately. Students must identify the email type from the question prompt and apply the correct conventions.
Tone and Language in Email Writing

Email tone depends on the recipient and purpose. Formal emails require: respectful language, no contractions, clear and direct statements, polite requests ('I would like to...', 'I kindly request...'), and professional sign-offs. Informal emails allow: contractions ('I'm', 'don't'), colloquial expressions, personal anecdotes, exclamations, and warm closings. A common error is mixing tones — writing an informal email with formal language or a formal email with casual expressions. Always match the tone to the recipient and purpose.
Common Mistakes in Email Writing

Avoid these errors: (1) No subject line — the most common and damaging mistake in email writing. (2) Wrong closing — using 'Yours faithfully' in an informal email, or 'Love' in a formal email. (3) Writing too much — emails should be concise; the body should not exceed 120 words. (4) Using letter format for email — including addresses and date placement from letter format. (5) Informal language in formal emails — slang, contractions, emotional language. (6) Vague subject line — 'Hello' or 'Important' instead of a descriptive subject. (7) Forgetting the signature — always include your name and designation for formal emails.
confusion: Email vs. Letter format: Emails do not require sender's or receiver's addresses at the top. Emails require a subject line; letters do not. Emails use 'Yours faithfully/sincerely' like formal letters, but informal emails use casual closings like 'Love' or 'Your friend'. The key difference is the subject line — it is mandatory for emails and absent in letters.

Subject line placement: In emails, the subject line appears at the top, after the salutation or before it. In NEB exams, it is typically placed after the salutation: 'Dear Sir/Madam, Subject: ....' The subject line should be concise (5-10 words) and descriptive. Forgetting the subject line is the most common error in email writing questions.

Formal email vs. Formal letter: Formal emails are shorter and more direct than formal letters. They omit addresses but include a subject line. The tone is similarly formal in both, but emails are generally more concise. In NEB exams, if the question says 'email', do not write addresses; if it says 'letter', do include addresses.

Informal email vs. Informal letter: Informal emails are essentially the same as informal letters in tone and content. The main difference is the subject line (present in emails, absent in letters) and the absence of addresses (present in letters, absent in emails). Otherwise, both use warm, personal language and first-name signatures.

Yours faithfully vs. Yours sincerely in emails: The same rule applies as in letters — 'Yours faithfully' when the salutation is 'Dear Sir/Madam' (name unknown), 'Yours sincerely' when the salutation uses a name (e.g., 'Dear Mr. Sharma'). This distinction is tested in NEB exams even for email questions.

data.title: Notice Writing
notes: What Is a Notice?

A notice is a brief, formal announcement posted in a public place or distributed to inform a specific group of people about an event, rule, or important information. In the NEB Class 11 English examination, notice writing is a commonly tested skill, typically carrying 5-8 marks. A well-written notice is concise, clear, and follows a standard format that includes a heading, date, body, and issuing authority.
Format of a Notice

The standard notice format includes: (1) Heading/Title — the word 'NOTICE' centred at the top in capital letters. (2) Issuer's name/organisation — the name of the school, institution, or authority issuing the notice. (3) Date — the date of issue (usually placed below the heading or at the bottom left). (4) Subject/Heading line — a concise title describing the notice's purpose (e.g., 'Annual Sports Day', 'School Closure Notice'). (5) Body — the main content: what the notice is about, when and where it applies, any instructions or actions required. (6) Signature and designation — the name and position of the person issuing the notice (e.g., 'Principal', 'School Captain', 'Head Boy'). The body should be 50-80 words — concise and to the point.
Key Features of a Notice

A notice must be: (1) Concise — every word matters; avoid unnecessary details. (2) Clear — the message should be understood immediately. (3) Precise — include exact dates, times, and venues. (4) Formal — use formal language; no contractions, slang, or emotional language. (5) Action-oriented — state clearly what readers need to do (e.g., 'All students are requested to...', 'Participation is mandatory for...'). A notice is not an essay — it should not include explanations, anecdotes, or lengthy descriptions.
Types of Notices

Common types of notices in NEB exams include: (1) Event notice — announcing a school event (sports day, function, visit). 'Annual Sports Day is scheduled for 15th November 2024. All students are required to participate.' (2) Closure notice — informing about school closure. 'The school will remain closed on 15th August on account of Janai Purnima.' (3) Instruction notice — giving specific instructions. 'All students must submit their project reports by Friday.' (4) Lost and found notice — reporting a lost item or found object. 'A blue school bag has been found in the library. The owner may claim it from the office.' (5) Safety notice — warning about a hazard. 'Caution: Wet floor. Please exercise care.'
Notice Writing Tips for NEB Exams

To score well in notice writing: (1) Follow the format precisely — missing any element (date, heading, signature) costs marks. (2) Keep the body within 50-80 words — too short loses content marks; too long wastes time. (3) Use formal, impersonal language — 'It is informed that...' or 'All students are requested to...' (4) Include all necessary details — date, time, venue, action required. (5) Write the issuing authority's name and designation — e.g., 'Ramesh Sharma, School Captain'. (6) Underline the heading — the word 'NOTICE' should be underlined and centred. These conventions are strictly followed by NEB examiners.
Common Mistakes in Notice Writing

Avoid these errors: (1) Forgetting the word 'NOTICE' at the top. (2) Writing in the first person ('I have decided...') — notices are impersonal. (3) Using contractions ('don't', 'can't'). (4) Making the body too long — a notice is not an essay. (5) Forgetting the date — essential for any formal notice. (6) Not mentioning the issuing authority — always sign off with name and designation. (7) Using emotional language — notices are factual and formal. (8) Writing an incomplete sentence — every sentence should be grammatically complete.
confusion: Notice vs. Letter: A notice is a public announcement meant for a broad audience (all students, all residents). A letter is a private communication to a specific person or authority. Notices are posted publicly; letters are sent privately. Notices use formal, impersonal language; letters (especially informal ones) use personal language.

Notice vs. Advertisement: A notice informs about an event, rule, or loss. An advertisement promotes a product, service, or event to attract customers. Notices are issued by institutions (schools, colleges, government offices). Advertisements are issued by businesses or individuals. Notices are formal; advertisements are persuasive and may use creative language.

Notice vs. Report: A notice announces information to a specific group. A report provides a detailed account of an event, investigation, or situation, usually for an authority. Notices are brief (50-80 words); reports are longer (150-200 words) and include observations, findings, and recommendations.

Date placement in notices: The date can appear either below the heading (top right or left) or at the bottom left of the notice. Both placements are acceptable in NEB exams, but consistency is key — do not place the date in different positions in different notices.

Signature in notices: A notice must be signed with the issuer's name and designation (e.g., 'Ramesh Sharma, School Captain'). Unlike letters, notices do not use complimentary closes ('Yours faithfully'). The signature is simply the name and title of the issuing authority.

data.title: Paragraph Writing
notes: What Is a Paragraph?

A paragraph is a group of related sentences that develop a single central idea. It is the basic unit of composition in English writing. A well-written paragraph has three essential elements: a topic sentence (states the main idea), supporting sentences (provide details, examples, explanations), and a concluding sentence (summarises or transitions). In NEB English exams, paragraph writing questions typically carry 5-8 marks and require students to write a coherent paragraph on a given topic within 100-150 words.
The Topic Sentence

The topic sentence is usually the first sentence of the paragraph and states the main idea that the paragraph will develop. It should be specific enough to guide the paragraph but broad enough to allow development. A good topic sentence: 'Regular exercise has numerous physical and mental health benefits.' A weak topic sentence: 'Exercise is good.' The topic sentence acts as a promise to the reader about what the paragraph will discuss. In NEB exams, a clear topic sentence is essential for earning marks for organisation and coherence.
Supporting Sentences

Supporting sentences develop the main idea introduced in the topic sentence. They can provide: examples (e.g., 'For instance, running improves cardiovascular health'), details (e.g., 'A 30-minute walk daily can reduce the risk of heart disease by 30%'), explanations (e.g., 'Exercise releases endorphins, which improve mood and reduce stress'), facts/statistics (e.g., 'According to WHO, physical inactivity is the fourth leading risk factor for global mortality'). Each supporting sentence should relate directly to the topic sentence. Unrelated sentences weaken the paragraph's coherence and cost marks.
The Concluding Sentence

The concluding sentence wraps up the paragraph by restating the main idea in different words, summarising the key points, or providing a final thought. It should not introduce new information. Examples: 'Therefore, incorporating regular physical activity into daily routine is essential for maintaining overall health.' 'In summary, the benefits of exercise extend beyond physical fitness to mental well-being as well.' The concluding sentence gives the paragraph a sense of closure and helps the reader remember the main point.
Coherence and Unity

Coherence means the paragraph flows logically — ideas connect smoothly and readers can follow the progression. Unity means every sentence relates to the single main idea. Achieving coherence requires: (1) Logical order — arrange supporting sentences in a sensible sequence (chronological, spatial, order of importance, cause-effect). (2) Transitional words — use connectors like 'first', 'second', 'moreover', 'however', 'for example', 'consequently', 'in addition'. (3) Pronoun reference — use pronouns (it, they, this, these) to avoid repetition and create links between sentences. A paragraph lacking coherence reads like a list of unrelated statements.
Types of Paragraphs

Paragraphs can be classified by their purpose: Descriptive paragraph — paints a picture using sensory details (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste). 'The marketplace was a vibrant tapestry of colours and sounds — piles of bright red tomatoes, the pungent aroma of cumin and turmeric, the chatter of vendors hawking their wares.' Narrative paragraph — tells a short story or recounts an event. 'That morning, I woke up to find the streets covered in a thin layer of snow, a rare sight in Kathmandu.' Expository paragraph — explains or informs about a topic. 'Renewable energy sources, such as solar and hydroelectric power, are increasingly vital to Nepal's energy security.' Argumentative paragraph — presents a claim with supporting evidence. 'School uniforms should be mandatory because they promote equality, reduce distraction, and foster school spirit.'
Organisational Patterns

Paragraphs can be organised using different patterns: Chronological order — events in time sequence (first, then, next, finally). Space order — description arranged by location (left to right, top to bottom, near to far). Order of importance — most important to least important, or vice versa. Compare and contrast — similarities and differences between two subjects. Cause and effect — reasons and results. Problem and solution — a problem and its possible solutions. Choosing the right organisational pattern depends on the paragraph's purpose and the nature of the topic. In NEB exams, a logical organisational pattern is essential for coherence marks.
Avoiding Common Paragraph Errors

Common errors in paragraph writing include: (1) Fragment paragraphs — a single sentence that does not develop a full idea (more than one sentence is needed). (2) Run-on paragraphs — a paragraph that is too long and tries to cover too many ideas (keep to one main idea per paragraph). (3) Missing topic sentence — the reader cannot identify the main point. (4) Irrelevant sentences — sentences that do not support the main idea. (5) No conclusion — the paragraph ends abruptly without wrapping up. (6) Poor transitions — sentences feel disconnected. (7) Repetition — stating the same idea multiple times without adding new information. Each of these errors reduces the paragraph's effectiveness and earns fewer marks in NEB exams.
Paragraph Writing in NEB Exams

In the NEB English examination, paragraph writing is typically worth 5-8 marks. Students are given a topic (e.g., 'Write a paragraph on the benefits of reading newspapers') and expected to write 100-150 words. Marking criteria include: Content (relevance and development of ideas), Organisation (logical structure, coherence), Linguistic accuracy (grammar, spelling, punctuation), and Language (vocabulary, variety of sentences). A well-structured paragraph with relevant content, correct grammar, and smooth transitions can earn full or near-full marks. Practising paragraph writing on common topics is the best preparation strategy.
confusion: Paragraph vs. Essay: A paragraph develops a single main idea with topic sentence, supporting sentences, and conclusion. An essay develops multiple related ideas across multiple paragraphs with an introduction, body, and conclusion. A paragraph is a building block of an essay, not a complete composition on its own.

Topic sentence vs. Thesis statement: A topic sentence introduces the main idea of a single paragraph. A thesis statement introduces the main argument of an entire essay. Both serve as central statements, but at different levels of organisation. A paragraph can have only one topic sentence; an essay has one thesis statement.

Descriptive vs. Narrative paragraph: A descriptive paragraph focuses on painting a sensory picture (what something looks, sounds, smells like). A narrative paragraph focuses on telling a story or recounting events (what happened, in what order). A descriptive paragraph answers 'what is it like?'; a narrative paragraph answers 'what happened?'.

Unity vs. Coherence: Unity means all sentences relate to one main idea. Coherence means the sentences flow logically and connect smoothly. A paragraph can have unity (all sentences about exercise) but lack coherence (sentences in random order). Both are required for a good paragraph.

Concluding sentence vs. Summary: A concluding sentence wraps up the paragraph by restating the main idea or providing a final thought. A summary condenses the entire essay's main points. A paragraph's concluding sentence should not introduce new information — it should bring the paragraph to a natural close.

data.title: Report Writing
notes: What Is a Report?

A report is a factual account of an event, situation, or investigation, written for a specific audience (usually a teacher, principal, or authority). In the NEB Class 11 English examination, report writing typically carries 5-8 marks. Unlike essays or letters, reports are objective, formal, and structured — they present facts and observations without personal opinion or emotional language. A good report answers the questions: What happened? When? Where? Who was involved? What were the results?
Format of a Report

The standard report format includes: (1) Heading/Title — a clear, descriptive title (e.g., 'Report on the Annual Science Exhibition'). (2) Date — the date of writing (placed below the title or at the end). (3) Introduction — briefly state the purpose of the report and the event/situation being reported. (4) Body — present the facts in a logical order (chronological, thematic, or by importance). Use headings and subheadings if the report is long. (5) Conclusion — summarise the key findings or outcomes. (6) Signature and designation — the reporter's name and role (e.g., 'Ramesh Sharma, Class Representative'). The body should be 100-150 words for NEB exams.
Key Features of Report Writing

A report must be: (1) Objective — present facts without personal opinion or emotion. Use 'It was observed that...' instead of 'I think that...'. (2) Concise — include only relevant information; avoid unnecessary details. (3) Organised — use headings, subheadings, and logical order (chronological or thematic). (4) Formal — use formal language; no contractions, slang, or informal expressions. (5) Third-person — write in third person, not first person. (6) Past tense — reports describe events that have already happened, so past tense is standard. These features distinguish reports from essays and narratives.
Types of Reports

Common types of reports in NEB exams include: (1) Event report — reporting on a school event (sports day, function, visit). 'The Annual Sports Day was held on 15th November. The event began with the flag hoisting ceremony...' (2) Incident report — reporting on an accident or unexpected event. 'An incident occurred on 10th November when a tree fell on the school boundary wall during the night storm...' (3) Investigation report — reporting findings from an inquiry. 'An inquiry was conducted into the matter of missing laboratory equipment...' (4) Progress report — reporting on the status of a project. 'The construction of the new science lab is 70% complete...' Each type follows the same basic format but differs in content and focus.
Writing an Event Report

An event report describes a function, ceremony, or activity that took place. Structure: (1) Opening — state the event, date, venue, and purpose. 'The Annual Cultural Festival of our school was held on 20th November 2024 in the school auditorium.' (2) Body — describe the key activities in chronological order. 'The function began with the lighting of the ceremonial lamp by the principal. This was followed by cultural programmes including dance, drama, and song performances by students from different classes...' (3) Conclusion — summarise the outcome and express satisfaction. 'The event concluded with the prize distribution ceremony at 5:00 PM. The festival was a great success, reflecting the artistic talent of the students.' Keep the language formal and factual.
Writing an Incident Report

An incident report records an unexpected or unfortunate event. Structure: (1) Opening — state what happened, when, and where. 'An accident occurred on the morning of 5th November 2024 at approximately 8:30 AM on the school campus.' (2) Body — describe the sequence of events factually. 'A student from Class 10, Ram Maharjan, slipped on a wet floor near the science laboratory and fractured his left wrist. The incident was reported immediately to the school nurse...' (3) Conclusion — state the outcome and any recommendations. 'The student was admitted to nearby hospital. It is recommended that warning signs be placed on wet floors to prevent similar incidents.' Maintain an objective, impersonal tone throughout.
Common Mistakes in Report Writing

Avoid these errors: (1) Using first person ('I saw...', 'We organised...') — reports are third-person and objective. (2) Including personal opinions ('I think the event was wonderful') — reports present facts, not feelings. (3) Using contractions ('don't', 'wasn't') — use full forms. (4) Making it too long — a report should be concise (100-150 words for NEB). (5) Using emotional language ('tragic', 'heartbreaking') — remain objective. (6) Omitting key details — date, time, venue, people involved must be mentioned. (7) Not using headings — a report with headings is more professional and easier to read. (8) Writing in present tense — reports about past events use past tense.
Report Writing in NEB Exams

In the NEB English examination, report writing typically carries 5-8 marks. Marking is based on: Format (heading, date, structure), Content (relevant facts, completeness), Organisation (logical flow, headings), Linguistic accuracy (grammar, spelling, punctuation), and Tone (formal, objective, impersonal). Students who practise writing reports on common topics (events, incidents, investigations) are well-prepared for this question type. The key to success is maintaining objectivity and following the standard format precisely.
confusion: Report vs. Essay: A report presents facts objectively with headings and a structured format. An essay presents the author's argument or analysis with an introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion. Reports use past tense and third person; essays may use first person (in narrative/descriptive essays) and present tense. Reports are formal and factual; essays can be personal and argumentative.

Report vs. Notice: A notice is a brief announcement (50-80 words) posted publicly to inform about an event or rule. A report is a detailed account (100-150 words) of an event that has already occurred. Notices use future or present tense (announcing what will happen); reports use past tense (describing what happened). Notices have a 'NOTICE' heading; reports have a descriptive title.

Report vs. Narrative: A report presents facts in an objective, formal tone with headings. A narrative tells a story with a plot, characters, and a chronological sequence, often using first person and emotional language. Reports answer 'what happened?'; narratives answer 'what happened and how did it feel?' In NEB exams, reports are always objective; narratives are personal and descriptive.

Third person in reports: Reports must be written in the third person (he, she, it, they, the student, the principal). Never use first person (I, we, my, our) in a report. This is because reports are objective accounts, not personal stories. Using 'I' or 'we' makes the report subjective and informal, which loses marks.

Date placement in reports: Unlike letters (date below sender's address), reports typically place the date below the title or at the end of the report. In NEB exams, either placement is acceptable, but the date must be present. Forgetting the date is a common error that costs marks.

data.title: Exercise 5.2 - Q3 & Q6: Proof-Type Determinant Identities
notes: Question 3: Without expanding the determinants, show that the value of each of the following determinants is zero

General approach pattern: Look for a row/column that is a linear combination of others (common factor, sum of two other rows, etc.) using Row/Column Operations (Râ†’R+kR or Câ†’C+kC). If you can reduce any row or column entirely to zeros, the determinant is instantly 0 by Property that says a zero row/column gives zero determinant.
Solution:
$$\begin{vmatrix}6&1&9\\2&4&7\\18&3&27\end{vmatrix}$$
Notice Row 3 = 3 Ã— Row 1 (18=3Ã—6, 3=3Ã—1, 27=3Ã—9). Take 3 common from Row 3:
$$= 3\begin{vmatrix}6&1&9\\2&4&7\\6&1&9\end{vmatrix}$$
Now Row 1 = Row 3, so by Property (iii):
Proved.
Pattern to recognize: whenever one row/column is a multiple of another, factor out the multiple first â€” this immediately reveals identical rows.
(ii) Show |1 a b+c; 1 b c+a; 1 c a+b| = 0
Solution: Adding Column 2 into Column 3 (Câ‚ƒ â†’ Câ‚ƒ + Câ‚‚):
$$= \begin{vmatrix}1&a&a+b+c\\1&b&a+b+c\\1&c&a+b+c\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (a+b+c) common from Column 3:
$$= (a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}1&a&1\\1&b&1\\1&c&1\end{vmatrix}$$
Since Column 1 = Column 3 (both all 1's):
Proved.

Pattern to recognize: whenever you see 'x, y, x+y' type entries, try adding the other column/row to combine them into a constant sum like (a+b+c) â€” this is the single most common trick in this whole exercise.
(iii) Show |(aâˆ’b) (bâˆ’c) (câˆ’a); (bâˆ’c) (câˆ’a) (aâˆ’b); (câˆ’a) (aâˆ’b) (bâˆ’c)| = 0
Solution: Using Câ‚ƒ â†’ Câ‚‚ + Câ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}(a-b)&(b-c)&(b-c+c-a)\\(b-c)&(c-a)&(c-a+a-b)\\(c-a)&(a-b)&(a-b+b-c)\end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix}(a-b)&(b-c)&(b-a)\\(b-c)&(c-a)&(c-b)\\(c-a)&(a-b)&(a-c)\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (âˆ’1) common from Column 3 (since bâˆ’a = âˆ’(aâˆ’b), etc.):
$$= -\begin{vmatrix}(a-b)&(b-c)&(a-b)\\(b-c)&(c-a)&(b-c)\\(c-a)&(a-b)&(c-a)\end{vmatrix}$$
Since Column 1 = Column 3:
Proved.
(iv) Show |1 bc a(b+c); 1 ca b(c+a); 1 ab c(a+b)| = 0
Solution: Expanding a(b+c) = ab+ac, b(c+a) = bc+ab, c(a+b) = ac+bc, so Column 3 becomes:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}1&bc&bc+ab+ca\\1&ca&ca+bc+ab\\1&ab&ab+ca+bc\end{vmatrix}$$
Each entry in Column 3 equals (ab+bc+ca):
$$= (ab+bc+ca)\begin{vmatrix}1&bc&1\\1&ca&1\\1&ab&1\end{vmatrix}$$
Since Column 1 = Column 3:
$$= (ab+bc+ca) \times 0 = 0$$
Proved.
(v) Show |1 bc bc(b+c); 1 ca ac(c+a); 1 ab ab(a+b)| = 0
Solution: Multiply Row 1 by a, Row 2 by b, Row 3 by c (and divide the whole determinant by abc to compensate):
$$= \frac{1}{abc}\begin{vmatrix}a&abc&abc(b+c)\\b&abc&abc(c+a)\\c&abc&abc(a+b)\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking abc common from Column 2 and Column 3:
$$= \frac{1(abc) \cdot abc}{abc}\begin{vmatrix}a&1&a+b+c\\b&1&a+b+c\\c&1&a+b+c\end{vmatrix}$$
$$= abc\begin{vmatrix}a&1&a+b+c\\b&1&a+b+c\\c&1&a+b+c\end{vmatrix}$$
Using Câ‚ƒ â†’ Câ‚ƒ + aÃ—Câ‚, and then noting Câ‚‚ = Câ‚ƒ after simplification:
$$= abc(a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}a&1&1\\b&1&1\\c&1&1\end{vmatrix}$$
Since Column 2 = Column 3:
$$= abc(a+b+c) \times 0 = 0$$
Proved.
(vi) Show |1 Ï‰ Ï‰Â²; Ï‰ Ï‰Â² 1; Ï‰Â² 1 Ï‰| = 0 (where Ï‰ is a cube root of unity)

data.title: Angle Bisector — Worked Example (a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method)
notes: **Bisector equations.** The angle bisectors of the lines a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0 are (a₁x + b₁y + c₁)/√(a₁² + b₁²) = ± (a₂x + b₂y + c₂)/√(a₂² + b₂²).
**Equal distance property.** Any point on a bisector is equidistant from the two lines, using the perpendicular distance |ax + by + c|/√(a² + b²).
**Acute vs obtuse.** The two bisectors are perpendicular; when a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ < 0 the '+' combination bisects the acute angle, and when a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ > 0 it bisects the obtuse angle.
**Worked steps.** Write both equations in general form, divide each by the square root of the sum of its squared coefficients, combine with ±, and simplify each result.
**Use of the result.** The bisector equations locate the in-centre of a triangle (intersection of internal bisectors) and solve locus problems requiring equal distance from two lines.
**Coefficients:** a₁ = −1, b₁ = −2, a₂ = 4, b₂ = 2 (constant terms already made positive)
Since the result is negative, the (+) sign bisector is acute and the (−) sign bisector is obtuse
**Acute Bisector (+ sign):** 6x + 6y − 1 = 0
**Obtuse Bisector (− sign):** 2x − 2y + 19 = 0

data.title: Angle Bisector — Verifying with the tan θ Method
notes: As a cross-check, find the angle θ between one of the original lines and one candidate bisector using: tan θ = |(m₁ − m_b)/(1 + m₁·m_b)|, where m₁ is the original line's slope and m_b is the bisector's slope
**If tan θ < 1** (θ < 45°): since θ is half the angle between the two original lines, the total angle is less than 90°, so this bisector is the **acute** angle bisector
**If tan θ > 1** (θ > 45°): this bisector is the **obtuse** angle bisector
**Worked check:** slope of Bisector 1 (6x + 6y − 1 = 0) is m_b = −6/6 = −1; with the original line's slope m₁ = −1/2: tan θ = |(−1/2 − (−1))/(1 + (−1/2)(−1))| = |(1/2)/(3/2)| = 1/3
Since tan θ = 1/3 < 1, this confirms 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 is definitively the **acute angle bisector** — matching the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ method

data.title: Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs …
notes: **Fact.** Indeterminate forms 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞ → L'Hôpital: lim f/g = lim f'/g' (when applicable).
**Fact.** Standard limits: lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1; lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e; lim_{x→∞} (1 + a/x)^x = e^a.
**Fact.** Continuity: f continuous at c iff lim_{x→c}f(x) = f(c). Types of discontinuity: removable, jump, infinite.

**Removable discontinuity (hole):** The limit $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, but either $f(a)$ is undefined or $f(a) \neq \lim_{x \to a} f(x)$. The graph has a "hole" at $x = a$. Example: $f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ at $x = 1$.

**Jump discontinuity:** The left-hand and right-hand limits both exist but are not equal: $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$. The graph "jumps" at $x = a$. Example: the floor function $f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor$ at every integer.
**Infinite discontinuity (asymptotic):** At least one of the one-sided limits is $\pm \infty$. The graph has a vertical asymptote at $x = a$. Example: $f(x) = 1/x$ at $x = 0$.
**Essential (oscillatory) discontinuity:** The function oscillates infinitely near the point, so the limit does not exist in any sense. Example: $f(x) = \sin(1/x)$ at $x = 0$.
**Removable discontinuity fix:** If $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ but $f(a) \neq L$ or is undefined, define a new function $g(x) = f(x)$ for $x \neq a$ and $g(a) = L$. Then $g$ is continuous at $a$.
**Graph sketching tips for discontinuous functions:** Mark open circles (holes) at removable discontinuities, closed dots at defined points, and draw vertical dashed lines at vertical asymptotes.
**Definition:** A function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = a$ if all three conditions hold: (i) $f(a)$ is defined, (ii) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, (iii) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$.
**Informally:** A function is continuous at a point if you can draw its graph through that point without lifting your pencil.
**Continuity on an interval:** $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ if it is continuous at every point in $(a, b)$, right-continuous at $a$, and left-continuous at $b$.
**Continuity of standard functions:** All polynomial, rational (where defined), trigonometric (where defined), exponential, and logarithmic functions are continuous on their domains.
**Algebra of continuous functions:** If $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $x = a$, then $f + g$, $f - g$, $f \cdot g$, and $f/g$ (if $g(a) \neq 0$) are all continuous at $x = a$.
**Composition of continuous functions:** If $g$ is continuous at $a$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(a)$, then the composite function $f \circ g$ is continuous at $a$.
**Intermediate Value Theorem:** If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a) \neq f(b)$, then $f$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ at least once on $[a, b]$.

A removable discontinuity can be "fixed" by redefining the function at one point. Jump and infinite discontinuities cannot be removed this way.
The function $f(x) = \sin(1/x)$ for $x \neq 0$ and $f(0) = 0$ has an essential discontinuity at $x = 0$ — no matter how you define $f(0)$, the limit does not exist.
A vertical asymptote always indicates an infinite discontinuity, but not all discontinuities involve vertical asymptotes.
A function can be continuous at a point but not differentiable there (e.g., $f(x) = |x|$ at $x = 0$). Continuity is a weaker condition than differentiability.
A function can have a limit at a point without being continuous there — the function might be undefined at that point, or its value might differ from the limit.

data.title: Continuity of Function
notes: **The three conditions:** $f$ is continuous at $x=a$ if (i) $f(a)$ is DEFINED, (ii) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ EXISTS, and (iii) the two are EQUAL. All three are required, and naming which one fails is exactly how discontinuity is classified.

**Intuitively:** the graph has no hole, no jump and no break at $a$ — it can be drawn without lifting the pencil. Since this is a limit statement, a function can be continuous everywhere yet fail to be differentiable at a corner (the case $|x|$ at 0).
**Elementary functions:** polynomials are continuous everywhere, so $\lim_{x\to a}P(x)=P(a)$ by direct substitution. $\frac1x$, $\tan x$, roots and logarithms are continuous only where defined.
**Continuity of a piece:** the test is $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=f(a)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$. For piece-wise functions this value-matches-both-sides check is almost always what a question intends.
**Removable discontinuity:** the limit exists but $f(a)$ is undefined or differs from it. Assigning the missing value equal to the limit repairs the function — a strong hint the break is removable.

**Composite and inverse:** $g\circ f$ is continuous wherever $f$ is continuous and $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$; the inverse of a continuous one-to-one function is continuous on its range, which is why $\sqrt{\tan x}$ is continuous exactly where both parts are.
formulas: Continuity at $a$: $f(a)$ defined, $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$, and $f(a)=L$
One-sided test: $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=f(a)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$
Composite: $g\circ f$ continuous if $f$ is and $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$
Polynomial: $\lim_{x\to a}P(x)=P(a)$
confusion: Checking only that $f(a)$ is defined and declaring continuity — the limit must exist and match.
Conflating continuity with differentiability — $|x|$ at 0 is continuous but not differentiable.
Using a one-sided limit in place of the two-sided one at a join point.
universalFacts: The intermediate value theorem — a continuous function on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ — is why a graph with a hole can skip a root but a graph with a jump cannot.
Physical laws are modelled as continuous because the world is, to measurement precision, free of instantaneous jumps; discontinuities in models are usually deliberate idealisations.
keyPoints: All three conditions must hold; the failing one names the type of discontinuity.
Continuity does not imply differentiability — $|x|$ at 0 proves it.
Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational functions except where the denominator vanishes.
data.summary: Continuity at $a$ requires three things at once: $f(a)$ defined, the two-sided limit existing, and the two being equal. Polynomials and elementary functions are continuous on their domains and composite functions inherit continuity from their parts. Continuity is strictly weaker than differentiability, which is why $|x|$ is continuous but not differentiable at 0.
specialNotes: Where a formula is quoted it is valid only under the conditions stated; Checking only that $f(a)$ is defined and declaring continuity — the limit must exist and match.
Every result here follows from the definitions, so a first-principles derivation is always a valid fallback in the exam.
importantStatements: Statement 1: $f$ is continuous at $a$ only if $f(a)$ is defined, the limit exists, and they are equal.
Statement 2: Every polynomial is continuous everywhere on the real line.
Statement 3: Continuity does not imply differentiability.
Statement 4: A continuous function on $[a,b]$ attains every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
Statement 5: $g\circ f$ is continuous wherever both factors are continuous.
importantNotes: Topic anchor: Composite and inverse  $g circ f$ is continuous wherever $f$ is continuous and $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$; the inverse of a continuous one-to-one function is continuous on its range, which is why $ sqrt{ tan x}$ is cont
examShortTricks: When asked 'is it continuous at $a$?', name which of the three conditions fails rather than answering only 'no'.
A hole with a well-defined limit is removable — always check for that case first.
examNotes: Testing continuity of a piece-wise function at a join point is a standard 2–3 mark question.

mcs.question: At $x=0$, $f(x)=|x|$ is:
mcs.explanation: Both one-sided limits equal $f(0)=0$ so it is continuous; the left derivative $-1$ and right derivative $+1$ disagree, so no derivative exists.

mcs.question: $f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ at $x=2$ fails which continuity condition?
mcs.explanation: The limit exists and equals 4; the failing condition is that $f(2)$ is not defined.

mcs.question: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, which must be true?
mcs.explanation: The extreme value theorem guarantees it attains a maximum and minimum, hence boundedness. Differentiability does not follow.

importantConcepts: All three conditions must hold; the failing one names the type of discontinuity.
Continuity does not imply differentiability — $|x|$ at 0 proves it.
Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational functions except where the denominator vanishes.
importantTasks: Work through the authored practice problems and re-derive each key formula from the definition.
numericals:
**1. [Idea: a parameter must make the limit finite, and the point must then be defined]** Find all $a$ for which $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2+ax+3}{x-1}$ has a removable discontinuity at $x = 1$, and give the repaired value.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** For the limit to be finite the numerator must also vanish at 1:$^{ ullet}$ $1 + a + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow a = -4$.
ewline
ewline**Check:** with $a=-4$, $x^2-4x+3 = (x-1)(x-3)$, so $f(x)=x-3$ for $x
e1$, giving $\lim_{x	o1}f = -2$.
ewline
ewline$f(1)$ is still undefined, but the break is removable: assign $f(1)=-2$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $a=-4$, repaired value $f(1)=-2$. **Trap:** cancelling the denominator makes the limit finite, but the function is not continuous until the point itself is defined.

**2. [Idea: fewer equations than unknowns — parameterise the family]** The function $f(x)=\dfrac{ax^2+bx+c}{x-1}$ has a finite limit at $x=1$ equal to 2. Find $a,b,c$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Finite limit requires the numerator to vanish at 1:$^{ ullet}$ $a+b+c=0 \quad (i)$.
ewline
ewlineThe removable value equals the derivative ratio, set equal to 2:$^{ ullet}$ $2a+b = 2 \quad (ii)$.
ewline
ewlineTwo equations in three unknowns — the question is deliberately **under-determined**. From (ii) $b=2-2a$; from (i) $c=-a-b = a-2$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $a$ arbitrary, $b=2-2a$, $c=a-2$. **Check with $a=1$:** $\dfrac{x^2+3}{x-1}$, and $\lim_{x	o1} rac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=2$. ✓ **Lesson:** recognising under-determination and giving a one-parameter family is the skill tested.

**3. [Idea: exhibit both one-sided limits rather than assert them]** Show that $f(x)=\dfrac{2^{1/x}-1}{2^{-1/x}+1}$ has no limit as $x 	o 0$, and classify the discontinuity.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Put $u = 1/x$.$^{ ullet}$ **$x	o0^+$: $u	o+\infty$**, so $2^u 	o \infty$. Divide numerator and denominator by $2^u$:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0^+}\dfrac{2^u-1}{2^{-u}+1} = \lim\dfrac{1-2^{-u}}{2^{-u}+1} = \dfrac{1-0}{0+1} = 1$.$^{ ullet}$ **$x	o0^-$: $u	o-\infty$**, so $2^u 	o 0$. Numerator $	o -1$, denominator $	o 2$, giving $- rac12$.
ewline
ewlineThe one-sided limits are $1$ and $- rac12$ — both finite but UNEQUAL.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** no limit; a **JUMP** discontinuity of size $\left|1+ rac12ight| =  rac32$.

**4. [Idea: the derivative test resolves $0/0$ at any point where the numerator also vanishes]** Classify the discontinuity of $g(x)=\dfrac{\sin(\pi x)}{x(x-1)}$ at $x=0$ and at $x=1$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** The form is $ rac00$ at both, so apply the ratio-of-derivatives test.$^{ ullet}$ **At 0:** $\lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{2x-1} = \dfrac{\pi}{1} = \pi$. Finite ⇒ **removable**, $g(0)=\pi$.$^{ ullet}$ **At 1:** $\lim_{x	o1}\dfrac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{2x-1} = \dfrac{-\pi}{1} = -\pi$. Finite ⇒ **removable**, $g(1)=-\pi$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** removable at both, repaired values $\pi$ and $-\pi$. **Note:** the test succeeds at both points only because $\sin(\pi x)$ vanishes at BOTH $0$ and $1$; had it vanished at 0 but not 1, $x=1$ would have been an infinite discontinuity.

**5. [Idea: compose the two limit statements, and notice where the hypothesis is used]** $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, $g$ is continuous on $[c,d]$, and $f([a,b])\subseteq[c,d]$. Prove $g\circ f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Fix $x_0\in[a,b]$.$^{ ullet}$ $f$ continuous at $x_0$: $\lim_{x	o x_0}f(x)=f(x_0)$.$^{ ullet}$ $f(x_0)\in[c,d]$ and $g$ continuous there: $\lim_{u	o f(x_0)}g(u)=g(f(x_0))$.
ewline
ewline$^{ ullet}$ As $x	o x_0$, $f(x)	o f(x_0)$, so substituting $u=f(x)$ in the second statement gives$
ewline\lim_{x	o x_0}g(f(x)) = g(f(x_0))$.
ewline
ewlineThat is precisely continuity of $g\circ f$ at $x_0$, and $x_0$ was arbitrary.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $g\circ f$ continuous on $[a,b]$. **Where the hypothesis matters:** the inclusion $f([a,b])\subseteq[c,d]$ ensures the second limit is taken where $g$ is actually continuous — otherwise $f(x_0)$ could land on a hole in $g$.

data.title: Indeterminate Forms
notes: **What 'indeterminate' means:** a form like $0/0$ describes the SHAPE the expression takes as $x$ approaches the point, never its value. The same form can give $0$, $1$, $7$, $\infty$, or no limit at all. $\frac{x^2}{x}\to0$, $\frac{x^2}{x^2}\to1$ and $\frac{x}{x^2}\to\infty$ are all $0/0$.

**The seven forms:** $0/0$, $\infty/\infty$, $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty-\infty$, $\infty^0$, $0^0$, $1^\infty$. Everything else is determinate — $\frac{0}{5}=0$ and $\frac{5}{0}=\infty$ need no further work. $0\cdot\infty$ is the classic trap because each factor is a LIMIT rather than a value.
**Technique 1 — factorise and cancel:** find the common vanishing factor. $\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}=\lim\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=4$. For powers use $a^n-b^n=(a-b)(a^{n-1}+\dots+b^{n-1})$.

**Technique 2 — rationalise with the conjugate:** $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\lim\frac{1-\cos^2x}{x^2(1+\cos x)}=\lim\frac{\sin^2x}{x^2(1+\cos x)}=\frac12$. The conjugate is chosen so a difference of squares appears.

**Technique 3 — L'Hôpital:** for $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$, differentiate numerator and denominator SEPARATELY and take the limit of the ratio, provided that limit exists. $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ becomes $\frac{2x}{1}\to4$.
**Technique 4 — logs for $1^\infty$:** with $y=(1+f)^{g}$ and $f\to0$, take logs and use $\lim\frac{\ln(1+f)}{f}=1$, giving $\lim y = e^{\lim g\ln(1+f)}$. Hence $\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\frac1n)^n=e$.
formulas: Forms: $0/0$, $\infty/\infty$, $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty-\infty$, $1^\infty$, $0^0$, $\infty^0$
Conjugate: $\frac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}=\frac{\sin^2x}{1+\cos x}$
L'Hôpital: $\lim\frac{f}{g}=\lim\frac{f'}{g'}$ for $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$
$\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\frac{k}{n})^n = e^k$
confusion: Reading $0/0$ as the answer — it means substitution failed, and the limit may be anything.
Applying L'Hôpital to $0\cdot\infty$ or $\infty-\infty$ without first rewriting as a quotient.
Differentiating only the numerator and forgetting the denominator.
universalFacts: Euler's number is defined as a limit, $e=\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\frac1n)^n$ — the compound-interest form of the $1^\infty$ case.
Numerical differentiation avoids $f(x+h)-f(x)$ over $h$ precisely because at tiny $h$ this $0/0$ suffers catastrophic cancellation.
keyPoints: An indeterminate form is a shape, not a value.
Factorise, rationalise, or use L'Hôpital — never substitute and stop.
L'Hôpital applies only to $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$.
For $1^\infty$, take logarithms to reduce to a $0/0$ quotient.
data.summary: An indeterminate form describes the shape an expression takes near a point, never its value — the same $0/0$ may resolve to $0$, $1$, or nothing at all. Four techniques cover essentially every case: factorise and cancel, rationalise with a conjugate, apply L'Hôpital to $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$, and take logarithms for $1^\infty$.
specialNotes: L'Hôpital requires the derivative quotient's limit to EXIST; if it does not, the rule is silent and another technique is needed.
Some $1^\infty$ forms have no limit, so writing the form down never licenses the exponential answer.
importantStatements: Statement 1: $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$ are indeterminate, but $5/0$ and $0/5$ are determinate.
Statement 2: L'Hôpital's rule may be applied only to $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$ forms.
Statement 3: Differentiating both parts is only part of L'Hôpital — the resulting limit must exist.
Statement 4: $0\cdot\infty$ and $\infty-\infty$ must be rewritten as a quotient first.
Statement 5: $\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+\frac{k}{n})^n = e^k$.
importantNotes: Topic anchor: Technique 4 — logs for $1^ infty$  with $y=(1+f)^{g}$ and $f to0$, take logs and use $ lim frac{ ln(1+f)}{f}=1$, giving $ lim y = e^{ lim g ln(1+f)}$.
examShortTricks: Match technique to form: $0/0$ → factorise, rationalise or L'Hôpital; $1^\infty$ → logs; $0\cdot\infty$ and $\infty-\infty$ → rewrite as a quotient.
If the expression contains a root, reach for the conjugate first.
examNotes: Naming the correct technique for a given form is a frequent 2-mark question in the limits block.

Factorise, rationalise, or use L'Hôpital — never substitute and stop.

numericals:
**1. [Idea: the denominator's limit does not exist, so the limit cannot either]** Determine $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x^2}{2x^2 + \sin^2(1/x)}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Substitute: the numerator tends to $0$ and the denominator oscillates, so the form is not even $ rac00$ and L'Hôpital is unavailable. Divide by $x^2$:$
ewline\dfrac{1}{2 + \left( rac{\sin(1/x)}{x}ight)^2}$. Put $u = 1/x$, so $u 	o \infty$ and the squared term becomes $u^2\sin^2 u$.
ewline
ewline**Examine two sequences:**$^{ ullet}$ $x_n =  rac{1}{n\pi}$ gives $\sin u = 0$, so the fraction is exactly $ rac12$.$^{ ullet}$ $y_n =  rac{1}{ rac\pi2 + 2n\pi}$ gives $|\sin u| = 1$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{1}{2+y_n^2} 	o 0$.
ewline
ewlineSince the two sequences give different values, **the limit does not exist**.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** DNE. **This is the concept the question tests** — students who see $ rac00$ and reach for L'Hôpital get a wrong answer.

**2. [Idea: repeated L'Hôpital, one application per order of vanishing]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x - \sin x}{x^3}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$. The numerator vanishes to **third order** because $x - \sin x$ starts with the $x^3$ term, so exactly three applications are needed.$^{ ullet}$ 1st: $\lim\dfrac{1 - \cos x}{3x^2}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 2nd: $\lim\dfrac{\sin x}{6x}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 3rd: $\lim\dfrac{\cos x}{6} =  rac16$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac16$. **Warning:** a fourth application would be differentiating an already non-zero limit, which is meaningless.

**3. [Idea: substitute $t = 1/x$ to convert an infinity-limit into a zero-limit]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o \infty} x^3\left(	an^{-1}\dfrac1x - \dfrac1xight)$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Naive substitution gives $\infty^3 \cdot 0$, so a change of variable is required. Let $t =  rac1x$, so $t 	o 0$ and $x^3 =  rac1{t^3}$:$
ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{	an^{-1}t - t}{t^3}$, a $ rac00$ form.
ewline
ewlineL'Hôpital:$
ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1}{1+t^2} - 1}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1-(1+t^2)}{1+t^2}}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{-t^2}{3t^2(1+t^2)} = -\lim_{t	o0}\dfrac{1}{3(1+t^2)}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $- rac13$. **Check:** $	an^{-1}t = t -  rac{t^3}{3} + \cdots$, so the difference is $- rac{t^3}{3}$ and multiplying by $x^3= rac1{t^3}$ indeed gives $- rac13$.

data.title: Limits of a Function
notes: **Meaning of a limit:** $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means that as $x$ gets arbitrarily close to $a$ (from either side, and without ever requiring $x = a$) the value of $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$. The point $x=a$ may be undefined and the limit still exist — which is why $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$, undefined at 2, has limit 4.

**The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition:** for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $0 < |x-a| < \delta$ implies $|f(x)-L| < \varepsilon$. The condition $0 < |x-a|$ EXCLUDES the point itself, and that exclusion is exactly what makes a limit independent of $f(a)$.

**One-sided limits:** $\lim_{x \to a^-}$ approaches from below, $\lim_{x \to a^+}$ from above. The two-sided limit exists **if and only if** both exist and are equal. Equal-but-different still means no limit — a jump discontinuity is the standard counter-example.

**Indeterminate forms are signals, not answers:** $0/0$, $\infty-\infty$, $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty/\infty$, $1^\infty$, $0^0$, $\infty^0$ mean direct substitution FAILED. **1. [Idea: the denominator's limit does not exist, so the limit cannot either]** Determine $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x^2}{2x^2 + \sin^2(1/x)}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Substitute: the numerator tends to $0$ and the denominator oscillates, so the form is not even $ rac00$ and L'Hôpital is unavailable. Divide by $x^2$:$
ewline\dfrac{1}{2 + \left( rac{\sin(1/x)}{x}ight)^2}$. Put $u = 1/x$, so $u 	o \infty$ and the squared term becomes $u^2\sin^2 u$.
ewline
ewline**Examine two sequences:**$^{ ullet}$ $x_n =  rac{1}{n\pi}$ gives $\sin u = 0$, so the fraction is exactly $ rac12$.$^{ ullet}$ $y_n =  rac{1}{ rac\pi2 + 2n\pi}$ gives $|\sin u| = 1$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{1}{2+y_n^2} 	o 0$.
ewline
ewlineSince the two sequences give different values, **the limit does not exist**.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** DNE. **This is the concept the question tests** — students who see $ rac00$ and reach for L'Hôpital get a wrong answer.

**2. [Idea: repeated L'Hôpital, one application per order of vanishing]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x - \sin x}{x^3}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$. The numerator vanishes to **third order** because $x - \sin x$ starts with the $x^3$ term, so exactly three applications are needed.$^{ ullet}$ 1st: $\lim\dfrac{1 - \cos x}{3x^2}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 2nd: $\lim\dfrac{\sin x}{6x}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 3rd: $\lim\dfrac{\cos x}{6} =  rac16$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac16$. **Warning:** a fourth application would be differentiating an already non-zero limit, which is meaningless.

**3. [Idea: substitute $t = 1/x$ to convert an infinity-limit into a zero-limit]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o \infty} x^3\left(	an^{-1}\dfrac1x - \dfrac1xight)$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Naive substitution gives $\infty^3 \cdot 0$, so a change of variable is required. Let $t =  rac1x$, so $t 	o 0$ and $x^3 =  rac1{t^3}$:$
ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{	an^{-1}t - t}{t^3}$, a $ rac00$ form.
ewline
ewlineL'Hôpital:$
ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1}{1+t^2} - 1}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1-(1+t^2)}{1+t^2}}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{-t^2}{3t^2(1+t^2)} = -\lim_{t	o0}\dfrac{1}{3(1+t^2)}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $- rac13$. **Check:** $	an^{-1}t = t -  rac{t^3}{3} + \cdots$, so the difference is $- rac{t^3}{3}$ and multiplying by $x^3= rac1{t^3}$ indeed gives $- rac13$.

**4. [Idea: the $1^\infty$ family with a trigonometric inner function]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\left(1+\sin xight)^{ rac{1}{\sin x}}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Let $y = \left(1+\sin xight)^{1/\sin x}$ and take logarithms:$
ewline\ln y = \dfrac{\ln(1+\sin x)}{\sin x}$, which is $ rac00$.
ewline
ewlineL'Hôpital:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{ rac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}}{\cos x} = \lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x} = 1$.
ewline
ewlineSo $\ln y 	o 1$, hence $y 	o e$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $e$. **Check:** this is the general identity $\lim_{u	o0}(1+u)^{1/u}=e$ with $u = \sin x$.

**5. [Idea: the standard limit $\lim rac{e^u-1}{u}=1$ does all the work]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{2^{\sin^2 x} - 1}{x^2}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** The form is $ rac00$. Direct differentiation is circular, and a squeeze using $-x^2 \le \sin^2x \le x^2$ only bounds the expression by $ rac{2^{x^2}-1}{x^2}$, which tends to $\ln 2$ — **a non-zero bound proves nothing**.
ewline
ewlineConvert the base instead: $2^{\sin^2x} = e^{\sin^2x \ln 2}$. Set $u = \sin^2 x\,\ln 2$, so $u 	o 0$, and factor the expression into three pieces each with a known limit:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0}\underbrace{ rac{e^u-1}{u}}_{	o\,1}\cdot\underbrace{ rac{u}{\sin^2x}}_{	o\,\ln2}\cdot\underbrace{ rac{\sin^2x}{x^2}}_{	o\,1}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $1 	imes \ln 2 	imes 1 = \ln 2$. **Lesson:** when a squeeze bound tends to a non-zero constant, switch to factorisation.

**6. [Idea: chain an unknown function's limit through a rationalising identity]** Given $\lim_{x 	o 2}\dfrac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2} = 3$ and $f(2) = 6$, evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 2}\dfrac{f^2(x) - 36}{x^2-4}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$ and nothing can be computed without more information, so factor both sides:$^{ ullet}$ Numerator: $f^2(x)-36 = \left(f(x)-f(2)ight)\left(f(x)+f(2)ight)$ since $36 = f^2(2)$.$^{ ullet}$ Denominator: $x^2-4 = (x-2)(x+2)$.
ewline
ewlineThen$
ewline\lim_{x	o2}\dfrac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2}\cdot\dfrac{f(x)+f(2)}{x+2} = 3 \cdot \dfrac{6+6}{2+2} = 3 \cdot 3$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $9$.

data.title: Limits of a Function
notes: **Meaning of a limit:** $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means that as $x$ gets arbitrarily close to $a$ (from either side, and without ever requiring $x = a$) the value of $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$. The point $x=a$ may be undefined and the limit still exist — which is why $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$, undefined at 2, has limit 4.

**The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition:** for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $0 < |x-a| < \delta$ implies $|f(x)-L| < \varepsilon$. The condition $0 < |x-a|$ EXCLUDES the point itself, and that exclusion is exactly what makes a limit independent of $f(a)$.

**One-sided limits:** $\lim_{x \to a^-}$ approaches from below, $\lim_{x \to a^+}$ from above. The two-sided limit exists **if and only if** both exist and are equal. Equal-but-different still means no limit — a jump discontinuity is the standard counter-example.

**Indeterminate forms are signals, not answers:** $0/0$, $\infty-\infty$, $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty/\infty$, $1^\infty$, $0^0$, $\infty^0$ mean direct substitution FAILED. Rewrite instead: factorise and cancel, rationalise with the conjugate, divide by the highest vanishing power, or use $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$.

**Infinite limits and asymptotes:** $\infty$ is never a value, only shorthand for unbounded growth. Opposite-sign one-sided limits give a VERTICAL asymptote; a finite limit at infinity gives a HORIZONTAL asymptote, found by the dominant-term rule.
**Sum and difference:** if $\lim f = L$ and $\lim g = M$ then $\lim(f\pm g)=L\pm M$. Limits commute with addition because they preserve the arithmetic structure of the reals.

**Product and quotient:** $\lim(fg)=LM$ and, provided $M\ne0$, $\lim\frac{f}{g}=\frac{L}{M}$. The condition $M\ne0$ is the whole reason $0/0$ is indeterminate — the product law guarantees $0$ while the quotient law is unavailable.

**Constant multiple and power:** $\lim(cf)=cL$ and $\lim f^n=L^n$. An even root additionally needs a non-negative limit, while an odd root does not, so sign information about $L$ decides whether $\lim\sqrt[n]{f}$ exists.

**Composition:** if $\lim f=L$ and $g$ is continuous at $L$ then $\lim g(f(x))=g(L)$. This licenses substituting into a continuous outer function, and it is why a discontinuous $g$ such as $\tan$ at $\pi/2$ breaks the rule.

**Squeeze (sandwich) theorem:** if $g(x)\le f(x)\le h(x)$ near $a$ and $\lim g=\lim h=L$ then $\lim f=L$. This is the only reliable tool for a vanishing factor times an oscillating one, and it proves $\lim_{x\to0}x\sin\frac1x=0$ from $-|x|\le x\sin\frac1x\le|x|$.

**Why the laws survive discontinuity:** none of these need $f$ defined at $a$, only the limits to exist. That is exactly why a removable discontinuity does not spoil a limit, while a jump does — unequal one-sided limits mean the laws cannot be applied at all.

**The three conditions:** $f$ is continuous at $x=a$ if (i) $f(a)$ is DEFINED, (ii) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ EXISTS, and (iii) the two are EQUAL. All three are required, and naming which one fails is exactly how discontinuity is classified.

**Intuitively:** the graph has no hole, no jump and no break at $a$ — it can be drawn without lifting the pencil. Since this is a limit statement, a function can be continuous everywhere yet fail to be differentiable at a corner (the case $|x|$ at 0).
**Elementary functions:** polynomials are continuous everywhere, so $\lim_{x\to a}P(x)=P(a)$ by direct substitution. $\frac1x$, $\tan x$, roots and logarithms are continuous only where defined.
**Continuity of a piece:** the test is $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=f(a)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$. For piece-wise functions this value-matches-both-sides check is almost always what a question intends.
**Removable discontinuity:** the limit exists but $f(a)$ is undefined or differs from it. Assigning the missing value equal to the limit repairs the function — a strong hint the break is removable.

**Composite and inverse:** $g\circ f$ is continuous wherever $f$ is continuous and $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$; the inverse of a continuous one-to-one function is continuous on its range, which is why $\sqrt{\tan x}$ is continuous exactly where both parts are.

ewline**Solution:** Substitute: the numerator tends to $0$ and the denominator oscillates, so the form is not even $ rac00$ and L'Hôpital is unavailable. Divide by $x^2$:$
ewline\dfrac{1}{2 + \left( rac{\sin(1/x)}{x}ight)^2}$. Put $u = 1/x$, so $u 	o \infty$ and the squared term becomes $u^2\sin^2 u$.
ewline
ewline**Examine two sequences:**$^{ ullet}$ $x_n =  rac{1}{n\pi}$ gives $\sin u = 0$, so the fraction is exactly $ rac12$.$^{ ullet}$ $y_n =  rac{1}{ rac\pi2 + 2n\pi}$ gives $|\sin u| = 1$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{1}{2+y_n^2} 	o 0$.
ewline
ewlineSince the two sequences give different values, **the limit does not exist**.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** DNE. **This is the concept the question tests** — students who see $ rac00$ and reach for L'Hôpital get a wrong answer.

**2. [Idea: repeated L'Hôpital, one application per order of vanishing]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{x - \sin x}{x^3}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$. The numerator vanishes to **third order** because $x - \sin x$ starts with the $x^3$ term, so exactly three applications are needed.$^{ ullet}$ 1st: $\lim\dfrac{1 - \cos x}{3x^2}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 2nd: $\lim\dfrac{\sin x}{6x}$ — still $ rac00$.$^{ ullet}$ 3rd: $\lim\dfrac{\cos x}{6} =  rac16$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac16$. **Warning:** a fourth application would be differentiating an already non-zero limit, which is meaningless.

**3. [Idea: substitute $t = 1/x$ to convert an infinity-limit into a zero-limit]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o \infty} x^3\left(	an^{-1}\dfrac1x - \dfrac1xight)$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Naive substitution gives $\infty^3 \cdot 0$, so a change of variable is required. Let $t =  rac1x$, so $t 	o 0$ and $x^3 =  rac1{t^3}$:$
ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{	an^{-1}t - t}{t^3}$, a $ rac00$ form.
ewline
ewlineL'Hôpital:$
ewline\lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1}{1+t^2} - 1}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{ rac{1-(1+t^2)}{1+t^2}}{3t^2} = \lim_{t 	o 0}\dfrac{-t^2}{3t^2(1+t^2)} = -\lim_{t	o0}\dfrac{1}{3(1+t^2)}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $- rac13$. **Check:** $	an^{-1}t = t -  rac{t^3}{3} + \cdots$, so the difference is $- rac{t^3}{3}$ and multiplying by $x^3= rac1{t^3}$ indeed gives $- rac13$.

**4. [Idea: the $1^\infty$ family with a trigonometric inner function]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\left(1+\sin xight)^{ rac{1}{\sin x}}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Let $y = \left(1+\sin xight)^{1/\sin x}$ and take logarithms:$
ewline\ln y = \dfrac{\ln(1+\sin x)}{\sin x}$, which is $ rac00$.
ewline
ewlineL'Hôpital:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{ rac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}}{\cos x} = \lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x} = 1$.
ewline
ewlineSo $\ln y 	o 1$, hence $y 	o e$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $e$. **Check:** this is the general identity $\lim_{u	o0}(1+u)^{1/u}=e$ with $u = \sin x$.

**5. [Idea: the standard limit $\lim rac{e^u-1}{u}=1$ does all the work]** Evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 0}\dfrac{2^{\sin^2 x} - 1}{x^2}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** The form is $ rac00$. Direct differentiation is circular, and a squeeze using $-x^2 \le \sin^2x \le x^2$ only bounds the expression by $ rac{2^{x^2}-1}{x^2}$, which tends to $\ln 2$ — **a non-zero bound proves nothing**.
ewline
ewlineConvert the base instead: $2^{\sin^2x} = e^{\sin^2x \ln 2}$. Set $u = \sin^2 x\,\ln 2$, so $u 	o 0$, and factor the expression into three pieces each with a known limit:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0}\underbrace{ rac{e^u-1}{u}}_{	o\,1}\cdot\underbrace{ rac{u}{\sin^2x}}_{	o\,\ln2}\cdot\underbrace{ rac{\sin^2x}{x^2}}_{	o\,1}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $1 	imes \ln 2 	imes 1 = \ln 2$. **Lesson:** when a squeeze bound tends to a non-zero constant, switch to factorisation.

**6. [Idea: chain an unknown function's limit through a rationalising identity]** Given $\lim_{x 	o 2}\dfrac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2} = 3$ and $f(2) = 6$, evaluate $\lim_{x 	o 2}\dfrac{f^2(x) - 36}{x^2-4}$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Direct substitution gives $ rac00$ and nothing can be computed without more information, so factor both sides:$^{ ullet}$ Numerator: $f^2(x)-36 = \left(f(x)-f(2)ight)\left(f(x)+f(2)ight)$ since $36 = f^2(2)$.$^{ ullet}$ Denominator: $x^2-4 = (x-2)(x+2)$.
ewline
ewlineThen$
ewline\lim_{x	o2}\dfrac{f(x)-f(2)}{x-2}\cdot\dfrac{f(x)+f(2)}{x+2} = 3 \cdot \dfrac{6+6}{2+2} = 3 \cdot 3$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $9$.

**1. [Idea: a parameter must make the limit finite, and the point must then be defined]** Find all $a$ for which $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2+ax+3}{x-1}$ has a removable discontinuity at $x = 1$, and give the repaired value.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** For the limit to be finite the numerator must also vanish at 1:$^{ ullet}$ $1 + a + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow a = -4$.
ewline
ewline**Check:** with $a=-4$, $x^2-4x+3 = (x-1)(x-3)$, so $f(x)=x-3$ for $x
e1$, giving $\lim_{x	o1}f = -2$.
ewline
ewline$f(1)$ is still undefined, but the break is removable: assign $f(1)=-2$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $a=-4$, repaired value $f(1)=-2$. **Trap:** cancelling the denominator makes the limit finite, but the function is not continuous until the point itself is defined.

**2. [Idea: fewer equations than unknowns — parameterise the family]** The function $f(x)=\dfrac{ax^2+bx+c}{x-1}$ has a finite limit at $x=1$ equal to 2. Find $a,b,c$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Finite limit requires the numerator to vanish at 1:$^{ ullet}$ $a+b+c=0 \quad (i)$.
ewline
ewlineThe removable value equals the derivative ratio, set equal to 2:$^{ ullet}$ $2a+b = 2 \quad (ii)$.
ewline
ewlineTwo equations in three unknowns — the question is deliberately **under-determined**. From (ii) $b=2-2a$; from (i) $c=-a-b = a-2$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $a$ arbitrary, $b=2-2a$, $c=a-2$. **Check with $a=1$:** $\dfrac{x^2+3}{x-1}$, and $\lim_{x	o1} rac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=2$. ✓ **Lesson:** recognising under-determination and giving a one-parameter family is the skill tested.

**3. [Idea: exhibit both one-sided limits rather than assert them]** Show that $f(x)=\dfrac{2^{1/x}-1}{2^{-1/x}+1}$ has no limit as $x 	o 0$, and classify the discontinuity.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Put $u = 1/x$.$^{ ullet}$ **$x	o0^+$: $u	o+\infty$**, so $2^u 	o \infty$. Divide numerator and denominator by $2^u$:$
ewline\lim_{x	o0^+}\dfrac{2^u-1}{2^{-u}+1} = \lim\dfrac{1-2^{-u}}{2^{-u}+1} = \dfrac{1-0}{0+1} = 1$.$^{ ullet}$ **$x	o0^-$: $u	o-\infty$**, so $2^u 	o 0$. Numerator $	o -1$, denominator $	o 2$, giving $- rac12$.
ewline
ewlineThe one-sided limits are $1$ and $- rac12$ — both finite but UNEQUAL.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** no limit; a **JUMP** discontinuity of size $\left|1+ rac12ight| =  rac32$.

**4. [Idea: the derivative test resolves $0/0$ at any point where the numerator also vanishes]** Classify the discontinuity of $g(x)=\dfrac{\sin(\pi x)}{x(x-1)}$ at $x=0$ and at $x=1$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** The form is $ rac00$ at both, so apply the ratio-of-derivatives test.$^{ ullet}$ **At 0:** $\lim_{x	o0}\dfrac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{2x-1} = \dfrac{\pi}{1} = \pi$. Finite ⇒ **removable**, $g(0)=\pi$.$^{ ullet}$ **At 1:** $\lim_{x	o1}\dfrac{\pi\cos(\pi x)}{2x-1} = \dfrac{-\pi}{1} = -\pi$. Finite ⇒ **removable**, $g(1)=-\pi$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** removable at both, repaired values $\pi$ and $-\pi$. **Note:** the test succeeds at both points only because $\sin(\pi x)$ vanishes at BOTH $0$ and $1$; had it vanished at 0 but not 1, $x=1$ would have been an infinite discontinuity.

**5. [Idea: compose the two limit statements, and notice where the hypothesis is used]** $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, $g$ is continuous on $[c,d]$, and $f([a,b])\subseteq[c,d]$. Prove $g\circ f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Fix $x_0\in[a,b]$.$^{ ullet}$ $f$ continuous at $x_0$: $\lim_{x	o x_0}f(x)=f(x_0)$.$^{ ullet}$ $f(x_0)\in[c,d]$ and $g$ continuous there: $\lim_{u	o f(x_0)}g(u)=g(f(x_0))$.
ewline
ewline$^{ ullet}$ As $x	o x_0$, $f(x)	o f(x_0)$, so substituting $u=f(x)$ in the second statement gives$
ewline\lim_{x	o x_0}g(f(x)) = g(f(x_0))$.
ewline
ewlineThat is precisely continuity of $g\circ f$ at $x_0$, and $x_0$ was arbitrary.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $g\circ f$ continuous on $[a,b]$. **Where the hypothesis matters:** the inclusion $f([a,b])\subseteq[c,d]$ ensures the second limit is taken where $g$ is actually continuous — otherwise $f(x_0)$ could land on a hole in $g$.

data.title: Trigonometric Equations and General Values
formulas: **Multiple & Submultiple Angles — the complete formula sheet for NEB.**
**Double angles — 2A**
$$\sin 2A = 2\sin A\cos A$$
$$\cos 2A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 A$$
$$\cos 2A = \frac{1-\tan^2 A}{1+\tan^2 A}$$
$$\sin 2A = \frac{2\tan A}{1+\tan^2 A}$$
$$\tan 2A = \frac{2\tan A}{1-\tan^2 A}$$
$$\cot 2A = \frac{\cot^2 A - 1}{2\cot A}$$
$$\sec 2A = \frac{1+\tan^2 A}{1-\tan^2 A}, \qquad \csc 2A = \frac{1+\tan^2 A}{2\tan A}$$
**Power & product rewiring — the bridge to submultiple angles**
$$\sin A\cos A = \frac{1}{2}\sin 2A$$
$$1 - \cos 2A = 2\sin^2 A, \qquad 1 + \cos 2A = 2\cos^2 A$$
$$\sin^2 A = \frac{1-\cos 2A}{2}, \qquad \cos^2 A = \frac{1+\cos 2A}{2}$$
$$\sin^2 A - \cos^2 A = -\cos 2A$$
**Triple angles — 3A**
$$\sin 3A = 3\sin A - 4\sin^3 A$$
$$\cos 3A = 4\cos^3 A - 3\cos A$$
$$\tan 3A = \frac{3\tan A - \tan^3 A}{1 - 3\tan^2 A}$$
$$\cot 3A = \frac{3\cot A - \cot^3 A}{3\cot^2 A - 1}$$
**Quadruple angles — 4A**
$$\sin 4A = 2\sin 2A\cos 2A = 4\sin A\cos A\cos 2A$$
$$\tan 4A = \frac{4\tan A - 4\tan^3 A}{1 - 6\tan^2 A + \tan^4 A}$$
**Submultiple angles — A/2**
$$\sin\frac{A}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos A}{2}}$$
$$\cos\frac{A}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos A}{2}}$$
$$\tan\frac{A}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos A}{1+\cos A}} = \frac{\sin A}{1+\cos A} = \frac{1-\cos A}{\sin A}$$
$$\cot\frac{A}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos A}{1-\cos A}} = \frac{\sin A}{1-\cos A} = \frac{1+\cos A}{\sin A}$$
$$\tan\frac{A}{2} = \csc A - \cot A, \qquad \cot\frac{A}{2} = \csc A + \cot A$$
$$1 - \cos A = 2\sin^2\frac{A}{2}, \qquad 1 + \cos A = 2\cos^2\frac{A}{2}$$
$$\sin A = 2\sin\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{A}{2}, \qquad \cos A = \cos^2\frac{A}{2} - \sin^2\frac{A}{2}$$
**± rule:** in $\sin\frac A2$, $\cos\frac A2$ and $\tan\frac A2$ take $+$ or $-$ from the quadrant in which $\frac A2$ lies — $A/2$ is not automatically acute.
**Any angle $nA$ — de Moivre, the source of every formula above**
$$\left(\cos A + i\sin A\right)^n = \cos nA + i\sin nA$$

Expand the left side with the binomial theorem and match the real and imaginary parts: $\cos nA$ and $\sin nA$ fall out as polynomials in $\sin A$ and $\cos A$ — that is exactly how the 2A, 3A and 4A identities above are generated.

data.title: शव्द-स्रोत (Word Sources)
notes: शब्दको परिभाषा (Definition of Word): एउटा वा एउटाभन्दा बढी अक्षरहरू मिलेर बनेको अर्थबोधक ध्वनिमय संयोजनलाई 'शब्द' भनिन्छ। शब्द नै भाषाको सबैभन्दा सानो इकाइ हो, जसलाई अझ सानो भागमा विभाजित गर्दा अर्थ नहोस्। नेपाली भाषामा शब्दहरू विभिन्न स्रोतबाट आएका छन् जुन भाषाको समृद्धिमा योगदान पुगेका छन्।

शब्दको उद्गम (Origin of Word): शब्दको उद्गम भनेको कुन भाषा वा कुन मूलबाट शब्दले जन्म लिएको छ भन्ने कुरा हो। नेपाली भाषाको शब्दभण्डारमा संस्कृत, प्राकृत, अपभ्रंश र अन्य भाषाहरूबाट आएका शब्दहरू समावेश छन्। शब्दको स्रोत थाहा पाउनु भाषाको ऐतिहासिक विकास बुझ्न र शब्दको शुद्ध प्रयोग गर्नका लागि आवश्यक छ।

शव्दको वर्गीकरण (Classification of Words by Source): शब्दको उद्गम स्रोतको आधारमा शब्दहरूलाई मुख्यतया तीन भागमा वर्गीकरण गरिएको छ: (१) तत्सम शब्दहरू — जो संस्कृतका शुद्ध रूपमा नेपालीमा प्रयोग हुने, (२) तद्भव शब्दहरू — जो संस्कृतबाट नेपाली स्वरूपमा विकसित भएर आएका, (३) आगन्तुक शब्दहरू — जो अरबୀ-फारसी, अंग्रेजी वा अन्य भाषाबाट आएका हुन्।

तत्सम शब्दहरू (Tatsama Words): तत्सम शब्दहरू भनेको संस्कृतका ती शब्दहरू हुन् जुन उच्चारण, वर्तनी, लिङ्ग-वचन-विभक्ति सबै पक्षमा संस्कृतकै रूपमा नेपाली भाषामा प्रयोग हुन्छन्। उदाहरण: पुस्तक (पुस्तक), विद्यालय (विद्यालय), शिक्षक (शिक्षक), ज्ञान (ज्ञान), धर्म (धर्म), कर्म (कर्म), सत्य (सत्य), अस्तित्व (अस्तित्व), शासन (शासन), आत्म (आत्मा)। यी शब्दहरूको वर्तनी संस्कृत नियमअनुसार हुन्छ।

तत्सम शब्दको पहिचान (Identifying Tatsama Words): तत्सम शब्दहरू पहिचान गर्नका लागि निम्न आधारहरू प्रयोग गरिन्छ: (१) चन्द्रबिन्दु (ं) र विस्गर्ग (ः) भएको शब्द तत्सम हुन्छ, (२) श, ष, ञ, ठ, ड, ण जस्ता वर्णहरू संस्कृत वर्तनीमा हुन्छन्, (३) बहुवचनमा 'हरू', 'हरू' प्रत्यय थपिन्छ, (४) शब्दको सम्पूर्ण रूप संस्कृतमै पाइन्छ। उदाहरण: 'विद्या' → 'विद्याहरू', 'शिक्षा' → 'शिक्षाहरू'।

तद्भव शब्दहरू (Tadbhava Words): तद्भव शब्दहरू भनेको संस्कृतका ती शब्दहरू हुन् जुन कालक्रममा प्राकृत, अपभ्रंश हुँदै आधुनिक नेपाली भाषामा पुगेका र आफ्नो मूल रूप त्यागेर नयाँ रूप लिएका हुन्। 'तद्भव' शब्दको अर्थ 'यसबाट भएको' वा 'यसबाट निस्किएको' हो। उदाहरण: संस्कृत 'दुग्ध' → नेपाली 'दूध', 'पत्र' → 'चिट', 'नाग' → 'साप', 'मत्स्य' → 'माछा', 'गगन' → 'आकाश', 'अश्व' → 'घोडा'।

तद्भव शब्दको पहिचान (Identifying Tadbhava Words): तद्भव शब्द पहिचान गर्ने आधारहरू: (१) चन्द्रबिन्दु र विस्गर्ग हुँदैन, (२) र्रे (र्), रे (रे), ककार परिवर्तन हुन्छ, (३) श, ष, ज, भ, य, र, ल, व जस्ता संस्कृत वर्णहरू नेपालीमा परिवर्तित भएर आउँछन्, (४) शब्द छोटो र सरल हुन्छ, (५) शब्दको अन्त्यमा स्वतन्त्र स्वर हुन्छ। उदाहरण: 'चिट' (पत्र), 'साँवा' (श्याम), 'आँखा' (नेत्र), 'कान' (कर्ण)।

तद्भव शब्दको परिवर्तन प्रकार (Types of Tadbhava Changes): तद्भव शब्दहरूमा निम्न प्रकारका परिवर्तनहरू देखिन्छन्: (१) स्वर परिवर्तन — जैसे: गगन → आकाश, (२) व्यञ्जन परिवर्तन — जैसे: पत्र → चिट, (३) स्वर-व्यञ्जन दुवैको परिवर्तन — जैसे: नाग → साप, (४) रूप परिवर्तन — जैसे: वक्षस् → छाती, (५) शब्द लोप — जैसे: सन्तान → सन्तान, (६) शब्द थप — जैसे: पिता → बुबा/आमा, (७) अर्थ परिवर्तन — जैसे: अश्व → घोडा।

आगन्तुक शब्दहरू (Aagantuk Words): आगन्तुक शब्दहरू भनेको नेपाली भाषाको आफ्नै मूल नभएर अन्य भाषाहरूबाट लिएका शब्दहरू हुन्। यी शब्दहरू मुख्यतया दुई विभागमा पर्छन्: (क) स्वदेशी आगन्तुक — हिन्दी, उर्दू, बङ्गाली, मराठी, गुजराती, तमिल, तेलुगु, मल्यालम, सिन्धी लगायत भारतीय भाषाहरूबाट आएका, (ख) विदेशी आगन्तुक — अंग्रेजी, अरबी-फारसी, फ्रान्सेली, पोर्चुगীज, जर्मान, जापानी, चीनीबाट आएका।

अरबी-फारसी आगन्तुक शब्दहरू (Arabic-Persian Loanwords): इस्लामको प्रभाव र मुगलकालीन शासनकालमा अरबी-फारसी शब्दहरू नेपाली भाषामा प्रवेश गरे। उदाहरण: अल्लाह, अलफ़, अमीर, अद्ल, इल्म, इन्साफ, इसलाम, इकराम, इकबाल, इकरार, इज्जत, अहवाल, इबादत, हुकुम, नसीब, दौलत, जहान, फितना, किस्मत, ख्वाजा। यी शब्दहरू धर्म, प्रशासन, साहित्य र दैनिक बोलचालमा प्रयोग हुन्छन्।

अंग्रेजी आगन्तुक शब्दहरू (English Loanwords): अंग्रेजी शासनकाल र आधुनिकीकरणसँगै अंग्रेजी शब्दहरू नेपाली भाषामा व्यापक रूपमा प्रवेश गरे। उदाहरण: अफिस (office), अलमारी (almirah/cupboard), एम्बुलेन्स (ambulance), एनिमल (animal), एजुकेशन (education), एक्ट (act), एक्टर (actor), एडिट (edit), एडमिन (admin), एप (app), बेस (base), बोर्ड (board), कम्प्यूटर (computer), डिग्री (degree), एक्साम (exam), फोन (phone), हस्पितल (hospital), इन्जिन (engine), नेटवर्क (network)।

अन्य विदेशी आगन्तुक शब्दहरू (Other Foreign Loanwords): पोर्चुगिसबाट: केशर (cauliflower), काजू (cashew), प्याज (pyaz/onion), बोटल (bottle), जेब (pocket), ड्रेस (dress), बेल्ट (belt)। फ्रान्सेलीबाट: गोभी (cabbage), फ्रेन्च फ्राइज, ब्रेड (bread)। जर्मनबाट: बोक्स (box), बैग (bag)। जापानीबाट: सुशी (sushi), कमि (kami), टेकि (take)। चीनीबाट: नूडल्स (noodles)। यी शब्दहरू आधुनिक जीवन, खाना, पोशाक र प्रविधिसँग सम्बन्धित छन्।

आगन्तुक शब्दको विशंस्कृतिकरण (Sanitization of Loanwords): आगन्तुक शब्दहरू नेपाली भाषाको ढाँचामा परिर्वतन भएर विशंस्कृत हुँदै आएका छन्। जस्तै: अंग्रेजी 'pocket' → 'जेब', 'bag' → 'ब्याग', 'bus' → 'बस', 'car' → 'कार', 'phone' → 'फोन', 'computer' → 'कम्प्युटर', 'electric' → 'इलेक्ट्रिक', 'radio' → 'रेडियो'। यो प्रक्रियाले आगन्तुक शब्दहरू नेपाली उच्चारण, वर्तनी र व्याकरणसँग मिल्दै जान्छन्।

आगन्तुक शब्दको उच्चारण नियम (Pronunciation Rules for Loanwords): आगन्तुक शब्दहरू उच्चारण गर्दा नेपाली ध्वनि प्रणालीअनुसार परिवर्तन हुन्छ: (१) अंग्रेजी 'th' ध्वनि → 'थ' वा 'द' (the → थ, three → थ्री), (२) 'v' ध्वनि → 'ब' वा 'भ' (very → बेरी, van → बन), (३) 'f' ध्वनि → 'फ' (farm → फार्म), (४) 'w' ध्वनि → 'व' (water → वटर), (५) 'z' ध्वनि → 'ज' (zoo → झू)। यसले आगन्तुक शब्दहरू नेपाली भाषामा स्वाभाविक लाग्छ।

शब्द निर्माणका माध्यमहरू (Means of Word Formation): नेपाली भाषामा शब्द निर्माणका विभिन्न माध्यमहरू छन्: (१) उपसर्ग जोड्द्वारा — प्रति+पत्र = प्रतिलिपी, सम+गर् = समग्र, (२) प्रत्यय जोड्द्वारा — गुरु + य = गुरुय, राज + इन् = राजिन, (३) समास बनाउँद्वारा — राजा+पुरुष = राजapurush, (४) द्वन्द्व समास — राम+लक्ष्मण = रामलक्ष्मण, (५) तत्पुरुष समास — राजाको पुरुष = राजapurush, (६) कर्मधारय समास — सुन्दर घर = सुन्दरगृह।

शब्दभण्डारको समृद्धि (Enrichment of Word Bank): नेपाली भाषाको शब्दभण्डार संस्कृत, प्राकृत, अपभ्रंश, अरबो-फारसी, अंग्रेजी र स्थानीय भाषाहरूबाट आएका शब्दहरूले भरिपूर्ण छ। यी सबै स्रोतहरूले नेपाली भाषालाई समृद्ध बनाएका छन्। शब्दभण्डारको समृद्धिले भाषाको विकास र विस्तारमा मद्दत गर्छ, विभिन्न क्षेत्रहरू (विज्ञान, प्रविधि, कानून, प्रशासन) को शब्दावली विकास गर्न सहज बनाउँछ।

शब्दको उद्गम र ऐतिहासिक विकास (Historical Development of Words): शब्दहरूको उद्गम र विकास एक दीर्घ प्रक्रिया हो। मानव समुदायले सञ्चारका लागि शब्दहरूको प्रयोग सुरु गरेपछि शब्दहरूको विकास हुँदै गयो। शब्दहरू समयसँगै परिवर्तित हुँदै गए, नयाँ शब्दहरू थपिए, पुराना शब्दहरू लोप भए। नेपाली भाषामा पनि यही प्रक्रिया देखिन्छ: प्राचीन संस्कृतबाट → प्राकृत → अपभ्रंश → अवधी/बज्जिका → आधुनिक नेपाली।

शब्दहरूको वर्तनी नियम (Spelling Rules of Words): नेपाली शब्दहरूको वर्तनीका लागि निम्न नियमहरू प्रयोग हुन्छन्: (१) तत्सम शब्दहरूको वर्तनी संस्कृत नियमअनुसार हुन्छ, (२) तद्भव शब्दहरूको वर्तनी नेपाली उच्चारणअनुसार हुन्छ, (३) आगन्तुक शब्दहरूको वर्तनी तिनीहरूको मूल भाषाअनुसार हुन्छ तर नेपाली उच्चारणमा ढल्किन्छ, (४) चन्द्रबिन्दु र विस्गर्ग तत्सम शब्दमा मात्र प्रयोग हुन्छ, (५) नेपाली वर्तनी नियम अनुसार 'क्ष' र 'ज्ञ' को प्रयोग तत्सम शब्दमा हुन्छ।

शब्दको उच्चारण र ध्वनि परिवर्तन (Pronunciation and Sound Changes): शब्दहरूको उच्चारण र वर्तनी शब्दको स्रोत र विकाससँग सम्बन्धित छ। तत्सम शब्दहरूको वर्तनी संस्कृत वर्तनी अनुसार हुन्छ, तद्भव शब्दहरूको वर्तनी नेपाली उच्चारण अनुसार हुन्छ, आगन्तुक शब्दहरूको वर्तनी तिनीहरूको मूल भाषा अनुसार हुन्छ तर नेपाली उच्चारणमा ढल्किन्छ। उदाहरण: अंग्रेजी 'knowledge' → 'नोलज' (नेपाली उच्चारण), 'समुद्र' → 'समुद' (तद्भव)।

शब्द भण्डारको महत्व (Importance of Word Bank): शब्दभण्डारको ज्ञान भाषा सीपको अभिन्न अंग हो। शब्दको स्रोत थाहा हुँदा शब्दको शुद्ध वर्तनी, उच्चारण र प्रयोग गर्न सकिन्छ। NEB परीक्षामा शब्दको स्रोत (तत्सम, तद्भव, आगन्तुक) पहिचान गर्ने प्रश्नहरू प्रायः आउँछन्। शब्दभण्डारको समृद्धिले भाषाको सौन्दर्य, प्रभावकारिता र विस्तारमा महत्वपूर्ण भूमिका खेल्छ।
confusion: तत्सम र तद्भव शब्दहरू एउटै हुन् — गलत। तत्सम शब्दहरू संस्कृतका शुद्ध रूपका हुन्छन् भने तद्भव शब्दहरू संस्कृतबाट विकसित भएका परिवर्तित रूपका हुन्छन्। तत्सममा चन्द्रबिन्दु/विस्गर्ग हुन्छ तर तद्भवमा हुँदैन।
आगन्तुक शब्द र तद्भव शब्दमा फरक छैन — गलत। आगन्तुक शब्दहरू अन्य भाषाहरूबाट आएका हुन्छन् भने तद्भव शब्दहरू संस्कृतबाट नेपालीमा विकसित भएर आएका हुन्छन्। दुवैको उद्गम स्रोत फरक हुन्छ।
नेपाली भाषामा आएका सबै शब्दहरू संस्कृतबाट आएका हुन् — गलत। नेपाली भाषामा अरबी-फारसी, अंग्रेजी, फ्रान्सेली, पोर्चुगिस, जर्मान लगायत धेरै भाषाहरूबाट शब्दहरू आएका छन्।
शब्दको स्रोत भनेको त्यसको अर्थ हो — गलत। शब्दको स्रोत भनेको त्यो शब्द कुन भाषाबाट आएको हो भन्ने हो, अर्थ होइन। स्रोत (source) = उद्गम स्थल।
आगन्तुक शब्दहरूमा चन्द्रबिन्दु र विस्गर्ग हुन्छ — गलत। आगन्तुक शब्दहरूमा चन्द्रबिन्दु र विस्गर्ग सामान्यतया हुँदैन। यी चिन्हहरू तत्सम शब्दहरूमा मात्र पाइन्छन्।
तद्भव शब्दहरू लामो र जटिल हुन्छन् — गलत। तद्भव शब्दहरू छोटो र सरल हुन्छन्, जबकि तत्सम शब्दहरू लामो र जटिल हुन्छन्। तद्भव शब्दहरू दैनिक बोलचालमा प्रयोग हुन्छन्।
