data.title: Applications of Banking
notes: **Banking of roads:** the practice of raising the outer edge of a curved road above the inner edge so that the normal reaction from the road surface provides part or all of the centripetal force needed to turn. This reduces reliance on friction and prevents skidding.

**Why banking is needed:** on a flat road, the entire centripetal force must come from friction: F_c = μmg. At high speeds or on slippery roads, friction may be insufficient and the vehicle skids outward. Banking tilts the road so the normal force has a horizontal component pointing toward the center.

**Forces on a banked road:** the road is tilted at angle θ. The normal reaction N acts perpendicular to the road surface. Resolving N: vertical component N cos θ balances weight (N cos θ = mg); horizontal component N sin θ provides centripetal force (N sin θ = mv²/r).

**Key equation — ideal banking angle (no friction needed):** dividing the two equations: tan θ = v²/(rg). For a given radius r and design speed v, the road should be banked at angle θ = arctan(v²/(rg)). At this angle, no friction is required.

**Friction on a banked road:** if the vehicle moves faster than the design speed, friction acts DOWN the slope (preventing outward skid). If slower, friction acts UP the slope (preventing inward sliding). The general formula: tan(θ + φ) = v²/(rg), where φ = arctan(μ).
**Maximum speed on a banked road with friction:** v_max = √[rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)]. When μ = 0 (no friction), this reduces to v = √(rg tan θ). When θ = 0 (flat road), it reduces to v = √(μrg).
**Worked example — car on banked curve:** a road of radius 100 m is banked at θ = 15°. Design speed (no friction): v = √(100 × 9.8 × tan 15°) = √(100 × 9.8 × 0.268) = √262.6 = 16.2 m/s (≈ 58 km/h).

**Railway banking (superelevation):** railways use the same principle. The outer rail is raised by height h above the inner rail. For track gauge w and banking angle θ: tan θ ≈ h/w. This prevents wear on rails and ensures passenger comfort.
**NEB exam focus:** deriving tan θ = v²/(rg); finding the design speed for a given banking angle; maximum speed with friction; railway superelevation problems.

**Force resolution on a banked road — detailed derivation:** draw the FBD with N perpendicular to the road and mg vertically down. Resolve N into: vertical component N cos θ (balances weight) and horizontal component N sin θ (provides centripetal force). From N cos θ = mg: N = mg/cos θ. From N sin θ = mv²/r: (mg/cos θ) sin θ = mv²/r → mg tan θ = mv²/r → tan θ = v²/(rg). This derivation is the standard NEB proof.

**Friction on a banked road — general case:** when friction is present, there are two limiting cases. Case 1 (going too fast): friction acts DOWN the slope, adding to the centripetal force. Case 2 (going too slow): friction acts UP the slope, preventing inward sliding. The general equation combining both: N sin θ ± f cos θ = mv²/r (horizontal) and N cos θ ∓ f sin θ = mg (vertical), where f = μN.

**Worked example — finding banking angle:** a curve of radius 150 m is designed for 90 km/h (25 m/s). Required banking angle: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 625/(150 × 9.8) = 0.425 → θ = 23.0°. At this angle, a car can negotiate the curve without any friction.

**Worked example — height of outer rail:** a railway track of gauge 1.5 m is banked at 5°. The height by which the outer rail is raised: h = w tan θ = 1.5 × tan 5° = 1.5 × 0.0875 = 0.131 m ≈ 13.1 cm. This is a typical NEB numerical problem.

**Why banking reduces tire wear:** on a flat road, friction must provide all centripetal force, causing lateral tire stress. On a banked road at the design speed, the normal force provides the centripetal component — no lateral friction needed. This dramatically reduces tire wear and fuel consumption.
formulas: Ideal banking angle (no friction): tan θ = v²/(rg)
Maximum speed with friction: v_max = √[rg(tan θ + μ)/(1 − μ tan θ)]
Minimum speed with friction: v_min = √[rg(tan θ − μ)/(1 + μ tan θ)]
Railway superelevation: h = w tan θ, where w = track gauge
Normal force on banked road: N = mg/cos θ
confusion: ❌ 'Banking eliminates friction entirely.' ✅ Banking REDUCES friction requirement. At the design speed (tan θ = v²/(rg)), friction is zero. At other speeds, friction is still needed.
❌ 'A steeper bank angle is always better.' ✅ Too steep a bank angle causes problems at low speeds — the vehicle may slide inward. The ideal angle depends on the design speed.
❌ 'The normal force equals mg on a banked road.' ✅ The normal force is N = mg/cos θ, which is GREATER than mg because the road is tilted.
❌ 'Banking angle depends on the mass of the vehicle.' ✅ The ideal banking angle tan θ = v²/(rg) is independent of mass — it depends only on speed and radius.
❌ 'On a banked road, friction always acts up the slope.' ✅ Friction direction depends on speed: if v > design speed, friction acts DOWN the slope; if v < design speed, friction acts UP.
❌ 'A higher banking angle means a lower maximum speed.' ✅ A HIGHER banking angle INCREASES the maximum speed — more of the normal force contributes to centripetal force.

With friction: A 50 m radius curve is banked at 20°. With μ = 0.4, max speed: v_max = √[50 × 9.8 × (0.364 + 0.4)/(1 − 0.4 × 0.364)] = √[490 × 0.764 / 0.854] = √438 = 20.9 m/s.
Railway: Track gauge w = 1.5 m, banking angle θ = 3°. Superelevation h = w tan θ = 1.5 × 0.0524 = 0.0786 m ≈ 7.9 cm.

data.title: Circular Motion Mindmap
notes: Circular motion: motion of a body along a circular path. Key quantities: angular displacement (θ), angular velocity (ω), angular acceleration (α), centripetal acceleration (a_c = v²/r = rω²).
Angular displacement: θ = s/r (radians); 2π rad = 360° = 1 revolution; vector along axis (right-hand rule).
Angular velocity: ω = dθ/dt; uniform circular motion has constant ω; unit: rad/s; rpm conversion: × 2π/60.
Angular acceleration: α = dω/dt; constant α gives kinematic equations mirroring linear motion.
Centripetal acceleration: a_c = v²/r = rω² — always directed toward the center; changes direction of velocity, not speed.
Centripetal force: F_c = mv²/r — not a new force; provided by tension, gravity, friction, or normal force.
Conical pendulum: bob moves in horizontal circle; string traces cone; period T = 2π√(L cos θ/g), independent of mass.
Vertical circle: speed varies with height; minimum top speed (string) = √(gr); minimum bottom speed = √(5gr).
Banking of roads: tan θ = v²/(rg) for ideal angle; reduces friction requirement; railway superelevation h = w tan θ.
NEB exam focus: converting rpm to rad/s; centripetal force identification; conical pendulum derivation; vertical circle min speeds; banking angle calculations.

data.title: Current-Voltage Relations and Ohmic/Non-Ohmic Resistance
notes: **Ohmic conductor:** obeys Ohm's law. The $I$-$V$ graph is a straight line through the origin. Resistance is constant.
**Non-ohmic conductor:** does not obey Ohm's law. The $I$-$V$ graph is curved. Resistance changes with voltage or current.

**Examples of non-ohmic:** diode (conducts easily in one direction only), filament lamp (resistance increases with temperature as current increases), thermistor (resistance decreases with temperature).
**Why filament lamp is non-ohmic:** as current increases, the filament heats up, increasing its resistivity. The $I$-$V$ curve bends because $R$ is not constant.
**Dynamic resistance:** $R_d = dV/dI$ at a point on the $I$-$V$ curve. For non-ohmic devices, this is the useful measure of resistance at a specific operating point.
**Forward bias diode:** current flows easily once the voltage exceeds the threshold ($\\\\approx 0.7$ V for silicon, $\\\\approx 0.3$ V for germanium). Below threshold, very little current flows.
**Reverse bias diode:** almost no current flows (except a tiny leakage current). At the breakdown voltage, current increases sharply and the diode may be damaged.
**Thermistor:** a semiconductor device whose resistance decreases sharply with temperature (NTC type). Used as temperature sensors and inrush current limiters.
**Zener diode:** operates in reverse breakdown at a precise voltage. It maintains a nearly constant voltage across it, used as a voltage regulator.

**Filament lamp $I$-$V$ curve:** starts linearly at low voltage (cool filament, low resistance). At higher voltages, the curve bends toward the voltage axis as the filament heats and resistance increases.

**Temperature coefficient of filament:** tungsten has $\\\\alpha \\\\approx 0.0045$ $^{\\\\circ}$C$^{-1}$. A 100 W, 230 V bulb has cold resistance of about $50\\\\,\\\\Omega$ but hot resistance of $529\\\\,\\\\Omega$.
confusion: Ohm's law $V = IR$ is a definition of resistance, not a law that all materials obey. Only ohmic conductors have a linear $I$-$V$ relationship. For non-ohmic devices, $R = V/I$ is still defined but varies.

A filament lamp becomes a better conductor (lower resistance) when cold. This is why bulbs often burn out at the moment they are switched on - the initial current surge is 10 times the steady-state current.

The dynamic resistance $dV/dI$ is different from the static resistance $V/I$. For a non-ohmic device, the static resistance is $V/I$ while the dynamic resistance is the slope of the $I$-$V$ curve at that point.

A diode is not simply a 'one-way valve' for current. In reverse bias, a tiny leakage current (nA to $\\\mu$A range) still flows. In forward bias, the current is exponentially related to voltage, not linearly.

Thermistors are not simply temperature-dependent resistors. Their resistance changes exponentially with temperature: $R = R_0 e^{\ eta(1/T - 1/T_0)}$, which makes them highly sensitive to small temperature changes.
data.topicTitle: Current-voltage relations; ohmic and non-ohmic resistance
practice: A filament lamp has a resistance of $20\\\\,\\\\Omega$ when cold and $240\\\\,\\\\Omega$ when glowing at full brightness. If connected to a 12 V supply, find the current when cold and when glowing. Solution: Cold: $I = V/R = 12/20 = 0.6$ A. Glowing: $I = V/R = 12/240 = 0.05$ A. The inrush current is 12 times the steady-state current.

A silicon diode has a forward voltage drop of 0.7 V at a current of 10 mA. It is connected in series with a 500 $\\\Omega$ resistor and a 5 V battery. Find the current. Solution: The diode drops 0.7 V, so the resistor sees $5 - 0.7 = 4.3$ V. $I = 4.3/500 = 8.6$ mA.

A thermistor has resistance $R_0 = 10\\\\,\	ext{k}\\\\Omega$ at 25$^{\\\\circ}$C and $R = 2\\\\,\	ext{k}\\\\Omega$ at 50$^{\\\\circ}$C. Find the resistance at 0$^{\\\\circ}$C assuming a linear temperature coefficient. Solution: $\\\\alpha = (R_0 - R)/(R \\\\cdot \\\\Delta T) = (10000 - 2000)/(2000 \	imes 25) = 0.16$ $^{\\\\circ}$C$^{-1}$. At 0$^{\\\\circ}$C: $R = R_0/(1 + \\\\alpha \\\\cdot 25) = 10000/(1 + 4) = 2000\\\\,\\\\Omega$.

A $I$-$V$ graph of a device shows that at $V = 3$ V, the current is 0.15 A, and the tangent at that point has slope $dI/dV = 0.02$ A/V. Find the static resistance and dynamic resistance. Solution: Static resistance $R_s = V/I = 3/0.15 = 20\\\\,\\\\Omega$. Dynamic resistance $R_d = 1/(dI/dV) = 1/0.02 = 50\\\\,\\\\Omega$.

A Zener diode with breakdown voltage 6 V is connected in parallel with a load resistor of 1 k$\\\Omega$ across a 10 V battery with series resistor of 500 $\\\Omega$. Find the current through the Zener diode. Solution: Voltage across load: 6 V (clamped by Zener). Current through 500 $\\\Omega$: $I = (10 - 6)/500 = 8$ mA. Current through load: $I_L = 6/1000 = 6$ mA. Current through Zener: $I_Z = 8 - 6 = 2$ mA.
universalFacts: A tungsten filament lamp has a resistance that changes by a factor of 10-15 between cold and hot, making it a classic example of non-ohmic behavior due to temperature-dependent resistivity.

The threshold voltage of a silicon diode is approximately 0.7 V because this is the energy needed to overcome the potential barrier of the p-n junction, corresponding to the band gap energy of silicon.
Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance (NTC thermistors) because more charge carriers are thermally excited across the band gap, increasing conductivity.
Ohmic materials include most metals at constant temperature. Non-ohmic materials include all semiconductors, electrolytes, and any device where temperature or other conditions change with current.
The $I$-$V$ characteristic of a diode is exponential: $I = I_0(e^{eV/kT} - 1)$, where $I_0$ is the reverse saturation current, $k$ is Boltzmann's constant, and $T$ is temperature.
specificConditions: **Ohmic Behavior Constraint:** A device is ohmic only if $I \propto V$ *and* the temperature is constant. Metals at constant temperature are ohmic; semiconductors, electrolytes, and gas discharges are inherently non-ohmic.

**Dynamic vs. Static Resistance:** For non-ohmic devices, the static resistance $R_s = V/I$ depends on the operating point, while the dynamic (small-signal) resistance $r_d = dV/dI$ describes the response to small AC signals superimposed on the DC bias.

**Temperature as Hidden Variable:** In filament lamps and thermistors, the non-ohmic behavior arises because the current heats the device, changing its resistivity. The $I$-$V$ curve actually represents a parametric plot where temperature varies with current.

data.title: EMF and Internal Resistance
notes: **EMF ($\\\\mathcal{E}$):** the open-circuit voltage of a source. It is the work done per unit charge in moving charge around the complete circuit.
**Internal resistance $r$:** the resistance inside the cell due to electrolyte and electrodes. It causes the terminal voltage to drop when current flows.
**Terminal voltage:** $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$. When no current flows ($I=0$), $V = \\\\mathcal{E}$. Under load, $V < \\\\mathcal{E}$.
**Cells in series:** $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = \\\\mathcal{E}_1 + \\\\mathcal{E}_2 + \\\\ldots$, $r_{total} = r_1 + r_2 + \\\\ldots$. Series adds both EMF and internal resistance.
**Cells in parallel:** $\\\\mathcal{E}_{total} = \\\\mathcal{E}$ (if all equal), $r_{total} = r/n$ for $n$ identical cells. Parallel reduces internal resistance, allowing higher current delivery.
**Maximum power transfer:** the power delivered to an external load $R$ is maximum when $R = r$. The maximum power is $P_{max} = \\\\mathcal{E}^2/(4r)$.
**Current in a simple circuit:** $I = \\\\mathcal{E}/(R + r)$, where $R$ is the external resistance and $r$ is the internal resistance.
**Efficiency:** the efficiency of power transfer is $\\\\eta = R/(R + r)$. Maximum efficiency approaches 100% when $R \\\\gg r$, but maximum power requires $R = r$.
**Short circuit current:** when $R = 0$, $I_{sc} = \\\\mathcal{E}/r$. This can be very large and dangerous, causing heating and damage.
**Cells with different EMFs:** when cells with different EMFs are connected in parallel, circulating currents flow between them. This can damage cells and should be avoided.
**Real cell behavior:** as a cell discharges, its EMF slowly decreases and its internal resistance increases. An old battery reads lower than its rated voltage even when not loaded.
confusion: EMF is not a force - it is a voltage (energy per unit charge). The name is historical. EMF is measured in volts, not newtons.

Terminal voltage $V = \\\\mathcal{E} - Ir$ is less than EMF when current flows out of the cell. But when charging the cell, current flows into the positive terminal, so $V = \\\\mathcal{E} + Ir$ - the terminal voltage is greater than EMF.
In series, both EMF and internal resistance add. In parallel, the equivalent EMF is the same as one cell, but the equivalent internal resistance is reduced, allowing more current.
Maximum power transfer ($R = r$) occurs at 50% efficiency. For efficient power delivery, you want $R \\\\gg r$ (high efficiency, low power). For maximum power, you sacrifice efficiency.
A fresh battery has a high open-circuit voltage (close to its EMF) but drops significantly under load if its internal resistance has increased with age. That is why old batteries seem weak.

data.title: Work and Power in Electrical Circuits
notes: **Electrical work:** $W = VIt = I^2Rt = V^2t/R$. Work done by a current is the energy transferred.
**Electrical power:** $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$. Power is the rate of energy transfer.
**Joule heating:** $P = I^2R$ is the power dissipated as heat in a resistor. This is also called $I^2R$ loss.
**Kilowatt-hour:** unit of electrical energy. $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6\\\\,\	ext{J}$. This is what electricity meters measure.
**Efficiency:** useful power output divided by total power input. Transmission lines use high voltage to reduce $I^2R$ losses because $P_{loss} \\\\propto I^2$.

**Power in different elements:** in a resistor, all electrical energy is converted to heat: $P = I^2R$. In a motor, electrical energy converts to mechanical work plus heat: $P_{input} = VI = I^2R + P_{mech}$. In a battery being charged, electrical energy is stored as chemical energy: $P_{input} = \\\\mathcal{E}I + I^2r$.

**Energy conservation in circuits:** the total electrical energy supplied equals the sum of energy dissipated as heat and energy converted to other forms: $V_{source} \\\\cdot I \\\\cdot t = I^2Rt + \	ext{other forms}$.
**Power rating of resistors:** resistors are rated by the maximum power they can dissipate without damage. Common ratings are 0.25 W, 0.5 W, and 1 W. Exceeding this causes overheating and failure.
**Domestic electrical cost:** the cost of running an appliance is $\	ext{Cost} = P(\	ext{kW}) \	imes t(\	ext{h}) \	imes \	ext{rate (per kWh)}$. A 100 W bulb running for 5 hours uses 0.5 kWh.
**Power factor:** for AC circuits, $P = VI\\\\cos\\\\phi$, where $\\\\cos\\\\phi$ is the power factor. For DC circuits, $\\\\cos\\\\phi = 1$, so $P = VI$ always.
**Heat energy in calories:** $H = 0.24 I^2 R t$ calories (mechanical equivalent of heat). In SI units, $H = I^2 R t$ joules.
confusion: Power $P = I^2R$ and $P = V^2/R$ are both correct but apply in different contexts. Use $I^2R$ when current is known (series circuits). Use $V^2/R$ when voltage is known (parallel circuits). Using the wrong one gives a wrong answer because $V$ and $I$ are not independent.
Electrical energy is measured in joules (J) or kilowatt-hours (kWh), NOT in watts (W). Watt is a unit of power (energy per time). $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6$ J.

A 100 W bulb connected to 230 V draws less current than a 60 W bulb (because $I = P/V$, so the 100 W bulb has $I = 0.43$ A vs $I = 0.26$ A for the 60 W bulb). The 100 W bulb actually has LOWER resistance.

In a series circuit, the higher-wattage bulb glows dimmer because it has lower resistance, and in series the same current flows through both: $P = I^2R$, so the higher resistance (60 W bulb) gets more power.
Power dissipated in internal resistance ($I^2r$) is wasted energy. This is why battery-powered devices get warm - the internal resistance converts some chemical energy to heat instead of useful work.
data.topicTitle: Work and power in electrical circuits
practice: A 60 W, 230 V bulb is connected to a 230 V supply. Find the current, resistance, and energy consumed in 5 hours. Solution: $I = P/V = 60/230 = 0.261$ A. $R = V/I = 230/0.261 = 881\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $W = Pt = 60 \	imes 5 = 300\\\\,\	ext{Wh} = 0.3\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 1.08 \	imes 10^6$ J.

A 12 V car headlamp draws 5 A. Find the power, resistance, and cost of running it for 4 hours at 8 pence per kWh. Solution: $P = VI = 12 \	imes 5 = 60$ W. $R = V/I = 12/5 = 2.4\\\\,\\\\Omega$. Energy $= 60 \	imes 4/1000 = 0.24\\\\,\	ext{kWh}$. Cost $= 0.24 \	imes 8 = 1.92$ pence.

A 100 $\\\Omega$ resistor carries a current of 2 A for 5 minutes. Find the heat produced in joules and calories. Solution: $H = I^2Rt = 4 \	imes 100 \	imes 300 = 120000$ J. In calories: $H = 120000/4.184 = 28681$ cal $\\\\approx 28.7$ kcal.

A transmission line carries 100 A at 11 kV over a total resistance of 5 $\\\Omega$. Find the power loss and the percentage of power lost. Solution: $P_{loss} = I^2R = 10000 \	imes 5 = 50000$ W $= 50$ kW. Power transmitted $= VI = 11000 \	imes 100 = 1.1 \	imes 10^6$ W $= 1100$ kW. Percentage loss $= 50/1100 = 4.5\\\\%$.

A 1.5 V cell with internal resistance 0.5 $\\\Omega$ is connected to a variable resistor. Find the resistance for maximum power transfer and the power delivered. Solution: $R = r = 0.5\\\\,\\\\Omega$. $I = 1.5/(0.5+0.5) = 1.5$ A. $P_{max} = I^2R = 2.25 \	imes 0.5 = 1.125$ W.
universalFacts: A 100 W incandescent bulb is only about 5% efficient - most electrical energy is converted to heat rather than visible light. LEDs are about 15-20% efficient but produce far more lumens per watt.

Electric transmission lines carry power at very high voltages (up to 765 kV) to minimize $I^2R$ losses. Halving the voltage doubles the current and quadruples the power loss, which is why high-voltage transmission is essential.
The unit of electrical energy consumption, the kilowatt-hour, is not an SI unit. The SI unit of energy is the joule: $1\\\\,\	ext{kWh} = 3.6 \	imes 10^6$ J.
A typical household circuit breaker is rated for 15-20 A at 120-240 V, giving a maximum power of 1.8-4.8 kW. Connecting too many high-power appliances can trip the breaker or cause a fire.
The heating effect of current was discovered by James Prescott Joule in 1841. His law $H = I^2Rt$ is a fundamental result of energy conservation in electrical circuits.
specificConditions: **Power Formula Context:** $P = I^2R$ is used when current is known (series circuits). $P = V^2/R$ is used when voltage is known (parallel circuits). Both are derived from $P = VI$ and Ohm's law; using the wrong one gives incorrect results because $V$ and $I$ are coupled through $R$.

**Joule Heating is Irreversible:** The power $P = I^2R$ dissipated in a resistor represents an irreversible conversion of electrical energy to heat. It cannot be recovered within the circuit. This is distinct from energy stored in inductors/capacitors or converted to mechanical work.

**Energy Units:** Electrical energy is measured in joules (SI) or kilowatt-hours (practical). $1 	ext{ kWh} = 3.6 	imes 10^6 	ext{ J}$. Power (watts) is the *rate* of energy transfer, not energy itself.

data.title: Chromatic and Spherical Aberration
notes: **Chromatic aberration:** a lens fails to focus all colours at the same point because $n$ varies with wavelength. Violet (higher $n$) focuses closer to the lens than red (lower $n$), producing coloured fringes around images.

**Spherical aberration:** rays passing through the edge (marginal rays) of a spherical lens focus at a different point from rays passing through the centre (paraxial rays). Marginal rays focus closer to the lens because the surface curvature is steeper at the edges.

**Why spherical aberration occurs:** the lens surface is part of a sphere, but the ideal focusing surface for parallel rays is a paraboloid, not a sphere. A spherical surface is only an approximation.

**Longitudinal chromatic aberration:** the distance between the focal points of the extreme colours (violet and red). For a thin lens, $\Delta f = f_v - f_r \approx -f \cdot \omega$, where $\omega$ is the dispersive power.
**Lateral chromatic aberration:** the difference in image heights for different colours, significant when the object is off-axis.

**Reducing spherical aberration:** use a diaphragm to block marginal rays (reduces brightness but improves sharpness), or use a compound lens with surfaces chosen so that aberrations of one surface cancel those of the other.

**Best-form lens:** a plano-convex lens has minimum spherical aberration when the curved face is oriented toward the more distant object (collimated light). For finite conjugates, the lens should be oriented so that the refraction is shared more equally between the two surfaces.

**Aplanatic surfaces:** certain combinations of object distance and lens shape eliminate both spherical aberration and coma. A sphere has two aplanatic points used in oil-immersion microscope objectives.
formulas: Application formula for Chromatic and spherical aberration
Derivation result for Chromatic and spherical aberration
confusion: Chromatic aberration is caused by dispersion (wavelength-dependent $n$); spherical aberration is caused by the spherical shape of the lens surface. They are fundamentally different phenomena that both degrade image quality.

Stopping down (using a diaphragm) reduces spherical aberration by blocking marginal rays, but it does NOT reduce chromatic aberration — all rays, regardless of height, still experience the same dispersion.
A plano-convex lens does not eliminate spherical aberration entirely; it only minimizes it for a particular object distance. Only a parabolic surface eliminates it completely for collimated light.
Spherical aberration affects all wavelengths equally (monochromatic aberration), while chromatic aberration affects different wavelengths differently (polychromatic aberration).

Using a thinner lens does not eliminate either aberration — it only reduces the magnitude. The fundamental cause (spherical shape for spherical aberration, dispersion for chromatic aberration) remains.

specificConditions: **Dispersion Definition:** Dispersion is the separation of white light into its constituent colors (spectrum) due to the dependence of the refractive index $n$ on the wavelength $\lambda$ of light ($n(\lambda)$).

**Cauchy's Equation:** For many transparent materials, the refractive index follows Cauchy's equation $n(\lambda) = A + B/\lambda^2 + C/\lambda^4$. This explains why blue light ($\lambda$ smaller) is refracted more than red light ($\lambda$ larger).

**Prism Validity:** The formula for dispersive power $\omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1)$ assumes small angle of deviation and that the prism is in air. For non-thin prisms or different mediums, angular dispersion depends on the geometry.
practice: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm is made of glass with $\omega = 0.02$. Calculate the longitudinal chromatic aberration. Solution: $\Delta f = f \cdot \omega = 20 \times 0.02 = 0.4$ cm $= 4$ mm. The focal length for violet is 0.4 cm shorter than for red.

A plano-convex lens of focal length 30 cm is used with the plane face toward the object. Explain why spherical aberration is worse than when the curved face faces the object. Solution: When the plane face faces the object, all refraction occurs at the curved surface, making marginal rays bend sharply. When the curved face faces the object, refraction is shared more equally between the two surfaces, reducing the bending at each surface and thus reducing spherical aberration.

A converging lens of focal length 50 cm is combined with a diverging lens to eliminate chromatic aberration. If the dispersive powers are in the ratio 2:3, find the focal length of the diverging lens. Solution: Condition: $\frac{\omega_1}{f_1} + \frac{\omega_2}{f_2} = 0$. Let $\omega_1 = 2\omega$, $\omega_2 = 3\omega$. Then $\frac{2\omega}{50} + \frac{3\omega}{f_2} = 0$, giving $f_2 = -\frac{3 \times 50}{2} = -75$ cm.

Describe two methods to reduce spherical aberration in a lens system. Solution: (1) Use a diaphragm/aperture stop to block the marginal rays that cause the greatest deviation from the paraxial focus. (2) Use an aplanatic lens combination, such as two thin lenses separated by a distance, chosen so that the spherical aberration of one lens cancels that of the other.

A telescope objective shows a coloured halo around bright stars. Is this chromatic or spherical aberration? Explain how to distinguish it. Solution: This is chromatic aberration — the halo is coloured because different wavelengths focus at different points. To distinguish from spherical aberration: observe a monochromatic source (e.g., sodium lamp); if the halo disappears, it is chromatic aberration. Spherical aberration persists with monochromatic light, showing as a general blur rather than coloured fringes.
universalFacts: All simple spherical lenses suffer from both chromatic and spherical aberration — no single spherical lens can form a perfect image.
The Hubble Space Telescope's initial primary mirror had a spherical aberration of about 2.2 micrometres — a tiny error that produced blurry images because of the mirror's 2.4-metre diameter.
Modern camera lenses contain 10–20 elements to correct both aberrations simultaneously, using combinations of crown and flint glass.
Aparabolic mirrors are used in telescopes instead of spherical mirrors because a paraboloid focuses all parallel rays to a single point, eliminating spherical aberration for on-axis objects.
The human eye has very little chromatic aberration because the cornea and lens have complementary dispersion properties, and the brain processes the colour information to compensate.

data.title: Achromatism
notes: **Achromatic doublet:** a convex crown-glass lens paired with a concave flint-glass lens. The crown lens converges all colours; the flint lens diverges more for violet than for red, cancelling the chromatic spread.

**Condition for achromatism (thin lenses in contact):** $\frac{\omega_1}{f_1} + \frac{\omega_2}{f_2} = 0$. Since $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are both positive, $f_1$ and $f_2$ must have opposite signs: one converging, one diverging.
**Result:** two colours (usually red and blue) are brought to the same focus. Intermediate colours fall close enough that the image appears colour-free to the eye.

**Power of the combination:** the total power is $P = P_1 + P_2 = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}$. For an achromatic doublet, $P = \frac{1}{f_1} - \frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2 f_1} = \frac{1}{f_1}\left(1 - \frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2}\right)$. The combination remains converging if $\omega_2 > \omega_1$.

**For a convex lens of crown glass ($\omega_c = 0.016$) and concave lens of flint glass ($\omega_f = 0.031$):** $\frac{f_f}{f_c} = -\frac{\omega_f}{\omega_c} = -\frac{0.031}{0.016} \approx -1.94$. The flint lens must have roughly twice the focal length (in magnitude) of the crown lens.
**Applications:** camera lenses, telescope objectives, and microscope objectives all use achromatic doublets or more complex multi-element designs to eliminate chromatic aberration.
**Apochromatic lenses:** advanced designs that bring three colours to the same focus using special glasses with anomalous dispersion (e.g., fluorite). These provide superior colour correction.
**Achromatic prism pair:** two prisms of different materials can be combined to produce dispersion without net deviation, or deviation without net dispersion, by adjusting the prism angles.

specificConditions: **Dispersion Definition:** Dispersion is the separation of white light into its constituent colors (spectrum) due to the dependence of the refractive index $n$ on the wavelength $\lambda$ of light ($n(\lambda)$).

**Cauchy's Equation:** For many transparent materials, the refractive index follows Cauchy's equation $n(\lambda) = A + B/\lambda^2 + C/\lambda^4$. This explains why blue light ($\lambda$ smaller) is refracted more than red light ($\lambda$ larger).

**Prism Validity:** The formula for dispersive power $\omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1)$ assumes small angle of deviation and that the prism is in air. For non-thin prisms or different mediums, angular dispersion depends on the geometry.
practice: An achromatic doublet is made by combining a crown glass convex lens of focal length 20 cm ($\omega_c = 0.016$) with a flint glass concave lens. Find the focal length of the flint lens and the focal length of the combination. Solution: $\frac{\omega_c}{f_c} + \frac{\omega_f}{f_f} = 0$. Taking $\omega_f = 0.031$: $\frac{0.016}{20} + \frac{0.031}{f_f} = 0$, so $f_f = -\frac{0.031 \times 20}{0.016} = -38.75$ cm. Combined focal length: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{38.75} = \frac{38.75 - 20}{20 \times 38.75} = \frac{18.75}{775}$, so $f \approx 41.3$ cm.

Show that for an achromatic doublet made of two thin lenses in contact, if the combination is to be converging, the converging lens must have the smaller dispersive power. Solution: Condition: $\frac{\omega_1}{f_1} + \frac{\omega_2}{f_2} = 0$. Let lens 1 be converging ($f_1 > 0$) and lens 2 be diverging ($f_2 < 0$). Then $\frac{\omega_2}{|f_2|} = \frac{\omega_1}{f_1}$, so $|f_2| = f_1 \cdot \frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1}$. For the combination to be converging: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} - \frac{1}{|f_2|} > 0$, so $f_1 < |f_2|$, which means $\omega_1 < \omega_2$. The converging lens must have the smaller dispersive power.

A telescope objective needs a focal length of 100 cm and must be achromatic. The crown glass has $\omega_c = 0.016$ and the flint glass has $\omega_f = 0.031$. Find the focal lengths of the two lenses. Solution: $\frac{1}{f_c} + \frac{1}{f_f} = \frac{1}{100}$ and $\frac{\omega_c}{f_c} + \frac{\omega_f}{f_f} = 0$. From the second equation: $f_f = -\frac{\omega_f}{\omega_c}f_c = -\frac{31}{16}f_c$. Substituting: $\frac{1}{f_c} - \frac{16}{31f_c} = \frac{1}{100}$, so $\frac{15}{31f_c} = \frac{1}{100}$, giving $f_c = \frac{1500}{31} \approx 48.4$ cm and $f_f = -\frac{31}{16} \times 48.4 \approx -93.8$ cm.

Explain why a single lens cannot be made achromatic. Solution: A single lens has one material with one dispersive power $\omega$. The focal length varies with wavelength as $f(\lambda) = \frac{1}{(n(\lambda)-1)K}$ where $K$ depends on surface curvatures. Since $n$ varies with $\lambda$, $f$ varies — there is no way to make $f$ independent of wavelength with a single material.

A converging lens of crown glass ($n_c = 1.514$ for red, $n_c = 1.524$ for violet) and a concave lens of flint glass ($n_f = 1.613$ for red, $n_f = 1.632$ for violet) are placed in contact. Find the ratio of their focal lengths for achromatism. Solution: For the crown lens: $\omega_c = \frac{1.524-1.514}{1.519-1} = \frac{0.010}{0.519} \approx 0.0193$. For the flint lens: $\omega_f = \frac{1.632-1.613}{1.6225-1} = \frac{0.019}{0.6225} \approx 0.0305$. Condition: $\frac{\omega_c}{f_c} + \frac{\omega_f}{f_f} = 0$, so $\frac{f_f}{f_c} = -\frac{\omega_f}{\omega_c} = -\frac{0.0305}{0.0193} \approx -1.58$.
universalFacts: The achromatic doublet was invented by Chester Moor Hall around 1733 and independently by John Dollond in 1758, who patented the design.

An achromatic doublet reduces but does not eliminate chromatic aberration — residual colour errors (secondary spectrum) remain because the dispersion curves of crown and flint glass are not perfectly linear.
Apochromatic objectives, used in high-end microscopy, bring three wavelengths to a common focus and are made with special low-dispersion materials like fluorite or extra-low dispersion (ED) glass.
The human eye has a small amount of longitudinal chromatic aberration (about 2 dioptres from red to violet), but the brain compensates and we do not normally perceive colour fringes.
In photography, "low dispersion" (LD) or "extra-low dispersion" (ED) glass elements are used in telephoto lenses to reduce chromatic aberration and produce sharper images at the edges.

data.title: Linear Momentum and Impulse
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version emphasises the momentum form of Newton's second law and the impulse–momentum theorem with force–time graphs — the framing NEB theory questions use.

**Impulsive Force:** A force that acts for a very short time but produces a finite change in momentum. Examples: hammer hitting a nail, bat hitting a ball, foot kicking a football. The force is extremely large, often thousands of Newtons, but the duration is milliseconds. The impulse is the area under the force-time curve, $J = \int F dt$.

**Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ — mass in motion, SI unit kg·m/s. It is a VECTOR along the velocity. A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J). Momentum is a measure of the 'difficulty' to stop an object. It is the 'inertia of motion'.

**Physical Significance:** Momentum is fundamentally linked to the translational symmetry of space (Noether's theorem). In quantum mechanics, momentum is related to the wave vector $k$ by $p = \hbar k$.
**Conservation:** Momentum is conserved in any system where the net external force is zero. This is a universal law, holding from subatomic particles to galactic collisions.

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$ for a constant force, and $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ in general — the AREA under a force–time graph. Impulse has units N·s = kg·m/s, the same as momentum — by design.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. Bending your knees on landing, catching a cricket ball with draw-back hands, and jumping with flexed legs are all the same physics.

**Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

**NEB exam focus:** define momentum and impulse with units; state and use $F = dp/dt$; compute impulse from force–time graphs; apply $J = \Delta p$ to catches, kicks and landings; explain safety devices via the force–time argument.

confusion: ❌ 'Momentum and kinetic energy are interchangeable measures of motion.' ✅ Momentum $mv$ is a vector conserved in ALL collisions; kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is a scalar conserved only in elastic ones. Both grow with speed but differently.
❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

❌ 'The ball exerts no force on the bat while being hit because the bat is harder.' ✅ Newton's third law: contact forces are equal and opposite during the collision — the ball's velocity change comes from the contact force acting on IT.
❌ 'A heavy object always has more momentum.' ✅ Momentum = mass × VELOCITY — a light fast bullet can out-momentum a heavy slow trolley; direction matters too.
❌ Using $F = ma$ for a rocket ejecting fuel. ✅ Mass changes with time, so $F = ma$ fails; the momentum form $F = dp/dt$ handles it and yields the rocket equation.
❌ Impulse has units of newtons. ✅ N·s (= kg·m/s) — momentum units. Dimensionally $[MLT^{-1}]$.

practice: A 60 kg runner at 8 m/s is stopped in 0.5 s. Find the impulse and the average force. — $J = 480$ kg·m/s; $F = 960$ N.
A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 12 m/s and rebounds at 8 m/s. Find the impulse. — $\Delta p = 0.5(8+12) = 10$ kg·m/s BACKWARD (note the sign reversal!).
From a triangular $F$–$t$ pulse peaking at 400 N over 0.02 s, find the impulse delivered to a 0.2 kg ball at rest. — Area $= \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(400) = 4$ N·s → $v = 20$ m/s.
A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s crashes into a barrier that stops it in 0.4 s. Find the average force, and compare with a crumple-zone stop in 1.0 s. — 50 kN vs 20 kN.
A machine-gun fires 30 g bullets at 400 m/s, 10 per second. Find the average recoil force. — $F = n\,mv = 10 \times 12 = 120$ N.
universalFacts: Airbags, crumple zones, helmets and safety nets are all impulse engineering: stretch the stopping time, cut the peak force, keep $\Delta p$ fixed.
The impulse–momentum theorem explains why follow-through matters in sports — prolonging contact time increases delivered impulse and exit speed.
Rocketry is continuous impulse: each second, expelling mass $dm$ at exhaust speed $v_e$ gives thrust $v_e\,dm/dt$ — momentum conservation making spaceflight possible.
Karate masters break boards by maximising $\Delta p$ in minimum $\Delta t$: peak contact forces of thousands of newtons in a few milliseconds.
The concept of 'impulse' is crucial in collision theory, where the duration of contact is often too short to measure the force directly, but the change in momentum is easily observed.
In relativistic mechanics, momentum is defined as $\vec{p} = \gamma m\vec{v}$, where $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$. At low speeds, $\gamma \approx 1$, and it reduces to the classical $m\vec{v}$.
**Fluid Impulse:** A jet of water hitting a wall exerts a force $F = \dot{m} v$, where $\dot{m}$ is the mass flow rate (kg/s). This is the principle behind Pelton wheels and jet engines.

**Impulse-Momentum Theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta \vec{p}$. This theorem is the foundation for analyzing collisions, explosions, and recoil. It allows us to relate the force-time history of a collision to the change in velocity of the objects involved.
examples: Example 1 (recoil): a 5 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 300 m/s — recoil speed $= \frac{0.02 \times 300}{5} = 1.2$ m/s backward.
Example 2 (kicking): a footballer gives a 0.45 kg ball at rest a speed of 20 m/s in 0.05 s — impulse 9 N·s, average force 180 N.
Example 3 (graph): a rectangular $F$–$t$ pulse of 250 N lasting 0.04 s delivers $J = 10$ N·s — a 2 kg cart leaves at 5 m/s.
Example 4 (safety): the same 4000 kg·m/s car momentum change stopped in 0.1 s (rigid wall) means 40 kN; in 0.5 s (crumple zone) only 8 kN — five times gentler.
Example 5 (jump landing): a 60 kg jumper hitting the ground at 6 m/s stops in 0.3 s with stiff legs (1200 N extra) vs 0.9 s with bent knees (400 N extra).

enrichedContent.summary: Linear momentum $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ measures 'quantity of motion'. Newton's second law in its general form is $\vec{F} = d\vec{p}/dt$, and integrating it over a collision interval gives the impulse–momentum theorem $\vec{J} = \int F\,dt = \Delta\vec{p}$ — impulse is the area under the force–time graph. Because a given momentum change can come from a big force briefly or a small force slowly, safety design (airbags, crumple zones, bent knees) is the art of stretching $\Delta t$. Recoil, ball games and rocket thrust are all direct applications.
specialNotes: Note 1: In rebound problems the velocity CHANGES SIGN — $\Delta p = m(v_f + v_i)$, not the difference. The commonest numerical error.
Note 2: Quote impulse in N·s and momentum in kg·m/s — numerically identical, and examiners check units.
Note 3: For force–time graphs, rectangular pulses are $F\Delta t$; triangular pulses are $\frac{1}{2}F_{max}\Delta t$.
Note 4: When a question says 'average force', it means $\Delta p/\Delta t$ — the constant force delivering the same impulse.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The linear momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity — a vector along the velocity.
Statement 2: The rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net force acting on it (general form of Newton's second law).
Statement 3: Impulse of a force is the product of the force and the time for which it acts, equal to the change in momentum produced.
Statement 4: For a fixed momentum change, the average force is inversely proportional to the collision time.
importantNotes: Note 1: Impulse units (N·s) and momentum units (kg·m/s) are identical — that is the theorem speaking.
Note 2: Momentum is directional: a rebound doubles the magnitude change versus a stop at the same speeds.
Note 3: The momentum form $F = dp/dt$ remains valid when mass varies (rockets, leaking trucks) where $F = ma$ fails.
Note 4: Force–time graph areas: rectangle = $F\Delta t$; triangle = $\frac{1}{2}F_{max}\Delta t$.

Trick 3: Recoil from rest: $V = mv/M$ instantly, with $V$ opposite the bullet.
Trick 4: Machine-gun/stream problems: average force = mass flow rate × exit speed ($n\,mv$).

A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J). Momentum is a measure of the 'difficulty' to stop an object. It is the 'inertia of motion'.

**Physical Significance:** Momentum is fundamentally linked to the translational symmetry of space (Noether's theorem). In quantum mechanics, momentum is related to the wave vector $k$ by $p = \hbar k$.
**Conservation:** Momentum is conserved in any system where the net external force is zero. This is a universal law, holding from subatomic particles to galactic collisions.

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$ for a constant force, and $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ in general — the AREA under a force–time graph. Impulse has units N·s = kg·m/s, the same as momentum — by design.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. Bending your knees on landing, catching a cricket ball with draw-back hands, and jumping with flexed legs are all the same physics.

**Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

**NEB exam focus:** define momentum and impulse with units; state and use $F = dp/dt$; compute impulse from force–time graphs; apply $J = \Delta p$ to catches, kicks and landings; explain safety devices via the force–time argument.

❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

❌ 'The ball exerts no force on the bat while being hit because the bat is harder.' ✅ Newton's third law: contact forces are equal and opposite during the collision — the ball's velocity change comes from the contact force acting on IT.

data.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
notes: **Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum:** In an isolated system (no external net force), the total linear momentum remains constant: $\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$. This is a fundamental law derived from the homogeneity of space (Noether's theorem). It is a direct consequence of the fact that the laws of physics are the same at all points in space.

**Isolated System:** A system where the net external force is zero. Internal forces (like collision forces) do not change the total momentum because they act in equal and opposite pairs (Newton's 3rd law). The system can be as small as two colliding particles or as large as the entire universe.

**Coefficient of Restitution (e):** A measure of elasticity in collisions: $e = (v_2 - v_1) / (u_1 - u_2)$. $e=1$ (perfectly elastic), $0 < e < 1$ (inelastic), $e=0$ (perfectly inelastic). This coefficient depends on the materials of the colliding objects and their surface properties.
**Collisions:** Events where momentum is conserved. Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy; inelastic collisions do not (energy is lost to heat, sound, deformation).
**Explosions:** A reverse collision where an object breaks apart. Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy increases (internal energy is converted to motion).
**Recoil:** A classic application. A gun firing a bullet: $M_g V_g + m_b v_b = 0$ (initially at rest).
**NEB exam focus:** State the law; apply it to 1D and 2D collisions; distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions; solve recoil and explosion problems.

**Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version derives the conservation law from Newton's third law and the impulse picture, then applies it to recoil, explosions and two-body systems — the application chain NEB numericals follow.

**The law:** if the net EXTERNAL force on a system is zero, its total linear momentum stays constant: $m_1\vec{u}_1 + m_2\vec{u}_2 = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2$. Internal forces (the pair between the two bodies) can change individual momenta but never the total.

**Why it holds (third-law derivation):** during contact, body 1 pushes body 2 with $\vec{F}_{12}$ and body 2 pushes back $\vec{F}_{21} = -\vec{F}_{12}$ for the SAME time $\Delta t$. Impulses: $\Delta\vec{p}_1 = \vec{F}_{21}\Delta t$ and $\Delta\vec{p}_2 = \vec{F}_{12}\Delta t$; adding gives $\Delta(\vec{p}_1 + \vec{p}_2) = (\vec{F}_{21} + \vec{F}_{12})\Delta t = 0$ — the total momentum cannot change.

**When it applies:** always for INTERNAL interactions; for the whole system even during explosions and collisions (internal forces are huge compared to external ones over the short interaction). Gravity/friction are external — momentum is conserved only along directions with zero net external force.

**Recoil (from rest):** initial momentum zero → $M\vec{V} + m\vec{v} = 0$, so $\vec{V} = -\dfrac{m}{M}\vec{v}$. Cannon–ball, rifle–bullet, rocket–exhaust, boat–passenger: the lighter body carries proportionally more speed.

**Explosions and separations:** a body of mass $(m_1 + m_2)$ at rest splits into pieces moving in opposite directions: $m_1 v_1 = m_2 v_2$. Kinetic energy is NOT conserved here (chemical energy converts to motion) — momentum alone is the reliable bookkeeper.

**Worked example:** a 60 kg skater at rest throws a 3 kg ball at 8 m/s. Recoil: $V = \frac{3 \times 8}{60} = 0.4$ m/s backward. If thrown at 30° above horizontal, only the horizontal component ($8\cos30°$) enters the horizontal recoil balance.

**Collision bookkeeping:** in ANY collision (elastic or not) total momentum is conserved: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$ (1-D). Two unknowns need a second equation — kinetic energy (elastic) or the coefficient of restitution $e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$.

**NEB exam focus:** state the law with its condition (no net external force); derive it from the third law; solve recoil and explosion numericals; explain rocket propulsion and the gun recoil by momentum conservation.

notes: **Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum:** In an isolated system (no external net force), the total linear momentum remains constant: $\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$. This is a fundamental law derived from the homogeneity of space (Noether's theorem). It is a direct consequence of the fact that the laws of physics are the same at all points in space.

**Isolated System:** A system where the net external force is zero. Internal forces (like collision forces) do not change the total momentum because they act in equal and opposite pairs (Newton's 3rd law). The system can be as small as two colliding particles or as large as the entire universe.

**Coefficient of Restitution (e):** A measure of elasticity in collisions: $e = (v_2 - v_1) / (u_1 - u_2)$. $e=1$ (perfectly elastic), $0 < e < 1$ (inelastic), $e=0$ (perfectly inelastic). This coefficient depends on the materials of the colliding objects and their surface properties.
**Collisions:** Events where momentum is conserved. Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy; inelastic collisions do not (energy is lost to heat, sound, deformation).
**Explosions:** A reverse collision where an object breaks apart. Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy increases (internal energy is converted to motion).
**Recoil:** A classic application. A gun firing a bullet: $M_g V_g + m_b v_b = 0$ (initially at rest).
**NEB exam focus:** State the law; apply it to 1D and 2D collisions; distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions; solve recoil and explosion problems.

specificConditions: **Isolated System Requirement:** Momentum conservation ($\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$) holds strictly only when the net *external* force on the system is zero. External forces like gravity, friction, or applied pushes must be absent or balanced.

**Collisions vs. Continuous Interaction:** In a collision, the interaction is brief and impulsive; internal forces dominate. In continuous interactions (e.g., rocket propulsion), momentum is conserved at each instant, but mass changes must be tracked using the variable-mass form $F = dp/dt$.

**Kinetic Energy Distinction:** Momentum is conserved in *all* isolated collisions (elastic or inelastic). Kinetic energy is conserved *only* in perfectly elastic collisions. In inelastic collisions, some KE is converted to heat, sound, or deformation energy.

importantStatements: The total linear momentum of an isolated system (zero net external force) remains constant in both magnitude and direction.
Newton's third law implies conservation of momentum: every action produces an equal and opposite reaction, so internal forces cannot change total momentum.
In a system of interacting bodies, the sum of individual momentum changes is zero: Δp₁ + Δp₂ + ... + Δpₙ = 0.
Momentum is conserved component-wise: if ΣF_x = 0, then Σp_x is constant even if forces act in other directions.
The law applies universally — from subatomic particles to galaxies — as long as the system is properly defined and isolated.
importantNotes: Note 1: Isolated system is key.
Note 2: Elastic vs Inelastic distinction.
Always define your system first — conservation applies to the chosen system, not to individual bodies within it.
Internal forces (collisions, explosions, attractions) can redistribute momentum among parts but never change the total.
External forces (gravity, friction, applied pushes) change the total momentum — account for them before applying conservation.
The law is derived from Newton's third law and is more fundamental than Newton's laws themselves (it holds in quantum mechanics and relativity too).
In NEB exams, the derivation from the third law is a standard 3-4 mark question — memorize the exact steps.

data.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version emphasises the momentum form of Newton's second law and the impulse–momentum theorem with force–time graphs — the framing NEB theory questions use.

**Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ — mass in motion, SI unit kg·m/s. It is a VECTOR along the velocity. A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J).

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$ for a constant force, and $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ in general — the AREA under a force–time graph. Impulse has units N·s = kg·m/s, the same as momentum — by design.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. Bending your knees on landing, catching a cricket ball with draw-back hands, and jumping with flexed legs are all the same physics.

**Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

**NEB exam focus:** define momentum and impulse with units; state and use $F = dp/dt$; compute impulse from force–time graphs; apply $J = \Delta p$ to catches, kicks and landings; explain safety devices via the force–time argument.
formulas: Momentum: $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$  [kg·m/s]
Second law (general): $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$; constant mass: $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$
Impulse (constant force): $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\Delta t$; general: $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ (area under $F$–$t$)
Impulse–momentum theorem: $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$
Average force: $F_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$
confusion: ❌ 'Momentum and kinetic energy are interchangeable measures of motion.' ✅ Momentum $mv$ is a vector conserved in ALL collisions; kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is a scalar conserved only in elastic ones. Both grow with speed but differently.
❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

❌ 'The ball exerts no force on the bat while being hit because the bat is harder.' ✅ Newton's third law: contact forces are equal and opposite during the collision — the ball's velocity change comes from the contact force acting on IT.
❌ 'A heavy object always has more momentum.' ✅ Momentum = mass × VELOCITY — a light fast bullet can out-momentum a heavy slow trolley; direction matters too.
❌ Using $F = ma$ for a rocket ejecting fuel. ✅ Mass changes with time, so $F = ma$ fails; the momentum form $F = dp/dt$ handles it and yields the rocket equation.
❌ Impulse has units of newtons. ✅ N·s (= kg·m/s) — momentum units. Dimensionally $[MLT^{-1}]$.

data.title: Application of Newton's Laws
notes: **The problem-solving framework (the 'FBD method'):** (1) isolate the body, (2) draw ALL forces acting ON it (weight, normal, friction, tension, applied), (3) choose axes (one along acceleration), (4) write ΣF = ma for each axis, (5) solve. Every single NEB numerical follows this pattern.

**Elevator weight paradox:** in an accelerating upward elevator, the normal force N = m(g + a) — you feel heavier. Accelerating downward: N = m(g − a) — you feel lighter. Free fall (a = g): N = 0 (weightlessness). The weight mg never changes; what changes is the apparent weight (the normal force).

**Atwood's machine (two masses on a pulley):** acceleration a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂); tension T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂). The string is massless and inextensible; the pulley is frictionless — if not, extra terms appear.

**Connected bodies (push and pull):** a single force F applied to a system of masses (m₁, m₂, m₃) gives a = F/(m₁ + m₂ + m₃). The contact force between m₁ and m₂ is the force needed to accelerate the trailing masses: N = (m₂ + m₃) × a.

**Inclined plane:** weight components: mg sin θ down the slope, mg cos θ into the plane. Normal N = mg cos θ. With friction: net force down slope = mg sin θ − μmg cos θ. The body slides when sin θ > μ cos θ, i.e., tan θ > μ — the critical angle depends only on μ, NOT on mass.
**Worked example:** a 5 kg block on a 30° rough slope (μ = 0.3) — does it slide? tan 30° = 0.577 > 0.3 → yes. Acceleration: a = g(sin 30° − 0.3 cos 30°) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.26) = 2.35 m/s² down the slope.

**Apparent weight in fluids:** an object submerged in a liquid appears lighter by the buoyant force (Archimedes): apparent weight = mg − ρVg. This is still a Newton's second law application: ΣF = mg − ρVg = ma.

**NEB exam focus:** elevator problems, Atwood's machine, connected bodies on horizontal surfaces, inclined plane with/without friction, apparent weight in accelerating systems — all use the same FBD → ΣF = ma framework.
formulas: Newton's second law (vector): ΣF = ma → ΣF_x = ma_x, ΣF_y = ma_y
Elevator apparent weight: N = m(g ± a) where + is upward acceleration, − is downward
Atwood's machine: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂); T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂)
Smooth inclined plane: a = g sin θ down the slope; N = mg cos θ
Rough inclined plane: a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ); slides when tan θ > μ
confusion: ❌ 'The normal force is always mg.' ✅ N = mg only on a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration. On a slope N = mg cos θ; in an accelerating elevator N = m(g ± a).

❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act in the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.
❌ 'The tension in a string equals the weight of the hanging mass.' ✅ Only if the system is in equilibrium. In an accelerating Atwood's machine, T ≠ mg — use ΣF = ma on each mass to find T.
❌ 'Action and reaction forces cancel each other.' ✅ They act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel in a single FBD. Include only forces acting ON the body you are analyzing.
❌ 'Heavier bodies slide slower down a slope.' ✅ a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) has no mass term — all bodies slide at the same rate (if μ is the same), just like free fall.
❌ 'A body at rest has no forces acting on it.' ✅ Static equilibrium means ΣF = 0, not zero forces — weight and normal (and possibly friction and tension) all act, they just balance.

❌ 'A body at rest has no forces acting on it.' ✅ Static equilibrium means ΣF = 0, not zero forces — weight and normal (and possibly friction and tension) all act, they just balance.

data.title: Moment, Torque and Equilibrium
notes: **Torque (moment of a force):** τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the pivot to the point of application, F is the force, and θ is the angle between r and F. The SI unit is Nm. Torque is positive for anticlockwise rotation, negative for clockwise.

**Equilibrium of a rigid body:** two conditions must BOTH hold: (1) translational equilibrium: ΣF = 0 (no net force → no linear acceleration); (2) rotational equilibrium: Στ = 0 (no net torque → no angular acceleration). A body at rest or rotating at constant angular velocity satisfies both.

**Couple:** two equal and opposite forces separated by a distance d produce a pure torque (independent of pivot): τ = F × d. The net force is zero, so there is no linear acceleration — only rotation. The turning effect is the same about ANY point.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the single point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. For regular uniform bodies, the CG is at the geometric centre. For irregular bodies, it can be found by balancing or suspension.

**Worked example — seesaw:** a 40 kg child sits 2 m from the fulcrum. Where must a 50 kg child sit to balance? Torque balance: 40×9.8×2 = 50×9.8×x → x = 1.6 m. The heavier child sits closer to the fulcrum.

**Worked example — ladder:** a uniform ladder of length L leans against a smooth wall at angle θ. The wall reaction is horizontal (smooth), the ground reaction has both normal and friction components. Torque about the base eliminates the unknown ground reaction: N_wall × L sin θ = mg × (L/2) cos θ.

**Equilibrium in the NEB exam:** the standard problem is a beam/ladder/plank with multiple forces — apply ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, and Στ = 0 (choosing the pivot wisely to eliminate unknowns). Three equations for up to three unknowns.

**Practical examples:** opening a door (push at the handle, not near the hinge — larger r gives more τ), using a spanner (longer handle = more torque for the same force), a wheelbarrow (load CG near the wheel reduces the lifting torque).

data.title: Solid Friction
notes: **What friction is:** a contact force that opposes relative motion (or its tendency) between two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the contact surface. Static friction (no sliding) and kinetic friction (sliding) are the two main types.

**Laws of friction:** (1) Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact (to a good approximation). (2) Maximum static friction and kinetic friction are both proportional to the normal reaction: f_s(max) = μ_sN, f_k = μ_kN. (3) μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

**Static friction is a variable force:** it matches the applied force up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_sN. If you push with 30 N and the object doesn't move, f_s = 30 N (not μ_sN). Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.

**Angle of friction (λ):** the angle between the normal reaction and the resultant reaction (normal + friction) when slipping is about to occur. tan λ = μ_s. The resultant reaction makes angle λ with the normal.

**Angle of repose (θ_r):** the steepest angle of a slope at which a body just remains at rest. At this angle, mg sin θ_r = μ_s mg cos θ_r → tan θ_r = μ_s. So θ_r = λ — the angle of repose equals the angle of friction.

**Worked example — body on a slope:** a 10 kg block on a 25° slope (μ_s = 0.5). Does it slide? tan 25° = 0.466 < 0.5 → no, it stays. Static friction = mg sin 25° = 41.5 N (less than μ_sN = 0.5 × 92.4 = 46.2 N).

**Worked example — pulling a block:** a 5 kg block on a horizontal surface (μ_k = 0.3). Pulled by a 20 N force at 30° above horizontal. Normal N = mg − F sin 30° = 49 − 10 = 39 N. Friction = 0.3 × 39 = 11.7 N. Net force = 20 cos 30° − 11.7 = 5.6 N. a = 5.6/5 = 1.12 m/s².

**NEB exam focus:** distinguish static vs kinetic friction; solve slope problems (does it slide? find acceleration); angle of repose and its equality with angle of friction; pulling/pushing at an angle (changes the normal, hence friction).
**Friction:** the force that opposes relative motion (or impending motion) between two surfaces in contact. It arises from microscopic irregularities and molecular adhesion between surfaces.
**Coefficient of friction $\mu$:** $\mu = \frac{F}{R}$, where $F$ is the limiting frictional force and $R$ is the normal reaction. $\mu$ is dimensionless — it is a ratio of two forces.

**Laws of friction:** (1) Friction acts opposite to the direction of impending motion. (2) Limiting friction $F_s = \mu_s R$, proportional to the normal reaction. (3) Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact (for a given normal force). (4) Friction depends on the nature and condition of the surfaces in contact.

**Static vs kinetic friction:** static friction adjusts up to a maximum $F_{s,max} = \mu_s R$; kinetic friction is approximately constant at $F_k = \mu_k R$, where typically $\mu_s > \mu_k$. This is why it is harder to start moving an object than to keep it moving.

**Angle of friction $\lambda$:** the angle between the resultant contact force and the normal reaction when limiting friction is reached. $\tan\lambda = \mu_s$. When the incline angle equals the angle of friction, the body is on the point of sliding.
**Angle of repose:** the maximum angle of an incline at which a body just rests on the plane without sliding. It equals the angle of friction: $\theta_{repose} = \lambda = \tan^{-1}\mu_s$.

**Verification of area independence:** experiments show that for a given normal force, doubling the contact area halves the pressure but leaves the frictional force unchanged because the increased number of molecular interactions compensates.
**Rolling friction:** much smaller than sliding friction because rolling deforms surfaces less and the contact time per point is shorter. Ball bearings use this principle to reduce friction.
**Units check:** $\mu = F/R$ — both numerator and denominator are forces, so $\mu$ is dimensionless. Friction force $F = \mu R$ has units of newtons.

Kinetic friction: f_k = μ_kN (acts during sliding; μ_k < μ_s)
Slope sliding condition: body slides when tan θ > μ_s; a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ)
Angle of friction: tan λ = μ_s (angle between normal and resultant reaction)
Angle of repose: tan θ_r = μ_s → θ_r = λ (steepest angle for rest)

confusion: ❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act IN the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.

❌ 'Friction depends on the area of contact.' ✅ For a given normal force, friction is (approximately) independent of area. A wide tyre and a narrow tyre with the same load have the same maximum friction (in the simple model).
❌ 'Static friction is always μ_sN.' ✅ Static friction is VARIABLE: it matches the applied force up to μ_sN. Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.
❌ 'μ_k > μ_s because sliding is faster.' ✅ μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding. This is why a heavy box jerks when you first push it.
❌ 'The angle of repose depends on the mass of the body.' ✅ tan θ_r = μ_s — mass cancels out. All bodies with the same μ_s have the same angle of repose.

❌ 'Pulling a block at an angle reduces friction because the force is smaller.' ✅ Pulling upward reduces the normal (N = mg − F sin θ), which reduces friction. Pushing downward increases the normal and friction.

Friction is NOT always opposite to the direction of motion — it is opposite to the direction of relative motion (or impending relative motion) between the two surfaces. For example, when you walk, friction on your foot points forward (in the direction of motion), preventing your foot from slipping backward.

The friction force is NOT always $\mu R$. This formula gives the LIMITING (maximum static) friction. For static friction, $f_s \leq \mu_s R$, and the actual value adjusts to match the applied force up to the maximum.

Friction being independent of area is an approximation that holds for rigid bodies with moderate contact pressures. For very soft materials (like rubber tyres) or very high pressures, the relationship becomes more complex.

$\mu_s > \mu_k$ is generally true but not universal. Some materials (like Teflon on Teflon) have nearly equal coefficients, and certain combinations can even have $\mu_k > \mu_s$ under specific conditions.

The normal reaction $R$ is NOT always equal to $mg$. On an inclined plane, $R = mg\cos\theta$. If an additional vertical force is applied, $R$ changes accordingly. Always determine $R$ from force equilibrium in the direction perpendicular to the surface.

specificConditions: **Static vs. Kinetic Threshold:** The maximum static friction $f_s^{\max} = \mu_s N$ is the *upper bound* for static friction. Static friction is a *variable* force that matches the applied force up to this limit. Kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ applies *only* when sliding occurs, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$.

**Normal Force Dependency:** Friction is proportional to the *normal reaction*, not the weight. Any vertical force component (pulling up, pushing down, incline) changes $N$, which directly changes the friction force. Always compute $N$ first.

**Area Independence (Ideal Model):** The laws of friction assume friction is independent of the apparent contact area (Coulomb's model). This holds well for dry, rigid surfaces but breaks down for soft materials, lubricated contacts, or adhesive forces where real contact area matters.

A 10 kg box rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Find the minimum horizontal force needed to start the box moving. Solution: $R = mg = 10 \times 9.8 = 98$ N. Limiting friction $F_s = \mu_s R = 0.5 \times 98 = 49$ N. Minimum force to start motion = 49 N.

A 5 kg block slides down an incline of angle 30° at constant velocity. Find the coefficient of kinetic friction. Solution: At constant velocity, acceleration is zero, so forces are balanced: $mg\sin\theta = \mu_k mg\cos\theta$. $\mu_k = \tan\theta = \tan 30° = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.577$.

A 20 kg crate is pushed across a floor with a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.3. If the crate moves at constant speed, find the applied force. Solution: $R = mg = 20 \times 9.8 = 196$ N. $F_k = \mu_k R = 0.3 \times 196 = 58.8$ N. Since velocity is constant, applied force = friction force = 58.8 N.

An inclined plane is raised until a block just begins to slide at angle 35°. Find the coefficient of static friction and the angle of friction. Solution: At the point of sliding, $\mu_s = \tan\theta = \tan 35° \approx 0.700$. The angle of friction $\lambda = \tan^{-1}(\mu_s) = 35°$. The angle of repose equals the angle of friction.

A 8 kg block is on a horizontal surface ($\mu_s = 0.6$, $\mu_k = 0.4$). A horizontal force of 30 N is applied. Find the friction force and acceleration. Solution: $R = mg = 8 \times 9.8 = 78.4$ N. $F_{s,max} = 0.6 \times 78.4 = 47.04$ N. Since applied force (30 N) < $F_{s,max}$ (47.04 N), the block does not move. Friction force = 30 N (equal and opposite to applied force). Acceleration = 0.

The laws of friction were first systematically studied by Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), but they were rediscovered and formalized by Guillaume Amontons in 1699 and further refined by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785.
The coefficient of friction for rubber on dry concrete is about 1.0, while for ice on steel it is only about 0.03 — a factor of 33 difference, explaining why ice skating is possible.
Friction generates heat: the work done against friction is converted into thermal energy. This is why brakes get hot and why meteoroids burn up in the atmosphere.

In ideal mathematical models, friction is treated as independent of contact area and sliding speed. In reality, both factors can affect friction, especially for rubber, polymers, and at very high or very low speeds.

The friction force can do positive, negative, or zero work depending on the reference frame. In the frame of the surface, friction on a sliding object does negative work; in the frame of a moving conveyor belt, friction can do positive work on an object placed on it.

data.title: Hooke's Law and Force Constant
notes: **Hooke's law statement:** For small deformations, the extension (or compression) of an elastic body is directly proportional to the applied force: F = kx, where F is the applied force, x is the deformation, and k is the spring (force) constant. This linear region is called the elastic limit.

**Force (spring) constant k:** k = F/x, measured in N/m. It measures the stiffness of the spring — a stiffer spring has a larger k and needs a bigger force for the same extension. k depends on the material, the wire diameter, the number of coils and the length of the spring.

**What Spring constant really means:** a spring of k = 200 N/m requires 200 N to stretch it by 1 metre. To stretch by any x, you need F = 200x N. It is the slope of the F–x graph in the linear (Hookean) region.

**Two ways to combine springs:** series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ (softer than either); parallel: k = k₁ + k₂ (stiffer than either). Series springs stretch more for the same load — think of a long telephone-cord spring vs two short springs joined.
**Worked example:** a force of 40 N stretches a spring by 8 cm. k = F/x = 40/0.08 = 500 N/m. A 100 N force will then stretch it by x = 100/500 = 0.2 m = 20 cm.

**Hooke's law on a graph:** the F–x graph is a straight line through the origin while the elastic limit is respected. Beyond it, the graph curves; after plastic deformation, a larger force is needed for the same extension or the body does not return to its original length.

**Application — weight balance (spring balance):** the extension of a calibrated spring measures the applied weight. Since F = kx and weight = mg, the scale can be marked directly in newtons or kilograms.

**Conditions for Hooke's law to hold:** the deformation must be small, elastic (the body returns to original shape when the load is removed), and within the proportional limit. Overstretching a spring permanently changes its k.
formulas: Hooke's law: F = kx
Spring constant: k = F/x (units N/m)
Series springs: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂
Parallel springs: k = k₁ + k₂
Elastic potential energy: U = ½kx²; oscillation ω = √(k/m)
confusion: ❌ 'F = kx means force depends on extension.' ✅ Precisely that — for a spring, doubling the extension doubles the stretching force needed. The spring PULLS back with force kx (restoring force) opposite to the applied load.

❌ 'k is a property only of the material.' ✅ k depends on the geometry too (length, coil radius, number of coils, wire thickness). It is the material property (Young's modulus) together with geometry that fixes k.
❌ 'A stiffer spring stretches more.' ✅ A stiffer spring stretches LESS for the same force — it has a larger k, so x = F/k is smaller.
❌ 'Extension is proportional to force at all loads.' ✅ Only within the elastic (proportional) limit. Beyond it the graph bends, and past the yield point the spring deforms permanently.
❌ 'Series springs are stiffer.' ✅ Series springs are SOFTER (smaller total k). Two identical springs in series have k/2; in parallel they have 2k.
❌ 'Force constant and friction constant (μ) are the same.' ✅ k (N/m) relates force to displacement of a spring; μ is a dimensionless friction coefficient relating friction to normal reaction.

**Application — weight balance (spring balance):** the extension of a calibrated spring measures the applied weight. Since F = kx and weight = mg, the scale can be marked directly in newtons or kilograms.

**Conditions for Hooke's law to hold:** the deformation must be small, elastic (the body returns to original shape when the load is removed), and within the proportional limit. Overstretching a spring permanently changes its k.
