confusion: ❌ 'F = kx means force depends on extension.' ✅ Precisely that — for a spring, doubling the extension doubles the stretching force needed. The spring PULLS back with force kx (restoring force) opposite to the applied load.

❌ 'k is a property only of the material.' ✅ k depends on the geometry too (length, coil radius, number of coils, wire thickness). It is the material property (Young's modulus) together with geometry that fixes k.
❌ 'A stiffer spring stretches more.' ✅ A stiffer spring stretches LESS for the same force — it has a larger k, so x = F/k is smaller.
❌ 'Extension is proportional to force at all loads.' ✅ Only within the elastic (proportional) limit. Beyond it the graph bends, and past the yield point the spring deforms permanently.
❌ 'Series springs are stiffer.' ✅ Series springs are SOFTER (smaller total k). Two identical springs in series have k/2; in parallel they have 2k.
❌ 'Force constant and friction constant (μ) are the same.' ✅ k (N/m) relates force to displacement of a spring; μ is a dimensionless friction coefficient relating friction to normal reaction.

data.title: Stress, Strain, Elasticity and Plasticity
notes: **Stress (σ):** the internal resisting force per unit area set up in a body when external forces are applied: σ = F/A. Empirical units are N/m² or Pa (pascal). Normal stress = force perpendicular to the area (tension/compression); shear stress = force parallel to the area.

**Strain (ε):** the fractional deformation produced: strain = change in dimension / original dimension. It is dimensionless. Linear strain = Δl/l, shear strain = θ (angle of shear), volumetric strain = ΔV/V.

**Elasticity and plasticity:** elasticity is the property of a body to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed. Plasticity is the property of remaining permanently deformed after the deforming force is removed. Bodies are elastic below the elastic limit and plastic beyond it.

**Hooke's law in stress-strain form:** within the elastic limit, stress ∝ strain: σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus (N/m²). This is the generalised Hooke's law — stress and strain are proportional until the elastic limit.

**Stress-strain curve regions:** (1) linear (proportional) region up to the proportional limit; (2) elastic region up to the elastic limit (still recovers fully); (3) yielding at the yield point (permanent deformation begins); (4) plastic deformation region where the material flows; (5) ultimate tensile strength (maximum stress), then (6) fracture/breaking point.

**Worked example — a wire under tension:** a steel wire of length 2 m and cross-section 1 mm² (10⁻⁶ m²) carries a 20 kg load. F = 196 N, σ = 196/10⁻⁶ = 1.96 × 10⁸ Pa. If E_steel = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, strain ε = σ/E = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴, so extension Δl = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴ × 2 = 1.96 mm.

**Thermal Stress:** If a wire is constrained and temperature changes, stress develops: $σ = EαΔT$, where α is the coefficient of linear expansion. This is crucial in bridge construction and railway tracks.

**Types of stress & strain (NEB focus):** tensile/compressive (longitudinal), shear (tangential), and volume (hydrostatic). Each has its own modulus: Young's modulus E = σ_t/ε_l, shear modulus G = τ/θ, bulk modulus B = −P/(ΔV/V).

**Ductile vs brittle materials:** ductile (copper, mild steel) show a long plastic region — they deform before breaking and are used for wires. Brittle (glass, cast iron) show little or no plastic region — they break suddenly near the elastic limit, which is why glass shatters.
formulas: Stress: σ = F/A (N/m² or Pa)
Strain: ε = Δl/l (dimensionless; ε_V = ΔV/V, shear ε = θ)
Hooke's law in stress–strain form: σ = Eε
Young's modulus: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl)
Bulk modulus: B = −P/(ΔV/V); Shear modulus: G = τ/θ

❌ 'Strain has units.' ✅ Strain is dimensionless — it is a ratio of lengths (or volumes/angles). This is essential for dimensional analysis.
❌ 'Elasticity means materials are always elastic.' ✅ Every material is elastic only up to its elastic limit; beyond it, plastic deformation occurs.
❌ 'Stress equals force.' ✅ Stress is force PER unit area (σ = F/A). Doubling the area halves the stress for the same force.
❌ 'The stress–strain graph is a straight line everywhere.' ✅ Only up to the proportional limit. After that it curves at the yield point and beyond.
❌ 'A ductile material breaks near the elastic limit.' ✅ DUCTILE materials deform plastically and stretch before fracturing; brittle materials break with little warning near the elastic limit.

data.title: Elastic modulus: Young modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus
notes: **Stress and strain.** Stress is the restoring force per unit area (F/A) and strain is the fractional deformation (ΔL/L); within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law).
**Young's modulus.** Y = longitudinal stress ÷ longitudinal strain = FL/AΔL; it measures a material's resistance to stretching or compression along its length.
**Bulk modulus.** K = −P ÷ (ΔV/V); the negative sign shows volume decreases under pressure, and its reciprocal is the compressibility of the material.
**Shear modulus.** G = shear stress ÷ shear strain = (F/A) ÷ (Δx/L); it measures resistance to change of shape at constant volume.
**Poisson's ratio.** σ = −(lateral strain ÷ longitudinal strain); for most stable materials it lies between 0 and 0.5, and elastic potential energy per unit volume is ½ stress × strain.

**Young's modulus (E):** the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl). It measures resistance to stretching/compression. For steel, E ≈ 2×10¹¹ N/m²; for aluminium ≈ 7×10¹⁰ N/m²; for rubber ≈ 5×10⁶ N/m².

**Bulk modulus (B):** the ratio of volume stress (pressure) to volume strain: B = −P/(ΔV/V). It measures resistance to uniform compression. The minus sign keeps B positive (ΔV is negative under pressure). For water B ≈ 2.2×10⁹ Pa; steel B ≈ 1.6×10¹¹ Pa.

**Shear modulus / modulus of rigidity (G or η):** the ratio of shear stress to shear strain: G = τ/θ = (F/A)/θ. It measures resistance to change of shape without change of volume. For steel G ≈ 8×10¹⁰ N/m².

**Key relation between moduli (for isotropic materials):** E = 2G(1 + σ) and E = 3B(1 − 2σ), where σ is Poisson's ratio. Combining them: 9/B = 3/G + 1/E or E = 9BG/(3B + G). These links let you compute one modulus from the others.

**Worked example — Young's modulus:** a wire of length 2 m and area 1 mm² extends 1 mm under a 50 kg load. F = 490 N, σ = 490/10⁻⁶ = 4.9×10⁸ Pa, ε = 10⁻³/2 = 5×10⁻⁴, E = 4.9×10⁸/5×10⁻⁴ = 9.8×10¹¹ ≈ 10¹¹ N/m².
**Worked example — bulk modulus:** 10⁵ Pa pressure on 1 m³ of water changes its volume by 4.5×10⁻⁵ m³. B = 10⁵/(4.5×10⁻⁵) = 2.2×10⁹ Pa.
**Compressibility:** the reciprocal of bulk modulus: k = 1/B. Fluids with high B are hard to compress; gases have very low B.
**Which modulus to use?** stretching a wire → Young's modulus; squeezing a sphere → bulk modulus; twisting/sliding layers → shear modulus. Choose by the type of deformation.

Elastic moduli: Young's Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L); Bulk K = −P/(ΔV/V); Shear G = (F/A)/(Δx/L).
Elastic potential energy U = ½FΔL = ½kx². Poisson's ratio σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) ≈ 0.25–0.35 for most metals.
Thomas Young established the concept of the modulus of elasticity in 1807 — his modulus E is one of the most fundamental material constants.
Rigidity (shear) modulus explains why liquids flow: their G = 0 — they cannot resist shear.
Diamond has the largest E of all materials (≈ 1.2×10¹² N/m²), which is why it is used for cutting tools.
Rubber has a low E but a very high elastic limit — it can stretch hundreds of percent before breaking.
Ultrasound techniques measure tissue Young's modulus for medical diagnosis (elastography).

**Anisotropic Materials:** In crystals and composites, elastic moduli depend on direction. Wood is much stronger along the grain than across it. This is described by the stiffness tensor with up to 21 independent constants for the most general anisotropic material.

specificConditions: **Material State Determines Available Moduli:** Solids have all three moduli ($E, B, G$). Fluids (liquids/gases) have *only* bulk modulus $B$ — they cannot sustain shear stress ($G=0$) and have no defined Young's modulus for stretching.

**Isotropic Material Relations:** For isotropic solids, the three moduli are linked via Poisson's ratio $\sigma$: $E = 2G(1+\sigma) = 3B(1-2\sigma)$. These relations *do not hold* for anisotropic materials (crystals, composites) where moduli depend on direction.

**Geometry Separation:** $E$ is an intensive material property (Pa), while spring constant $k = EA/L$ is extensive. Changing a wire's length or cross-section changes $k$ but not $E$ — this distinction is essential for connecting spring problems to material science.

data.title: Poisson's Ratio
notes: **Poisson's ratio (σ):** when a body is stretched (or compressed), it becomes thinner (or thicker) in the perpendicular directions. Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain: σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) = −(β/α). The minus sign keeps σ positive because lateral strain is opposite in sign to longitudinal strain.
**Why it is dimensionless:** Poisson's ratio divides one strain by another — strain is dimensionless, so σ has no units and no dimensions. Its value for most materials lies between 0 and 0.5.

**Typical values:** cork ≈ 0 (no lateral change), concrete ≈ 0.1–0.2, steel ≈ 0.25–0.3, copper ≈ 0.33, aluminium ≈ 0.34, rubber ≈ 0.5 (nearly incompressible). A hypothetical material with σ = 0.5 would conserve volume exactly.

**Worked example — wire stretch:** a wire of length 2 m and diameter 1 mm is stretched by 2 mm. Longitudinal strain = 2×10⁻³/2 = 10⁻³. If σ = 0.3, lateral strain = −0.3×10⁻³, so diameter change = 0.3×10⁻³ × 1 mm = 3×10⁻⁴ mm = 0.3 μm (a fractional diameter change of 3×10⁻⁴).

**Relation with the moduli:** σ links Young's modulus E, bulk modulus B and shear modulus G: E = 2G(1 + σ) and E = 3B(1 − 2σ). From these: 1/σ can be used to check material consistency, and σ = (3B − E)/(6B).
**Connection to volume change:** the fractional volume change under uniaxial stretch is ΔV/V = ε(1 − 2σ). For a perfectly incompressible material (σ = 0.5), ΔV/V = 0 — the volume is unchanged.

**Limits on σ:** the thermodynamic bound is −1 < σ < 0.5. Nearly all common materials have 0 < σ < 0.5. Materials with negative Poisson's ratio (auxetics) actually thicken when stretched — rare and exotic.

**Applications:** σ matters in designing cables, stretching films, and geological materials; cork (σ≈0) is chosen for bottle stoppers because it doesn't change width when squeezed, so it seals without expanding.

Relation with moduli: E = 2G(1 + σ); E = 3B(1 − 2σ)
σ from E and B: σ = (3B − E)/(6B)
σ from E and G: σ = E/(2G) − 1
Fractional volume change: ΔV/V = ε(1 − 2σ)
confusion: ❌ 'Poisson's ratio has units of strain.' ✅ It is a RATIO of two strains — dimensionless.
❌ 'Poisson's ratio can be greater than 1.' ✅ No — the thermodynamic limit is 0.5 for isotropic materials (a few exotic anisotropic materials exceed 0.5 but never 1).
❌ 'Lateral strain equals longitudinal strain.' ✅ Lateral strain = −σ × longitudinal strain, with σ typically between 0 and 0.5.
❌ 'When stretched, volume always increases.' ✅ If σ = 0.5 the volume is constant; for σ < 0.5 the volume increases slightly (ΔV/V = ε(1−2σ)).
❌ 'Cork and rubber have similar σ.' ✅ Cork ≈ 0, rubber ≈ 0.5 — at opposite ends of the range.
❌ 'Poisson's ratio is a force.' ✅ It is a pure, dimensionless ratio of deformation (strain) — not a force or modulus.

data.title: Elastic Potential Energy
notes: **Young's modulus (E):** the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain: E = (F/A)/(Δl/l) = Fl/(AΔl). It measures resistance to stretching/compression. For steel, E ≈ 2×10¹¹ N/m²; for aluminium ≈ 7×10¹⁰ N/m²; for rubber ≈ 5×10⁶ N/m².

**Bulk modulus (B):** the ratio of volume stress (pressure) to volume strain: B = −P/(ΔV/V). It measures resistance to uniform compression. The minus sign keeps B positive (ΔV is negative under pressure). For water B ≈ 2.2×10⁹ Pa; steel B ≈ 1.6×10¹¹ Pa.

**Shear modulus / modulus of rigidity (G or η):** the ratio of shear stress to shear strain: G = τ/θ = (F/A)/θ. It measures resistance to change of shape without change of volume. For steel G ≈ 8×10¹⁰ N/m².

**Key relation between moduli (for isotropic materials):** E = 2G(1 + σ) and E = 3B(1 − 2σ), where σ is Poisson's ratio. Combining them: 9/B = 3/G + 1/E or E = 9BG/(3B + G). These links let you compute one modulus from the others.

**Worked example — Young's modulus:** a wire of length 2 m and area 1 mm² extends 1 mm under a 50 kg load. F = 490 N, σ = 490/10⁻⁶ = 4.9×10⁸ Pa, ε = 10⁻³/2 = 5×10⁻⁴, E = 4.9×10⁸/5×10⁻⁴ = 9.8×10¹¹ ≈ 10¹¹ N/m².
**Worked example — bulk modulus:** 10⁵ Pa pressure on 1 m³ of water changes its volume by 4.5×10⁻⁵ m³. B = 10⁵/(4.5×10⁻⁵) = 2.2×10⁹ Pa.
**Compressibility:** the reciprocal of bulk modulus: k = 1/B. Fluids with high B are hard to compress; gases have very low B.
**Which modulus to use?** stretching a wire → Young's modulus; squeezing a sphere → bulk modulus; twisting/sliding layers → shear modulus. Choose by the type of deformation.

data.title: Electric charges
notes: **Nature of charge.** Charge is the property that produces electric force; like charges repel and unlike attract, and the SI unit is the coulomb (C).
**Quantisation and conservation.** Charge is quantised in units of e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (q = ne) and is conserved — the net charge of an isolated system never changes.
**Conductors and insulators.** Conductors (metals) allow charge to move freely, while insulators hold charge in place; excess charge resides on the outer surface of a conductor.
**Charging methods.** Bodies are charged by friction (transfer of electrons), conduction (contact) and induction (redistribution without contact, followed by earthing).
**Coulomb's law.** Two point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by r exert force F = (1/4πε₀)q₁q₂/r²; the constant 1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².

**Electric Charge & Elementary Charge:** Electric charge is an intrinsic physical property of elementary matter that governs all electromagnetic interactions. Charges exist in two polarities designated by Benjamin Franklin as positive (carried by protons, $+e$) and negative (carried by electrons, $-e$). The elementary charge quantum is $e \approx 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. Charge is a scalar quantity with SI unit Coulomb ($\text{C} = \text{A}\cdot\text{s}$) and dimensions $[I\,T]$.

**Quantization of Charge:** Electric charge is not continuous; it exists only in discrete integral multiples of the elementary electronic charge: $q = \pm n e$, where $n \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. Quantization was first demonstrated macroscopically by Robert Millikan's oil-drop experiment (1909). At macroscopic scales involving microcoulombs, the graininess is obscured ($1\,\mu\text{C} \approx 6.24 \times 10^{12}$ electrons), allowing charge to be treated as continuous.

**Conservation & Additivity of Charge:** In any isolated thermodynamic system, the algebraic sum of all electric charges remains strictly constant regardless of physical or chemical transformations: $\sum q_{initial} = \sum q_{final}$. In addition, charge is additive (total charge of an extended body is the scalar algebraic sum $\sum q_i$) and relativistically invariant (the magnitude of charge is independent of the reference frame speed, unlike mass).

**Methods of Charging — Friction & Conduction:** Neutral matter is charged by electron transfer: (1) **Triboelectric effect (Friction):** When two differing materials (e.g., glass and silk, or amber and wool) are rubbed, work function differences drive electron transfer from the lower to higher work function material; (2) **Conduction (Contact):** Direct contact between a charged conductor and a neutral conductor allows electron flow until both bodies achieve identical electrostatic potentials.

**Charging by Electrostatic Induction:** Charging by induction produces a net static charge on a conductor without physical contact with the charging source. Bringing a positively charged rod near an isolated neutral conductor repels positive ions conceptually while attracting mobile free conduction electrons toward the near face (polarization). Grounding the far face discharges positive potential by drawing electrons from Earth. Severing the ground connection before withdrawing the rod permanently traps an opposite negative charge on the conductor.

**Gold-Leaf Electroscope & Charge Detection:** The gold-leaf electroscope is a classical electrostatic apparatus comprising a brass rod, brass disc, and two ultra-thin gold leaves housed in an evacuated glass enclosure. Divergence of the leaves signals the presence of charge via mutual electrostatic repulsion. The electroscope can identify charge sign by observing leaf divergence when an unknown charge is brought near a pre-charged electroscope.

Thinking induction creates new charge: Induction does not generate charge from nothing; it redistributes existing mobile valence electrons within the conductor while preserving net charge conservation of the combined system.

Believing grounding always pulls electrons down to Earth: If a positively charged rod is inducing negative charge near it, grounding pulls electrons UP from the Earth into the conductor. If a negative rod is near, electrons flow DOWN into the Earth.

Assuming insulators can be charged permanently by induction: Only materials with delocalized mobile charges (conductors) can be charged by induction and grounding. Insulators experience only molecular dielectric polarization.

(b) How many electrons must be removed from the sphere? Solution: (a) To induce a net positive charge on the conductor, a negatively charged rod must be brought near it, driving electrons to ground when earthed. (b) Using quantization $q = ne$: $n = \frac{q}{e} = \frac{3.2 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{C}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 2.0 \times 10^9$ electrons transferred to Earth.

Potential V = kq/r; ΔV = W/q; U of a charge in potential = qV. Equipotential surfaces are ⟂ to field lines.

Charge is an absolute relativistic invariant: an electron's charge remains exactly $1.602176634 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$ whether at rest in a laboratory or traveling at $99.999\%$ the speed of light in the Large Hadron Collider.

Quarks carry fractional charges ($+\frac{2}{3}e$ and $-\frac{1}{3}e$), but because of quantum chromodynamic color confinement, quarks never exist as isolated free particles; all observable free entities have integer charge multiples $ne$.

data.summary: Electric charge is a fundamental, quantized ($q = ne$), and conserved property of matter. Objects can be charged by triboelectric friction, conduction, or electrostatic induction. Charging by induction polarizes mobile electrons in an insulated conductor; momentary grounding allows electron exchange with Earth, permanently trapping an opposite net charge on the conductor without losing inducing charge.

data.title: Coulomb's Law
notes: **Coulomb's Law of Electrostatics:** Formulated by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785, the electrostatic force between two stationary point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: $F = k \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$. The electrostatic force acts along the line connecting the centers of the two charges, being repulsive for like charges ($q_1 q_2 > 0$) and attractive for unlike charges ($q_1 q_2 < 0$).

**Electrostatic Constant & Permittivity of Free Space:** The proportionality constant in vacuum/air is $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \approx 8.98755 \times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2 \approx 9 \times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$. Here $\varepsilon_0$ denotes the electric permittivity of free space, with value $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^2/(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2) = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}$ and dimensions $[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 I^2]$.

**Vector Formulation & Newton's Third Law:** In vector notation, the force $\vec{F}_{12}$ exerted on charge $q_1$ by charge $q_2$ located at position vector $\vec{r}_2$ is: $\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{|\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2|^3} (\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{21}$. Because $\hat{r}_{12} = -\hat{r}_{21}$, it follows rigorously that $\vec{F}_{12} = -\vec{F}_{21}$. Thus, electrostatic forces between two charges constitute an action-reaction pair satisfying Newton's Third Law in its strong central-force form.

**Dielectric Medium & Relative Permittivity:** When point charges are embedded within an insulating medium of permittivity $\varepsilon$, dielectric polarization shields the charges, reducing the net force to $F_m = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon} \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2} = \frac{F_0}{\varepsilon_r} = \frac{F_0}{\kappa}$. The dimensionless quantity $\kappa = \varepsilon_r = \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0} \ge 1$ is the dielectric constant (relative permittivity) of the medium (for vacuum $\kappa = 1$, dry air $\approx 1.0006$, water $\approx 80$, ideal conductor $\kappa \to \infty$).

**Principle of Linear Superposition:** Electrostatic interaction between any pair of charges is completely unaffected by the presence of other surrounding charges. Consequently, the net electrostatic force on a test charge $q_0$ due to a discrete distribution of $N$ point charges $q_1, q_2, \dots, q_N$ is the vector sum: $\vec{F}_{net} = \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{F}_{0i} = \frac{q_0}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{q_i}{|\vec{r}_0 - \vec{r}_i|^3} (\vec{r}_0 - \vec{r}_i)$.

**Electrostatic Equilibrium & Earnshaw's Theorem:** A system of charges is in equilibrium if the net electrostatic force on each constituent charge vanishes ($\sum \vec{F} = 0$). By Earnshaw's theorem (derived from Gauss's law $\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{E} = 0$ in charge-free regions), a collection of stationary point charges cannot be maintained in a state of stable equilibrium solely under the influence of inverse-square electrostatic interactions.
formulas: Coulomb's Law (magnitude): $F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$
Coulomb's Law (vector form): $\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\hat{r}_{21} = -\vec{F}_{21}$
Force in dielectric medium: $F_m = \frac{F_0}{\varepsilon_r} = \frac{F_0}{\kappa} = \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\varepsilon_0} \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$
Principle of Superposition: $\vec{F}_{net} = \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{F}_i$
Proportionality constant in vacuum: $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \approx 8.99 \times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$
confusion: Adding electrostatic forces as scalar algebraic quantities: Electric forces are vectors! When calculating the net force exerted by multiple charges, one must resolve each pairwise force into Cartesian orthogonal components ($F_x, F_y$) before summing: $F_{net} = \sqrt{(\sum F_x)^2 + (\sum F_y)^2}$.

Ignoring the medium's dielectric screening: In water ($\kappa \approx 80$), the electrostatic force between ions drops to $\frac{1}{80}$ of its vacuum value, explaining why table salt ($NaCl$) spontaneously dissociates into hydrated $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$ ions in water.

Applying Coulomb's law to extended charge distributions at close range: Coulomb's inverse-square formula applies strictly to point charges or non-overlapping spherical charge distributions (via Shell Theorem). At close range, induction distorts charge distribution on real conductors.
data.topicTitle: Coulomb's law; force between multiple charges
practice: Two identical positive point charges $q_1 = q_2 = +2.0\,\mu\text{C}$ are placed at coordinates $(0, 0.3\text{ m})$ and $(0, -0.3\text{ m})$ along the y-axis. A third point charge $q_0 = +4.0\,\mu\text{C}$ is placed on the x-axis at $(0.4\text{ m}, 0)$. Find the magnitude and direction of the net electrostatic force acting on $q_0$. Solution: Distance from each charge to $q_0$ is $r = \sqrt{0.4^2 + 0.3^2} = 0.5\text{ m}$. Force magnitude from one charge: $F_1 = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(2 \times 10^{-6})(4 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.5)^2} = \frac{0.072}{0.25} = 0.288\text{ N}$. Angle with x-axis: $\cos\theta = 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8$, $\sin\theta = 0.3 / 0.5 = 0.6$. By symmetry, vertical components cancel ($F_{1y} - F_{2y} = 0$). Net horizontal force: $F_{net} = 2 F_1 \cos\theta = 2(0.288)(0.8) = 0.461\text{ N}$ directed along $+x$ axis.
universalFacts: The electrostatic force between two protons inside a nucleus is approximately $10^{36}$ times stronger than the gravitational force between them: $\frac{F_e}{F_g} = \frac{e^2 / (4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2)}{G m_p^2 / r^2} \approx 1.24 \times 10^{36}$, showing the colossal dominance of electromagnetism over gravity at microscopic scales.

Coulomb's law has been tested experimentally to an accuracy of better than 1 part in $10^{16}$, establishing the inverse power $r^{-(2+\delta)}$ with $|delta| < 10^{-16}$, proving the photon has zero rest mass.
examples: Ionic lattice cohesion in minerals: Table salt crystals ($NaCl$) are held together by Coulomb attraction between alternating $Na^+$ cations and $Cl^-$ anions, providing a high melting point of 801 °C.

Atomic electron orbitals: In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the electrostatic Coulomb attraction between the single proton nucleus and orbiting electron ($F = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$) provides the required centripetal acceleration ($m v^2 / r$).

Dissolution in polar solvents: The high dielectric constant of liquid water ($\kappa \approx 80$) reduces ionic attraction by a factor of 80, permitting thermal agitation to break ionic bonds and dissolve salts.

keyPoints: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square central force acting along the line connecting two stationary point charges.
Vector formulation demonstrates mutual symmetry: $\vec{F}_{12} = -\vec{F}_{21}$, fulfilling Newton's third law.
Presence of a dielectric medium with relative permittivity $\kappa > 1$ reduces electrostatic force by a factor of $\kappa$.
The principle of superposition allows independent pairwise summation of forces in multi-charge configurations.
Earnshaw's theorem establishes that stable electrostatic equilibrium of stationary point charges is impossible without non-electrostatic constraints.
data.summary: Coulomb's Law quantifies the electrostatic force between two stationary point charges as directly proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: F = k|q₁q₂|/r². In vector form, forces obey Newton's third law (F₁₂ = -F₂₁). When immersed in a dielectric medium of relative permittivity κ, the force reduces to F₀/κ. For multiple charges, the net force is determined via the principle of linear superposition by vector addition of all individual pairwise interactions.
specialNotes: Coulomb's law is strictly valid only for stationary point charges in an inertial reference frame. Accelerating charges radiate electromagnetic energy.
Definition of 1 Coulomb: That charge which, when placed in vacuum at a distance of 1 meter from an identical charge, repels it with a force of 9 × 10⁹ N.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The electrostatic force between two stationary point charges varies inversely with the square of the distance between them.
Statement 2: Electrostatic forces are central forces acting strictly along the straight line joining the centers of two interacting charges.
Statement 3: Electrostatic forces satisfy Newton's third law: the force on charge 1 by charge 2 is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force on charge 2 by charge 1.
Statement 4: The electrostatic force between two charges is independent of the presence of any other surrounding charges.
Statement 5: In any dielectric medium with relative permittivity κ, the electrostatic force between two charges is attenuated by a factor of κ.
importantNotes: Remember that the permittivity of free space ε₀ has SI units of C²/(N·m²) or F/m, with value 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m.
examShortTricks: Equilibrium between like charges q₁ and q₂ at distance L: Third charge of opposite sign placed at x = L / (√(q₂/q₁) + 1) from q₁ achieves equilibrium.
Ratio of forces in dielectric medium: F_air / F_medium = κ.
Two identical charges in symmetrical polygons: Net electrostatic force at the geometric center of any regular polygon with equal vertices charges is identically ZERO.
examNotes: State Coulomb's law in vector form and derive the condition for third charge equilibrium along a line joining two point charges (frequent 3-4 mark NEB question).

mcs.explanation: In a dielectric medium, the force is reduced by the relative permittivity: F_medium = F_air / κ = F / 4.

data.title: Electric Field due to Point Charges
notes: **Electric Field Concept & Definition:** An electric field $\vec{E}$ is an intrinsic vector property of space surrounding any charged distribution. It is defined quantitatively as the electrostatic force experienced per unit positive infinitesimal test charge placed at that location: $\vec{E} = \lim_{q_0 \to 0} \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$. The limiting operation $q_0 \to 0$ ensures the test charge does not disturb the source charge configuration. The SI unit of electric field is Newton per Coulomb ($\text{N/C}$) or equivalently Volt per meter ($\text{V/m}$), with dimensional formula $[M L T^{-3} I^{-1}]$.

**Electric Field due to an Isolated Point Charge:** Applying Coulomb's law to a source charge $q$ at position vector $\vec{r}'$ and test charge $q_0$ at field point $\vec{r}$, the electric field is: $\vec{E}(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|^3} (\vec{r} - \vec{r}') = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}\hat{r}$. The electric field radiates spherically outward in all directions for a positive source charge ($q > 0$) and converges radially inward for a negative source charge ($q < 0$), exhibiting strict inverse-square attenuation with radial distance $r$.

**Superposition Principle for Discrete & Continuous Charges:** The net electric field created by an ensemble of $N$ discrete point charges is the vector sum of individual fields: $\vec{E}_{net} = \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{E}_i = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{q_i}{r_i^2}\hat{r}_i$. For continuous charge distributions, summation transitions to volume, surface, or linear integrals: $\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \int \frac{dq}{r^2}\hat{r}$, where $dq = \lambda dl$ (linear charge density), $dq = \sigma dA$ (surface charge density), or $dq = \rho dV$ (volume charge density).

**Properties of Electric Field Lines:** Introduced by Michael Faraday, electric field lines (lines of force) provide an intuitive geometric mapping of electrostatic vector fields: (1) Lines originate perpendicularly on positive charges and terminate on negative charges (or extend to infinity); (2) The tangent to a field line at any point indicates the direction of $\vec{E}$ at that point; (3) Two field lines can NEVER cross, because intersecting lines would imply two distinct field vectors at the same spatial coordinate; (4) The local areal density of lines is directly proportional to field magnitude $E$; (5) Electrostatic field lines never form closed loops, reflecting the conservative nature of electrostatic forces ($\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} = 0$).

**Electric Dipole & Dipole Moment:** An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite point charges $\pm q$ separated by a small distance $2a$. The electric dipole moment vector is defined as $\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$, directed by convention from the negative charge $-q$ to positive charge $+q$, with SI unit $\text{C}\cdot\text{m}$. In an external electric field $\vec{E}$, a dipole experiences a net aligning torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$ and possesses electrostatic potential energy $U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}$. In a non-uniform field, it experiences both torque and a net translational force $\vec{F} = (\vec{p} \cdot \vec{\nabla})\vec{E}$.

**Electric Field of a Dipole at Axial & Equatorial Points:** For a dipole of moment $p = 2qa$ at distances $r \gg a$: (1) **Axial point (End-on position):** $\vec{E}_{axial} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2\vec{p}}{r^3}$, parallel to $\vec{p}$; (2) **Equatorial point (Broadside-on position):** $\vec{E}_{equatorial} = -\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{\vec{p}}{r^3}$, antiparallel to $\vec{p}$. Notice that for any dipole, $E \propto 1/r^3$ (faster fall-off than a point charge's $1/r^2$), and $E_{axial} = 2 E_{equatorial}$ at the same radial distance $r$.
formulas: Electric field definition: $\vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$
Field of a point charge: $\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}\hat{r}$
Electric dipole moment: $\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$
Dipole field (axial, $r \gg a$): $\vec{E}_{axial} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2\vec{p}}{r^3}$
Dipole field (equatorial, $r \gg a$): $\vec{E}_{equatorial} = -\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{\vec{p}}{r^3}$
Dipole torque in uniform field: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$
Dipole potential energy: $U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}$
confusion: Confusing field line direction with trajectory of a moving charge: An electric field line represents the direction of electrostatic force on a stationary positive charge, NOT the trajectory of a moving charge. A moving charge accelerates along $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$, so velocity and field vectors generally diverge due to inertia.

Assuming field lines can intersect: If two field lines crossed, a test charge at the intersection would experience two distinct electrostatic forces in different directions simultaneously, which violates the uniqueness theorem of vector fields.

Confusing the radial fall-off of dipoles versus point charges: Point charge field scales as $1/r^2$, whereas an electric dipole field decays as $1/r^3$ because the positive and negative charges largely cancel each other out at long distances ($r \gg a$).
data.topicTitle: Electric field due to point charges and field lines
practice: Two point charges $q_1 = +5.0\,\mu\text{C}$ and $q_2 = -5.0\,\mu\text{C}$ are separated by $10\text{ cm}$ along the x-axis ($2a = 0.1\text{ m}$). (a) Find the electric dipole moment. (b) Find the electric field magnitude at an axial point $20\text{ cm}$ from the dipole center. Solution: (a) $p = q(2a) = (5.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C})(0.1\text{ m}) = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\cdot\text{m}$. (b) Using the axial field formula with $r = 0.2\text{ m}$ ($r \gg a$ approximation): $E_{axial} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2p}{r^3} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(2 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-7})}{(0.2)^3} = \frac{9000}{0.008} = 1.125 \times 10^6\,\text{N/C}$, directed along the dipole axis in the direction of $\vec{p}$.
universalFacts: The terrestrial fair-weather atmosphere maintains a downward-directed vertical electric field of approximately $100\,\text{to}\,150\,\text{V/m}$ near the Earth's surface due to the global electrical thunderstorm battery circuit.

Electric fields in nerve cells (action potentials) reach immense intensities of roughly $10^7\,\text{V/m}$ across thin ($7\text{ nm}$) phospholipid bilayer cell membranes, driving ion pumps that enable animal thought and heartbeat.
examples: Inkjet printers: Electrically deflected microscopic ink droplets pass between high-voltage deflection plates generating a uniform electric field, steering droplets precisely onto paper to render text and images.

Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO): An electron beam accelerated by an electron gun is deflected horizontally and vertically by orthogonal electric fields between parallel plates, projecting waveforms onto a fluorescent screen.
Laser toner transfer: Controlled electrostatic fields attract charged polymer toner particles from the photoconductor drum onto paper, which is subsequently thermally fused.
practiceQuestions: Q2. State four essential characteristics of electric field lines and explain why two field lines can never intersect each other.

keyPoints: Electric field intensity is force per unit positive test charge ($E = F/q_0$) in N/C or V/m.
Point charge field obeys inverse square law ($E \propto 1/r^2$); short dipole field obeys inverse cube law ($E \propto 1/r^3$).
Field lines point outward from positive charges and inward toward negative charges, never intersecting.
Axial field of a short dipole is exactly twice the magnitude of equatorial field at equal distance ($E_{axial} = 2 E_{equatorial}$).
In a uniform electric field, an electric dipole experiences zero net force but a restoring torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$.
data.summary: The electric field E is a vector field describing electrostatic force per unit test charge (E = F/q₀). Point charges produce radially symmetric fields falling off as 1/r², mapped visually by continuous non-intersecting field lines originating on positive and terminating on negative charges. Electric dipoles (p = 2qa) generate fields decaying as 1/r³, with axial field intensity twice that of the equatorial position at the same large distance, experiencing aligning torque τ = p × E in an external field.
specialNotes: Electrostatic field lines do not form closed loops because electrostatic fields are conservative: the closed loop line integral ∮ E · dr = 0.
A charged particle projected perpendicularly into a uniform electric field follows a parabolic trajectory, analogous to projectile motion in a uniform gravitational field.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The electric field at any point in space is the electrostatic force experienced per unit infinitesimal positive test charge.
Statement 2: Electric field lines originate on positive charges, terminate on negative charges, and cannot intersect at any point.
Statement 3: The electric field due to a point charge obeys an inverse-square distance relationship (E ∝ 1/r²).
Statement 4: The electric field due to a short electric dipole decays inversely with the cube of distance (E ∝ 1/r³).
Statement 5: In a uniform electric field, an electric dipole experiences zero translational net force but a net aligning torque τ = p × E.
importantNotes: Remember that the SI units N/C and V/m are completely interchangeable: 1 N/C = 1 (J/m) / C = 1 (J/C) / m = 1 V/m.
examShortTricks: Dipole field ratio trick: At identical large distance r, E_axial / E_equatorial = 2.
Neutral point between like charges: E_net = 0 lies between them at distance x = d / (√(q₂/q₁) + 1) from q₁.
Acceleration of charged particle in field: a = qE / m (direction along E for positive charge, opposite E for electron).
examNotes: Derivation of electric field due to an electric dipole at axial and equatorial points is a premier 4-mark question in NEB Class 11 Physics exams.

mcs.question: The electric field intensity at an axial point distance r from a short electric dipole is E. The electric field at an equatorial point at the same distance r is:
mcs.explanation: For a short dipole (r ≫ a), E_axial = 2kp/r³ and E_equatorial = kp/r³. Therefore, E_equatorial = E_axial / 2 = E / 2.

mcs.question: An electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field experiences:
options: both a net force and a torque
a net force only, but no torque
a torque only, but no net force
neither a net force nor a torque
mcs.explanation: In a uniform field, equal and opposite forces act on +q and -q (+qE and -qE), so net force is zero. However, their lines of action do not coincide, producing a net torque τ = p × E.

mcs.question: Electric field lines can never intersect each other because:
options: at the point of intersection, the electric field would have two distinct directions
they form closed loops in vacuum
mcs.explanation: The tangent to a field line gives the direction of E. If two lines intersect, there would be two tangents, meaning two distinct field directions at a single point, which is physically impossible.

Electric field of a point charge and principle of linear superposition.
Rules governing electric field lines and why they never form closed loops.
Electric dipole moment and derivation of axial and equatorial dipole fields.
Behavior of dipoles in uniform and non-uniform electric fields.

data.title: Gauss law: electric flux
notes: Electric flux through a surface is Φ = ∫ E·dS = E A cos θ for a uniform field over a flat area; its SI unit is N m² C⁻¹ (equivalently V m).
Gauss's law: the total electric flux through any closed surface equals the net charge enclosed divided by ε₀ — Φ = q_enclosed / ε₀.
Gauss's law is equivalent to Coulomb's inverse-square law in electrostatics but is more convenient for charge distributions with symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, planar).
The law holds for any closed surface regardless of shape; charges outside the surface contribute zero net flux because every field line entering also leaves.
Gauss's law also implies that the net flux through a closed surface is independent of the surface's size or the positions of the enclosed charges.

**Electric Flux Concept & Definition:** Electric flux $\Phi_E$ is a macroscopic scalar measure of the total number of electric field lines passing perpendicularly through a given geometric surface. For an infinitesimal surface area vector $d\vec{A} = dA\,\hat{n}$ (where $\hat{n}$ is the unit normal pointing outward for a closed surface), the elemental flux is $d\Phi_E = \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = E\,dA\,\cos\theta$. The total electric flux through an arbitrary finite surface $S$ is given by the surface integral: $\Phi_E = \iint_S \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A}$. The SI unit of electric flux is $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}$ or $\text{V}\cdot\text{m}$, with dimensions $[M L^3 T^{-3} I^{-1}]$.

**Gauss's Law in Electrostatics:** Formulated by Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1835, Gauss's law states that the net outward electric flux through any arbitrary closed imaginary surface (known as a Gaussian surface) is directly proportional to the total net electric charge enclosed by that surface: $\Phi_{net} = \oint_S \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{enclosed}}{\varepsilon_0}$. Gauss's law is one of Maxwell's four fundamental equations of classical electrodynamics, valid for any static or moving charge distribution and any choice of closed surface.

**Proof of Gauss's Law for a Point Charge:** Consider an isolated positive point charge $+q$ enclosed by a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$. Due to spherical symmetry, the electric field has constant radial magnitude $E = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$ and is everywhere parallel to the outward area vector $d\vec{A}$ ($\theta = 0^\circ$). The total flux is: $\oint_S \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \oint E\,dA = E \oint dA = \left(\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\right)(4\pi r^2) = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$. By superposition, this result holds for any arbitrary shape and any number of enclosed discrete charges.

**Physical Implications of Gauss's Law:** (1) Charges located strictly outside the Gaussian surface contribute zero net flux through the closed surface, as every entering field line must exit elsewhere; (2) The total flux depends only on the net interior charge $Q_{enc} = \sum q_i$ and the medium permittivity $\varepsilon_0$, independent of the size, shape, or position of charges inside; (3) While the total flux depends only on enclosed charge, the electric field $\vec{E}$ at any specific point on the surface is the resultant field produced by ALL charges (both inside and outside).

**Gauss's Law in Differential Form (Maxwell's 1st Equation):** Applying the Gauss Divergence Theorem to convert the surface integral to a volume integral yields: $\oint_S \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \iiint_V (\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{E})\,dV = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0} \iiint_V \rho\,dV$. Equating integrands for an arbitrary infinitesimal volume gives the differential form: $\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{E} = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}$, stating that electric field divergence at any spatial point is directly proportional to local volume charge density $\rho$.

**Selection Criteria for Gaussian Surfaces:** Gauss's law is always fundamentally true, but it is practically useful for calculating electric fields only when the charge configuration exhibits high geometric symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, or planar). A Gaussian surface must satisfy: (1) $\vec{E}$ is either perpendicular or parallel to the surface; (2) $|\vec{E}|$ is constant over the portions of the surface where flux is non-zero; (3) The surface passes through the point where the field is to be evaluated.

Believing that zero net flux implies zero electric field everywhere: If a Gaussian surface encloses zero net charge, $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0$, but the electric field $\vec{E}$ at points on the surface need not be zero (e.g., an uncharged sphere placed in a uniform external field has entering flux equal to exiting flux).

Confusing the field $\vec{E}$ in Gauss's law with the field produced only by enclosed charges: $\vec{E}$ in the integral $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A}$ is the total resultant electric field produced by ALL charges in the universe, whereas the right-hand side $Q_{enc}$ counts strictly enclosed charges.

A point charge $q = +8.854\,\text{nC}$ is placed at the center of an imaginary cube of side $10\text{ cm}$. (a) Calculate the total electric flux emerging through the entire surface of the cube. (b) Find the electric flux passing through each of the six individual faces of the cube. Solution: (a) By Gauss's Law, total flux through the closed cube is $\Phi_{total} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{8.854 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^2/(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2)} = 1000\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}$. (b) By symmetry, the charge is equidistant from all six faces, so flux distributes equally: $\Phi_{face} = \frac{\Phi_{total}}{6} = \frac{1000}{6} = 166.7\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}$.

Gauss's law is mathematically equivalent to the inverse-square power in Coulomb's law. If Coulomb's force varied as $1/r^{2+\delta}$, Gauss's law would break down because flux through concentric spheres would depend on their radius.

Gauss's law for magnetism is $\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0$, signifying that magnetic field lines never originate or terminate on isolated sources; magnetic monopoles have never been observed in nature.

Faraday Cage: A closed conducting mesh or metal box shields its interior completely from external electric fields because any enclosed charge is zero and mobile charges redistribute along exterior surfaces, making $\vec{E} = 0$ inside.

Airplane lightning safety: Commercial aircraft bodies made of aluminum act as hollow Gaussian surfaces. When struck by lightning, immense electrostatic current flows across the outer skin without penetrating the passenger cabin.

Microwave oven shielding: The wire mesh on a microwave door has holes much smaller than the 12 cm wavelength of 2.45 GHz radiation, acting as a conducting Gaussian barrier that keeps radiation safely inside.

mcs.explanation: An electric dipole consists of equal and opposite charges (+q and -q). The net enclosed charge is Q_enc = +q - q = 0. By Gauss's Law, total flux Φ = Q_enc / ε₀ = 0.

mcs.question: A point charge q is placed at the center of an imaginary sphere of radius R. If the radius of the sphere is doubled, the total electric flux passing through the sphere will:

data.title: Applications of Gauss Law
notes: **Overview of Gauss's Law Applications:** Gauss's law provides an elegant and straightforward analytical method for determining electric fields produced by symmetric charge distributions where direct Coulomb integration is cumbersome. The three standard canonical geometries required by the NEB curriculum are: (1) an infinitely long straight line of charge (cylindrical symmetry); (2) an infinite uniformly charged plane sheet (planar symmetry); and (3) a uniformly charged spherical shell or conducting sphere (spherical symmetry).

**Electric Field of an Infinitely Long Straight Wire (Line Charge):** Consider a straight thin wire of infinite length having uniform linear charge density $\lambda$ ($\text{C/m}$). By cylindrical symmetry, the electric field is purely radial, pointing perpendicular to the wire. Construct a coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius $r$ and length $L$. The electric flux through the two circular flat end caps is zero because $\vec{E} \perp d\vec{A}$ ($\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0$). Through the curved cylindrical surface of area $2\pi r L$, $\vec{E}$ is parallel to $d\vec{A}$ everywhere and constant in magnitude: $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = E (2\pi r L)$. Enclosed charge is $Q_{enc} = \lambda L$. Applying Gauss's law: $E(2\pi r L) = \frac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$. The field decays inversely with distance ($E \propto 1/r$).

**Electric Field due to an Infinite Uniform Plane Sheet of Charge:** Consider an infinite non-conducting thin plane sheet carrying uniform surface charge density $\sigma$ ($\text{C/m}^2$). By symmetry, $\vec{E}$ is everywhere perpendicular to the sheet, directed away from both faces if $\sigma > 0$. Construct a Gaussian pillbox (a cylinder of cross-sectional area $A$ piercing perpendicular to the sheet with ends parallel to it). Flux through the curved surface is zero as $\vec{E}$ is parallel to the surface. Flux through the two end caps is $\Phi = E A + E A = 2 E A$. Enclosed charge is $Q_{enc} = \sigma A$. By Gauss's law: $2 E A = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$. Crucially, the electric field is completely independent of distance $r$ from the sheet, forming a perfectly uniform field.

**Electric Field of a Charged Conducting Plate & Between Parallel Plates:** For a conducting plate of finite thickness, mobile free electrons ensure that the internal electric field is strictly zero ($E_{inside} = 0$). The charge redistributes onto both outer faces with surface density $\sigma$. Constructing a pillbox with one face inside the conductor and one outside yields $E A = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ (twice that of an isolated non-conducting sheet). For two oppositely charged parallel conducting plates ($\pm \sigma$), fields add constructively between plates: $E_{between} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$, while cancelling outside: $E_{outside} = 0$.

**Electric Field due to a Uniformly Charged Thin Spherical Shell:** Consider a thin spherical shell of radius $R$ carrying total charge $Q$ distributed uniformly with surface density $\sigma = \frac{Q}{4\pi R^2}$. Construct a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$: (1) **Outside the shell ($r > R$):** $\oint E\,dA = E(4\pi r^2) = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r^2} = \frac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 r^2}$. The shell acts as if all its charge were concentrated at the geometric center; (2) **On the surface ($r = R$):** $E_{surface} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{R^2} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ (maximum magnitude); (3) **Inside the shell ($r < R$):** The Gaussian surface encloses zero charge ($Q_{enc} = 0$), so $E(4\pi r^2) = 0 \implies E_{inside} = 0$.

**Electric Field of a Uniformly Charged Non-Conducting Solid Sphere:** For an insulating solid sphere of radius $R$ with uniform volume charge density $\rho = \frac{Q}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$: (1) **Outside ($r \ge R$):** $E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2}$; (2) **Inside ($r < R$):** A concentric Gaussian sphere of radius $r$ encloses charge $Q_{enc} = \rho \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right) = Q \left(\frac{r^3}{R^3}\right)$. Applying Gauss's law: $E(4\pi r^2) = \frac{Q r^3}{\varepsilon_0 R^3} \implies E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q r}{R^3} = \frac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0}$. Thus, the electric field increases linearly with radial distance $r$ from zero at the center up to maximum at the surface ($E \propto r$ for $r \le R$), then decays as $1/r^2$ for $r > R$.
formulas: Infinite line charge: $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$
Infinite non-conducting plane sheet: $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$
Conducting surface boundary: $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$
Between oppositely charged plates: $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$
Spherical shell (outside, $r \ge R$): $E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2}$
Spherical shell (inside, $r < R$): $E = 0$
Non-conducting sphere (inside, $r \le R$): $E = \frac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q r}{R^3}$
confusion: Confusing field of a non-conducting infinite sheet with a conducting plate: An isolated non-conducting sheet has $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ on both sides because charge is embedded in a single layer. A conducting plate has charge on two separate faces; just outside any conducting surface, the boundary condition gives $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.

Assuming field inside a charged sphere is always zero: Inside a hollow shell or conductor, $E = 0$. However, inside a uniformly charged *non-conducting solid sphere*, the field increases linearly with radius: $E = \frac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0} = \frac{k Q r}{R^3}$.

Neglecting Gaussian end-caps in line charge: Students often forget to justify why the two flat circular ends of a Gaussian cylinder contribute zero flux (because $\vec{E} \perp d\vec{A}$, making $\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0$).
practice: An infinite line of charge produces an electric field of $9.0 \times 10^4\,\text{N/C}$ at a perpendicular distance of $2.0\text{ cm}$ in air. Calculate the linear charge density $\lambda$. Solution: The electric field of a long wire is $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$. Rearranging for $\lambda$: $\lambda = \frac{E \cdot r}{2k} = \frac{(9.0 \times 10^4\,\text{N/C})(0.02\text{ m})}{2 \times (9.0 \times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2)} = \frac{1800}{1.8 \times 10^{10}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C/m} = 0.10\,\mu\text{C/m}$.
universalFacts: Electrostatic shielding (Faraday cage effect) is an exact consequence of Gauss's law: because $E = 0$ inside any empty conducting cavity, sensitive electronics or occupants in an automobile or airplane are immune to external high-voltage discharges and lightning.

The linear dependence of electric field $E \propto r$ inside a uniform non-conducting charge sphere is mathematically identical to the gravitational acceleration $g(r) \propto r$ inside a hypothetical uniform planetary Earth.
examples: Van de Graaff Generator: Charges carried to the hollow metallic upper terminal immediately transfer to the outer sphere surface because E = 0 inside, allowing accumulation of potentials up to millions of volts.

Electrostatic air precipitators: High-voltage central wire electrodes generate intense radial fields (E ∝ 1/r) that ionize air molecules, charging smoke particles which then migrate to grounded collection plates.

Coaxial cable design: In transmission lines, the electric field is strictly contained between the inner cylinder and outer grounded shielding conductor (E = λ / (2πε₀r)), preventing signal radiation and electromagnetic interference.

Q4. A spherical conductor of radius 10 cm has a charge of 3.2 × 10⁻⁷ C distributed uniformly on its surface. What is the electric field at (a) a point 15 cm from the center, and (b) inside the conductor at 5 cm from the center?
keyPoints: Line charge field decreases inversely with radial distance: $E \propto 1/r$.
Infinite sheet field is completely uniform and distance-independent: $E = \sigma / (2\varepsilon_0)$.
Inside any hollow conductor or spherical shell in electrostatic equilibrium, $E = 0$ (electrostatic shielding).
Outside a spherical charge distribution, the field behaves as if all charge is concentrated at the center ($E \propto 1/r^2$).
Inside a uniformly charged solid dielectric sphere, field increases linearly from center to surface ($E \propto r$).
data.summary: Gauss's law enables straightforward derivation of electric fields for symmetric charge systems: an infinite line charge yields E = λ / (2πε₀r) showing inverse distance decay; an infinite planar sheet produces a uniform, distance-independent field E = σ / (2ε₀); and a spherical shell creates an inverse-square field externally (E = Q / (4πε₀r²)) while maintaining strictly zero internal field (E = 0), establishing electrostatic shielding.
specialNotes: The electric field just outside any arbitrarily shaped conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is always perpendicular to the surface and has magnitude E = σ / ε₀.
A graph of E versus r for a thin spherical shell shows zero field for 0 ≤ r < R, a step discontinuity to E_max = kQ/R² at r = R, and smooth 1/r² decay for r > R.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The electric field due to an infinitely long straight wire carrying uniform linear charge density is inversely proportional to distance from the wire (E ∝ 1/r).
Statement 2: The electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge is uniform and completely independent of the distance from the sheet.
Statement 3: The electric field inside a uniformly charged conducting spherical shell is identically zero everywhere.
Statement 4: Outside a spherically symmetric charge distribution, the field is identical to that of a point charge located at the sphere's geometric center.
Statement 5: Inside a uniformly charged non-conducting sphere, the electric field increases linearly with radial distance from the center (E ∝ r).

data.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = Gm₁m₂/r².

**The universal constant G:** G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg². It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.
**Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is F₁₂ = −G(m₁m₂/r²) r̂₁₂, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: F₁₂ = −F₂₁.
**Superposition:** when several masses act on one particle, the net force is the vector sum of the individual forces: F_net = Σ Fᵢ. Each pair obeys the inverse-square law independently.
**Worked example — Earth and Moon:** m_Earth = 6×10²⁴ kg, m_Moon = 7.4×10²² kg, r = 3.84×10⁸ m. F = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 6×10²⁴ × 7.4×10²² / (3.84×10⁸)² = 2.0×10²⁰ N — enough to hold the Moon in orbit.
**Gravitational field strength:** g = F/m = GM/r², the force per unit mass at a distance r from mass M. On Earth's surface g = 9.8 m/s², which gives Earth's mass: M = gR²/G ≈ 5.97×10²⁴ kg.
**Why G is used in orbits:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force (GMm/r² = mv²/r) gives orbital velocity v = √(GM/r) and period T = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law follows directly.

**Important comparisons:** gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces — between two protons the gravitational force is ~10⁻³⁶ times the electric force — yet it dominates cosmology because mass adds up while electric charges cancel.
formulas: Newton's law of gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r²
Gravitational field strength: g = GM/r²
Orbital velocity: v = √(GM/r)
Orbital period: T = 2π√(r³/GM)
g at height h: g' = g(R/(R+h))²
confusion: ❌ 'There is a force of gravity only near Earth.' ✅ Gravity acts between ANY two masses anywhere in the universe — it never switches off, it only weakens with the square of distance.
❌ 'G can change with temperature or medium.' ✅ G is a universal constant — independent of temperature, pressure, medium, or the objects involved.
❌ 'The force depends on the square of the distance — it dies quickly.' ✅ It dies as 1/r² but never reaches zero; at double distance the force is a quarter, at ten times it is one-hundredth.

❌ 'Heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls them harder.' ✅ Gravity pulls harder on heavier objects (F = mg), but their acceleration is the same: a = F/m = g, hence all bodies in free fall accelerate equally (ignoring air resistance).

❌ 'Earth pulls the Moon but the Moon does not pull Earth.' ✅ The forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Earth and Moon pull on each other with equal forces — the Moon's acceleration is larger because its mass is smaller.
❌ 'Inside Earth gravity stops.' ✅ Inside a uniform sphere, g decreases linearly with distance from the centre, reaching zero at the centre — it is not zero except exactly at the centre.

data.title: Gravitational Potential and Potential Energy
notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$. At infinity $V = 0$, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply $GMm/r$ of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — its total mechanical energy is $E = K + U = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, $U = mgh$. This is the constant-g approximation of $-\frac{GMm}{r}$: since $\Delta(1/r) \approx -h/R^2$, the change matches $mgh$. Use $mgh$ only for $h \ll R$; use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply $GMm/R$. Numerically for m = 1 kg: $\frac{6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 5.97\times 10^{24}}{6.37\times 10^6} \approx 6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J} \approx 62.5 \text{ MJ}$ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.

**Superposition:** for multiple masses, $V = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i}{r_i}\right)$ and $U = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i m}{r_i}\right)$ — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.
formulas: Gravitational potential: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ (J/kg)
Gravitational potential energy: $U = mV = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ (J)
Near the surface: $U = mgh$ ($h \ll R$)
Field from potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$
Total orbital energy: $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = U/2$
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$ (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ '$U = mgh$ and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: $mgh$ is the CHANGE in $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface ($-\frac{GM}{R}$) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes $-\frac{GMm}{2r}$ (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but $U \approx 0$). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

universalFacts: Gravitational potential energy is exactly the 'missing' energy that binds systems — this is why the binding energy of Earth + satellite equals $|U|$.
The concept of potential is useful because it is scalar: complex many-body problems reduce to addition rather than vector resolution.

The Voyager probes were launched using the escape-energy budget — their final trajectory traced the potential wells of the Sun and giant planets.

data.title: Variation in g due to Altitude and Depth
notes: **g above the surface (altitude):** at height h above Earth's surface, $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$. As h increases, g decreases. For small h ($h \ll R$), a binomial expansion gives $g' \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$ — a useful approximation.

**g below the surface (depth):** at depth d, only the mass inside the concentric sphere of radius ($R-d$) contributes: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$ — gravity DECREASES linearly with depth. At the centre ($d = R$), $g' = 0$.

**Why they differ:** above the surface, whole-earth mass acts from a larger distance ($1/r^2$ law); below the surface, the shell above the point exerts zero net force (shell theorem) and only the inner sphere matters, whose mass scales as ($R-d$)^3 while distance scales as ($R-d$) — giving linear decrease.

**Worked example — altitude:** at $h = R$ (one Earth radius up), $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{2R}\right)^2 = g/4 = 2.45 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $h = 100$ km, using the small-h formula, the fractional decrease is $2h/R = 2\times 100/6400 = 0.031$, so $g' \approx 9.5 \text{ m/s}^2$.
**Worked example — depth:** at $d = R/2$ (3200 km deep), $g' = g(1 - 1/2) = g/2 = 4.9 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $d = R$ (centre) → $g' = 0$ (weightlessness, though pressure is immense).
**Graphs (NEB favourite):** $g$ vs $r$ rises linearly from 0 at the centre to g at the surface, then falls as $1/r^2$ beyond the surface. The maximum value of g on Earth is at the surface.

**Other causes of variation:** (1) rotation of Earth: g reduced by $\omega^2 R \cos^2 \lambda$ ($\lambda$ = latitude), maximum at the equator; (2) shape: Earth is an oblate spheroid — g is larger at the poles ($\approx 9.832$) than the equator ($\approx 9.78$); (3) local density anomalies (mountains, mineral deposits) cause tiny local changes used in geophysics.

**Altitude formula for satellites:** for an orbit at height h, effective $r = R + h$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R+h}}$ and the orbital g is $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$ — the same g formula used at that radius.
formulas: g at altitude h: $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$
Small-h approximation: $g' \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$
g at depth d: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$
g at latitude λ due to rotation: $g' = g - \omega^2 R \cos^2 \lambda$
g inside a uniform sphere: $g' = \frac{gr}{R}$ ($r \le R$)
confusion: ❌ 'g increases with altitude.' ✅ Above the surface g DEcreases as $\frac{1}{(R+h)^2}$; below the surface it also decreases (linearly). g is max at the surface.
❌ 'From height h, g falls by $h/R$.' ✅ The small-h approximation is $2h/R$ (from the square), not $h/R$. At $h = 100$ km, that is ≈ 3%.
❌ 'Deep inside Earth, g keeps growing.' ✅ It decreases linearly: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$, zero at the centre. The shell above you pulls equally in all directions (zero net).
❌ 'g is the same at poles and equator.' ✅ Rotation and the oblate shape make g slightly larger at the poles (~0.5% difference).
❌ 'At altitude 6400 km, g is half of surface.' ✅ At $h = R$, $g' = g/4$ — the height doubles the distance, so the square halves twice.
❌ 'Weightlessness in orbit means no gravity.' ✅ Astronauts at 400 km still feel ~88% of surface gravity — they float because they are in free fall around Earth.

**Worked example — altitude:** at $h = R$ (one Earth radius up), $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{2R}\right)^2 = g/4 = 2.45 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $h = 100$ km, using the small-h formula, the fractional decrease is $2h/R = 2\times 100/6400 = 0.031$, so $g' \approx 9.5 \text{ m/s}^2$.
**Worked example — depth:** at $d = R/2$ (3200 km deep), $g' = g(1 - 1/2) = g/2 = 4.9 \text{ m/s}^2$. At $d = R$ (centre) → $g' = 0$ (weightlessness, though pressure is immense).
**Graphs (NEB favourite):** $g$ vs $r$ rises linearly from 0 at the centre to g at the surface, then falls as $1/r^2$ beyond the surface. The maximum value of g on Earth is at the surface.

**Other causes of variation:** (1) rotation of Earth: g reduced by $\omega^2 R \cos^2 \lambda$ ($\lambda$ = latitude), maximum at the equator; (2) shape: Earth is an oblate spheroid — g is larger at the poles ($\approx 9.832$) than the equator ($\approx 9.78$); (3) local density anomalies (mountains, mineral deposits) cause tiny local changes used in geophysics.

**Altitude formula for satellites:** for an orbit at height h, effective $r = R + h$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R+h}}$ and the orbital g is $g' = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$ — the same g formula used at that radius.
confusion: ❌ 'g increases with altitude.' ✅ Above the surface g DEcreases as $\frac{1}{(R+h)^2}$; below the surface it also decreases (linearly). g is max at the surface.
❌ 'From height h, g falls by $h/R$.' ✅ The small-h approximation is $2h/R$ (from the square), not $h/R$. At $h = 100$ km, that is ≈ 3%.
❌ 'Deep inside Earth, g keeps growing.' ✅ It decreases linearly: $g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$, zero at the centre. The shell above you pulls equally in all directions (zero net).
❌ 'g is the same at poles and equator.' ✅ Rotation and the oblate shape make g slightly larger at the poles (~0.5% difference).
❌ 'At altitude 6400 km, g is half of surface.' ✅ At $h = R$, $g' = g/4$ — the height doubles the distance, so the square halves twice.
❌ 'Weightlessness in orbit means no gravity.' ✅ Astronauts at 400 km still feel ~88% of surface gravity — they float because they are in free fall around Earth.

data.title: Centre of Mass and Centre of Gravity
notes: **Centre of mass (COM):** the point where the entire mass of a body (or system) may be considered to be concentrated for translational (linear) motion analysis. Position: $R_{cm} = \frac{\Sigma m_i r_i}{\Sigma m_i}$. For continuous bodies: $R_{cm} = \frac{\int r dm}{M}$.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. In a uniform gravitational field, the CG coincides exactly with the COM. If the field is non-uniform (very large bodies, varying g), the CG may shift slightly relative to the COM.

**Why CG equals COM in uniform g:** weight $W = mg$ at each point, and since $g$ is the same everywhere, the torque balance condition that defines the CG reduces to the same weighted average that defines the COM. The two centres coincide.
**Solved example — two masses:** masses 2 kg at x = 0 and 8 kg at x = 3 m. COM: $x_{cm} = \frac{2 \times 0 + 8 \times 3}{2+8} = \frac{24}{10} = 2.4 \text{ m}$. The COM is closer to the heavier mass.

**Solved example — system of three:** 1 kg at (0,0), 2 kg at (2,0), 3 kg at (0,4). $x_{cm} = \frac{1 \times 0 + 2 \times 2 + 3 \times 0}{6} = \frac{4}{6} = 0.67 \text{ m}$; $y_{cm} = \frac{1 \times 0 + 2 \times 0 + 3 \times 4}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = 2 \text{ m}$. COM at (0.67, 2) m.

**Properties:** (1) The COM of a uniform, symmetric body lies at its geometric centre. (2) The COM of two bodies lies on the line joining them. (3) For irregular bodies the COM can lie OUTSIDE the material (e.g., a ring, a boomerang, a bent L-shape). (4) The total linear momentum of a system equals $M \cdot V_{cm}$ — external forces alone can change $V_{cm}$.

**Finding CG experimentally (NEB practical):** suspend the body from two different points; the two vertical lines through the suspension points intersect at the centre of gravity. Plumb lines are used — the intersection of the two suspension lines locates the CG.

**Applications:** designing stable structures (ships, cars, tables) keeps the CG low and inside the base; balancing acts use alignment of the CG above the support; in projectiles, the COM follows a smooth parabola even if the object rotates; spacecraft alignment uses the COM.

**Why CG equals COM in uniform g:** weight W = mg at each point, and since g is the same everywhere, the torque balance condition that defines the CG reduces to the same weighted average that defines the COM. The two centres coincide.
**Solved example — two masses:** masses 2 kg at x = 0 and 8 kg at x = 3 m. COM: x_cm = (2×0 + 8×3)/(2+8) = 24/10 = 2.4 m. The COM is closer to the heavier mass.

**Properties:** (1) The COM of a uniform, symmetric body lies at its geometric centre. (2) The COM of two bodies lies on the line joining them. (3) For irregular bodies the COM can lie OUTSIDE the material (e.g., a ring, a boomerang, a bent L-shape). Satellites and spacecraft align around their COM for stable attitude control — even small COM shifts change flight behaviour.

enrichedContent.summary: The centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position of a body or system: $R_{cm} = \frac{\Sigma m_i r_i}{M}$; the centre of gravity is the point where total weight acts. They coincide in a uniform gravitational field. The COM may lie outside the material and its motion is controlled only by external forces — the key to rigid-body and stability analysis.
specialNotes: In a uniform gravitational field the location of CG equals COM — that is almost always true in school problems.
For symmetric uniform bodies, COM = geometric centre (no calculation needed).
The COM of a system of two masses divides the connecting line inversely to the masses.

notes: **Centre of mass (COM):** the point where the entire mass of a body (or system) may be considered to be concentrated for translational (linear) motion analysis. Position: $R_{cm} = \frac{\Sigma m_i r_i}{\Sigma m_i}$. For continuous bodies: $R_{cm} = \frac{\int r dm}{M}$.

**Centre of gravity (CG):** the point where the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. In a uniform gravitational field, the CG coincides exactly with the COM. If the field is non-uniform (very large bodies, varying g), the CG may shift slightly relative to the COM.

**Why CG equals COM in uniform g:** weight $W = mg$ at each point, and since $g$ is the same everywhere, the torque balance condition that defines the CG reduces to the same weighted average that defines the COM. The two centres coincide.
**Solved example — two masses:** masses 2 kg at x = 0 and 8 kg at x = 3 m. COM: $x_{cm} = \frac{2 \times 0 + 8 \times 3}{2+8} = \frac{24}{10} = 2.4 \text{ m}$. The COM is closer to the heavier mass.

**Solved example — system of three:** 1 kg at (0,0), 2 kg at (2,0), 3 kg at (0,4). $x_{cm} = \frac{1 \times 0 + 2 \times 2 + 3 \times 0}{6} = \frac{4}{6} = 0.67 \text{ m}$; $y_{cm} = \frac{1 \times 0 + 2 \times 0 + 3 \times 4}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = 2 \text{ m}$. COM at (0.67, 2) m.

**Properties:** (1) The COM of a uniform, symmetric body lies at its geometric centre. (2) The COM of two bodies lies on the line joining them. (3) For irregular bodies the COM can lie OUTSIDE the material (e.g., a ring, a boomerang, a bent L-shape). (4) The total linear momentum of a system equals $M \cdot V_{cm}$ — external forces alone can change $V_{cm}$.

**Finding CG experimentally (NEB practical):** suspend the body from two different points; the two vertical lines through the suspension points intersect at the centre of gravity. Plumb lines are used — the intersection of the two suspension lines locates the CG.

**Applications:** designing stable structures (ships, cars, tables) keeps the CG low and inside the base; balancing acts use alignment of the CG above the support; in projectiles, the COM follows a smooth parabola even if the object rotates; spacecraft alignment uses the COM.
confusion: ❌ 'COM and CG are always at the material centre.' ✅ Only for uniform, symmetric bodies. A ring's COM is at its empty centre; an L-shaped body has its COM outside its material.

❌ 'COM is a force point.' ✅ COM is a mass-weighted average position — a geometric point for translational dynamics, not a force.
❌ 'To find the COM, only the largest mass matters.' ✅ All masses contribute proportionally: $R_{cm} = \frac{\Sigma m_i r_i}{\Sigma m_i}$.
❌ 'The COM moves when the body spins.' ✅ The COM of an isolated system moves uniformly (or stays still); spinning happens about the COM.
❌ 'The CG of an object must lie within the object.' ✅ It can lie outside the material — ring, hollow sphere, L-shape, boomerang.

data.title: Motion of a satellite: orbital velocity and time period o…
notes: **Fact.** Newton: F = G m₁m₂/r²; g = GM/r²; at Earth's surface g = GM/R² ≈ 9.8 m/s².
**Fact.** Orbital velocity v = √(GM/r); time period T = 2π√(r³/GM); escape velocity v_esc = √(2GM/r) = √2·v_orbital (at same r).
**Fact.** For a uniform sphere, g ∝ r inside and g = 0 at the centre; g decreases as 1/r² outside.

**Orbital velocity (v₀):** a satellite stays in a circular orbit when the gravitational pull GMm/r² provides the required centripetal force mv²/r. Equating: GMm/r² = mv₀²/r → v₀ = √(GM/r). Near Earth's surface, v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s.

**Why v₀ matters:** too slow → the satellite spirals in; too fast → it escapes to a higher ellipse. The orbital speed depends only on the radius (GM/r), not on the satellite's mass — heavy and light satellites share the same orbit speed.

**Time period (T):** T = circumference/velocity = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM) — Kepler's third law. Squaring: T² ∝ r³. A higher orbit has a longer period: the Moon (r ≈ 3.84×10⁸ m) takes ~27.3 days; the ISS (r ≈ 6.8×10⁶ m) takes ~92 minutes.

**Energy of an orbiting satellite:** K = ½mv₀² = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, so E_total = −GMm/2r. Notice K = −U/2 and E = U/2 — a signature of circular orbits. To raise a satellite to a higher orbit you must ADD energy, but the KE actually decreases (higher orbit = slower speed).
**Worked example — geostationary orbit:** for T = 24 h, r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m ≈ 35,800 km above the equator with v₀ ≈ 3.08 km/s.

**Low Earth vs geostationary comparison:** LEO (200–2000 km): v ≈ 7.8 km/s, T ≈ 90 min, covers Earth rapidly (imaging, ISS). Geostationary (35,800 km): v ≈ 3.07 km/s, T = 24 h, appears fixed over one spot (communications, weather).

**Orbit changes:** to transfer between circular orbits, a Hohmann ellipse uses two engine burns; near perigee/apogee speeds change by Δv = v₂ − v₁. Firing thrust ahead slows the satellite and lowers the orbit; firing backward raises it.
